Assigning two people to the same position causes a lack of clarity about who is responsible for what and about whose orders and priorities are to be followed

让两个人担任同一职位会导致职责划分不清，不清楚谁负责什么，以及应该遵循谁的命令和优先事项。

Overcompensating an employee who received another job offer

对收到另一份工作邀请的员工给予过高的补偿

Lack of fairness

缺乏公平性

Undercompensating an employee until he is offered another job and then overcompensating him is doubly unfair: to the employee himself before he is offered the job and to the rest of his team afterwards.

在员工找到另一份工作之前给予其过低的薪酬，然后再给予其过高的薪酬，这是双重不公平的：对员工本人在找到新工作之前不公平，对之后他的团队其他成员也不公平。

No performance management / employee feedback process

没有绩效管理/员工反馈流程

Lack of consistency

缺乏一致性

Once clear objectives have been issued, performance management is mostly about consistency in applying consequences.

一旦明确了目标，绩效管理主要就是在执行相应措施时保持一致性。

Good managers try to avoid incurring management debt as much as possible. They do so by always choosing to do the work of setting unambiguous, individual and rewardable objectives and by always requesting their subordinates to be accountable for them. Doing so helps a team and an organization to avoid far more costly and difficult situations later.

优秀的管理者会尽可能避免背负管理债务。他们通过设定明确、具体且可奖励的目标，并始终要求下属对这些目标负责来实现这一点。这样做有助于团队和组织避免日后出现代价更高、更棘手的情况。

It is easier to spend a career taking hard choices than spending it taking easy ones.

职业生涯中，做艰难的选择比做容易的选择要容易得多。

# ↩


Summary

概括

Bad managers fail to set clear objectives because of mental patterns that make them believe that setting unclear objectives is the optimal choice. However, if they set unclear objectives, they remove the motivation for employees to complete them and make it less comfortable for themselves to follow-up with individual outcomes correlated to individual performance.

糟糕的管理者往往因为固有的思维模式而无法设定清晰的目标，他们认为设定模糊的目标才是最佳选择。然而，如果目标不明确，就会削弱员工完成目标的动力，也会让管理者更难跟进与员工个人绩效相关的具体结果。

Therefore, good managers spend a considerable amount of their time and energy to set objectives which are: unambiguous, individual and rewardable.

因此，优秀的管理者会花费大量时间和精力来设定明确的、个性化的、可获得奖励的目标。

Failing to do so equals to fail their subordinates, who rely on their manager for clarity and direction towards objectives worth fulfilling – objectives which, when completed, are necessarily followed by good outcomes both for organization and for the individuals who contributed to them.

如果做不到这一点，就等于辜负了下属，下属依靠经理提供清晰的指示和方向，朝着值得实现的目标前进——这些目标一旦实现，必然会给组织和为之做出贡献的个人带来良好的结果。

# ↩

The 2nd Principle
of Operational Excellence:

Good managers always explicitly assign full accountability together with objectives

卓越运营的第二原则：优秀的管理者总是明确地将全部责任与目标结合起来。

In his book “High Output Management”, former Intel CEO Andy Grove shares the following allegory for delegation. Imagine having to delegate to a subordinate of yours the task of writing his name on a piece of paper. You tell him what is requested from him and hand him a pencil. However, you do not release your grip on the pencil. Your subordinate struggles to write the first letter: your holding onto the pen prevents him from moving his hand. You recognize the difficulty, and you offer to help. As he moves his hand to write the second letter, you try to help by guiding the pen. The result is a mess.

在《高产出管理》一书中，英特尔前首席执行官安迪·格鲁夫分享了一个关于授权的寓言。想象一下，你得把在纸上写名字的任务委托给你的下属。你告诉他需要做什么，然后递给他一支铅笔。但是，你没有松开握着铅笔的手。你的下属费力地写第一个字母：你握着笔的手限制了他的手移动。你意识到他的困难，并主动提出帮忙。当他移动手写第二个字母时，你试图引导笔尖。结果却是一团糟。

Your subordinates cannot do what is required from them unless, after you provide them with the tools, you release your grip on them.

除非你给下属提供必要的工具，然后放开对他们的控制，否则他们无法完成你要求他们做的事情。

With this allegory, let me introduce the topic of delegation.

借此寓言，让我引出授权这个话题。

# ↩


Delegation

代表团

When delegating a task, a manager can either prescribe the result or the method. For example, he can ask an employee to fix a broken machine (the result) or he can ask him to change that broken component on the machine (the method).

在委派任务时，管理者可以指定结果或方法。例如，他可以要求员工修理一台坏掉的机器（结果），也可以要求他更换机器上损坏的部件（方法）。

The difference is that in the latter case, if the broken component is changed but the machine still doesn’t work or malfunctions again shortly after, technically, the employee completed his task. This is problematic, because it will result either in the employee ending up frustrated for having been told his job was not good enough even though he did what was requested from him, or in the employee being “trained” to ignore the results which matter (in this case, whether the machine works properly).

区别在于，在后一种情况下，如果更换了损坏的部件，但机器仍然无法工作或不久后再次出现故障，从技术上讲，员工已经完成了他的任务。这会带来问题，因为要么员工会因为被告知工作做得不够好而感到沮丧（即使他已经完成了要求），要么员工会被“训练”去忽略真正重要的结果（在本例中，即机器是否正常工作）。

If an employees’ task is to apply a method, he will have to apply it, even if he knows that the method is not appropriate to the situation at hand and even if he believes that the method will not be helpful in the long term.

如果员工的任务是应用某种方法，即使他知道该方法不适用于当前情况，即使他认为该方法从长远来看没有帮助，他也必须应用该方法。

Instead, if an employee’s task is to achieve a result, he will choose the most appropriate method and, in case that would not reach a satisfactory result, he will try another one until the task is completed. Especially if he had evidence from the past that he will be held accountable, both in positive and in negative terms, for the ultimate result of his task.

相反，如果员工的任务是达成某个结果，他会选择最合适的方法；如果这种方法未能达到令人满意的结果，他会尝试另一种方法，直到任务完成为止。尤其是在他过去的经验表明，他将对任务的最终结果承担责任（无论好坏）的情况下，他更是如此。

Prescribing methods removes accountability, whereas prescribing results enable it.

按方法开处方会消除问责制，而按结果开处方则可以实现问责制。

Assigning problems to solve (rather than tasks to complete) is a great way to ask for results without prescribing methods.

布置需要解决的问题（而不是需要完成的任务）是一种在不规定方法的情况下要求取得成果的好方法。

How to provide instructions

如何提供说明

An employee’s job is to complete whatever objective is set by his manager. If an employee is prescribed a result, then his job becomes to achieve the result. Instead, if the employee is prescribed a method, such as a list of instructions, then his task becomes to follow a list of instructions. This is okay if and only if there is absolute certainty that following the instructions is sufficient for reaching the desired result. In the real world, this is seldom the case. This does not mean that the result cannot contain instructions or boundaries that cannot be overstepped, such as a budget to be respected or an action which has to be carried in a certain way. However, a manager should only prescribe the instructions and boundaries as part of the result, never as the result itself. This is the difference between prescribing “fix the oil filter and make the machine work again” (good) and “fix the oil filter” (bad). At the end of this chapter, you will find some example scripts that will show you how to correctly delegate tasks.

员工的工作是完成经理设定的目标。如果经理为员工设定了结果，那么他的工作就是达成结果。相反，如果经理为员工设定了方法，例如一系列指令，那么他的任务就是遵循这些指令。只有当绝对确定遵循这些指令足以达到预期结果时，这种方法才是可行的。但在现实世界中，这种情况很少发生。这并不意味着结果中不能包含不可逾越的指令或界限，例如必须遵守的预算或必须以特定方式执行的操作。然而，经理应该只将指令和界限作为结果的一部分来设定，而绝不能将其作为结果本身。这就好比设定“修理机油滤清器，让机器重新运转”（好的）和“修理机油滤清器”（坏的）之间的区别。在本章末尾，您将找到一些示例脚本，这些脚本将向您展示如何正确地委派任务。

Bad managers are unclear about the result they want. They spend too little time talking about the result and too much time talking about the methods, to the point that they induce their subordinates to think that the objective of the task being delegated is the method.

糟糕的管理者不清楚自己想要的结果。他们花在谈论方法上的时间太多，却很少谈论结果，以至于让下属误以为任务的目标就是方法本身。

The subordinates of such managers are both puzzled and frustrated when their boss (or their boss’ boss) doesn’t seem happy for their results even after they fully followed the instructions they’ve been given.

这样的经理的下属，即使完全按照上级指示行事，如果上级（或上级）的上级对他们的工作成果不满意，他们就会感到困惑和沮丧。

Instead, good managers spend most of their time talking about results. If they do also talk about methods, they make clear that they are not the results.

相反，优秀的管理者会把大部分时间花在谈论结果上。即使他们也谈到方法，也会明确指出方法并非结果本身。

Sometimes, to mark the difference, good managers outsource the explanation of the methods to someone else, such as an experienced employee. However, they always make sure to never outsource the definition of the results. For example, a CEO would rarely be the one delivering safety trainings to his employees; however, a good CEO would talk for a few minutes to his employees before the start of such a training to communicate his expectations about what they should get out of it (or, in large companies, he would personally send a company-wide email mentioning that trainings will take place over the next weeks and that employees are expected to learn this and that).

为了体现差异，优秀的管理者有时会将方法的解释工作外包给其他人，例如经验丰富的员工。但是，他们始终确保不会将结果的定义外包出去。例如，首席执行官很少会亲自为员工进行安全培训；但是，优秀的首席执行官会在培训开始前花几分钟时间与员工沟通，说明他对员工的期望（或者，在大公司里，他会亲自发送一封全公司邮件，告知员工未来几周将进行培训，并说明员工需要学习哪些内容）。

For example, a great CEO would send a sales-team-wide email reading “over the next couple of months, all members of all sales team will be invited to follow a training on how to price maintenance service in commercial proposals. I expect every single member of the sales team to attend one of such trainings by the 1 st of March, and I expect that the number of contracts where maintenance service brings a negative contribution is reduced to 5%. Starting from next year, unprofitable maintenance service on their contracts will affect the personal bonuses of all salespeople and of their managers.”

例如，一位优秀的CEO会向整个销售团队发送一封电子邮件，内容如下：“在接下来的几个月里，所有销售团队成员都将受邀参加关于如何在商业提案中对维护服务进行定价的培训。我希望每位销售团队成员都能在3月1日前参加其中一项培训，并且我希望维护服务产生负收益的合同数量能够减少到5%。从明年开始，合同中不盈利的维护服务将影响所有销售人员及其经理的个人奖金。”

Some comments on the text above:

对以上文字的一些评论：

  • It sets clear expectations about who is supposed to do what and by when.
    它明确规定了谁应该做什么以及何时完成。
  • It paints a clear image of what is considered a success (5% contracts where maintenance service brings a negative contribution).
    它清晰地描绘了何为成功（5% 的合同，其中维护服务带来负面影响）。
  • It sets clear individual consequences.
    它明确规定了个人应承担的后果。
  • It creates a chain of accountability (not only the employees who should attend the training will be held accountable, but their managers as well – the topic of the chain of accountability will be explored more in detail in the following pages).
    它建立了一条问责链（不仅参加培训的员工要承担责任，他们的经理也要承担责任——问责链这一主题将在后续页面中进行更详细的探讨）。

Delegate problems, not tasks

委派问题，而不是任务。

If you delegate a task to a subordinate, the underlaying problem will get solved, but only if the subordinate is competent and proactive enough. An incompetent or reactive subordinate will limit himself to complete the task regardless of whether the underlaying problem is solved.

如果你把任务委派给下属，问题的根源最终会得到解决，但这前提是下属必须足够胜任且积极主动。如果下属能力不足或反应迟钝，他只会完成任务本身，而忽略了根本问题是否得到解决。

Instead, if you delegate a problem to solve, it will get solved, regardless of whether the subordinate is competent and proactive. An incompetent subordinate will have to acquire the necessary skills or enlist the help of someone who has them; a reactive subordinate will have no choice but to solve the problem, because there is no doubt that that’s what’s being required from him.

相反，如果你把问题委派给下属解决，无论下属是否胜任或积极主动，问题最终都会得到解决。能力不足的下属必须学习必要的技能或寻求具备相关技能的人的帮助；而被动的下属则别无选择，只能解决问题，因为毫无疑问，这就是上级对他的要求。

I f you delegate tasks other than problems, you’re basically crossing fingers on whether completing the task will achieve meaningful results.

如果你委派的任务不是解决问题，那么你基本上就是在祈祷完成任务后能否取得有意义的结果。

A full assignment of accountability

全面落实问责制

Good managers perform the assignment of full accountability immediately after assigning the objective. They do so in an explicit way, by describing how, when and by whom results will be evaluated. They explicitly mention that the subordinate is accountable for the results.

优秀的管理者在设定目标后会立即明确责任归属。他们会以清晰明确的方式，说明如何、何时以及由谁来评估结果。他们会明确指出，下属要对结果负责。

Good managers always assign full accountability to the subordinate for the objectives he is given. This does not mean that the manager isn’t accountable as well for the results – he is, to his own boss – but that the manager being accountable together with the subordinate does not result in the latter being left off the hook.

优秀的管理者总是会把完成任务的全部责任都交给下属。这并不意味着管理者自己就无需对结果负责——他当然要对自己的上级负责——而是说，管理者与下属共同承担责任并不意味着下属可以逃脱责任。

Contrary to popular belief, multiple people can be accountable for the same result, as long as they are on the same vertical hierarchical line (one is the manager of another) so that there is exactly one single person accountable at any given level of the hierarchy. This is a rather counterintuitive concept, so let’s see three examples.

与普遍认知相反，多人可以对同一结果负责，只要他们处于同一垂直层级（一人是另一人的经理），这样在层级的任何特定级别上都只有一个人负责。这是一个相当违反直觉的概念，所以让我们来看三个例子。

In companies with poor Operational Culture, accountability is not defined.

在运营文化较差的公司中，问责制没有明确界定。

In good-but-not-great companies, there is a single person accountable for any given area. This is good in the measure it avoids situations in which “everyone is accountable so no one is”. On the other side, if the company is large, a tradeoff must be made. Either the person accountable is at a low level, with little ability to move the necessary resources to achieve the objective, or he is at a high level, and in this case the problem is in ensuring that the low-level employees which will be tasked with carrying over the task will be motivated towards an effective action – something which could only be achieved by making them accountable.

在一些优秀但并非卓越的公司中，每个领域都由一人负责。这样做的好处在于避免了“人人负责，结果却无人负责”的局面。但另一方面，如果公司规模庞大，就必须做出权衡。要么负责人级别较低，缺乏调动必要资源达成目标的能力；要么负责人级别较高，在这种情况下，问题在于如何确保负责后续工作的基层员工能够积极主动地开展工作——而这只有通过赋予他们责任才能实现。

In great companies, objectives are tricked down from the CEO and accountability for a given objective is owned by everyone on the hierarchical line from the CEO to each employee whose actions might influence that objective. For example, the CEO is accountable for safety; he delegates this objective to the COO (between others), who delegates it to each plant manager, who delegate it to their Operations Manager, who delegates it to each Line Supervisor, who delegate it to each line worker. Individual objectives are scaled down accordingly, for example:

在优秀的公司里，目标由首席执行官逐级下达，每个员工都对特定目标负有责任，从首席执行官到每一位可能影响该目标的员工。例如，首席执行官负责安全；他将这一目标委派给首席运营官（以及其他人员），首席运营官再委派给各工厂经理，工厂经理委派给运营经理，运营经理委派给各生产线主管，生产线主管再委派给每一位一线工人。个人目标也相应地逐级下达，例如：

  • CEO & COO: less than 10 serious injuries company wide.
    CEO和COO：公司范围内严重受伤人数不到10人。
  • Plant Managers & Operation Managers: less than 3 serious injuries in their plant.
    工厂经理和运营经理：其工厂内发生的严重工伤事故少于 3 起。
  • Line Supervisors: no serious injuries in their line.
    生产线主管：其负责的生产线上没有发生严重工伤事故。
  • Workers: no serious injury.
    工人：无严重受伤。

(Do not focus on the specific numbers, as they are heavily dependent on the industry being considered, the team size, etc. Instead, focus on the concept of trickling down objectives across the whole hierarchical line.)

（不要过于关注具体数字，因为它们很大程度上取决于所考虑的行业、团队规模等因素。相反，应该关注如何将目标层层下达给整个层级。）

In this case, if a line worker breaks his leg while at the plant, each of these people on the hierarchical line of the worker who injured himself, including himself, should be hold accountable for the injury. This would mean: the line worker himself, the Line Supervisor, the Operations Manager, the Plant Manager, the COO and the CEO.

在这种情况下，如果一名流水线工人在工厂工作时摔断了腿，那么从该工人开始，沿着这条层级向上的所有人员，包括他本人，都应该对这起事故承担责任。这意味着：流水线工人本人、生产线主管、运营经理、工厂经理、首席运营官和首席执行官。

When I present this concept to my clients, some react with skepticism. Why should the line worker be accountable for his own injury? Or why should the CEO? My answer is always the same: both should be accountable, together with everyone in between, not to allow any blind spot. The line worker should be accountable, because he has both the ultimate responsibility upon his actions and because he has the ultimate knowledge of the place he operates in. The CEO should be hold accountable, because otherwise he could set competing priorities or orders which could be interpreted as superseding other priorities (if the CEO is accountable, he will be more likely to remind everyone to behave safely also during a production sprint to fulfill a rush order, for example). Everyone in between the CEO and the line worker should be accountable too, both to remove any gap in accountability and because only someone’s boss has both the technical knowledge and the authority to spot an employee taking a shortcut which can compromise long-term objectives (for example, a CEO might not know when an employee is rushing production in an unsafe way, but his direct supervisor should).

当我向客户介绍这个概念时，有些人会持怀疑态度。为什么一线工人要为自己的受伤负责？为什么CEO要负责？我的回答始终如一：两者都应该负责，中间所有人员也都应该负责，以避免任何盲点。一线工人应该负责，因为他对自己的行为负有最终责任，并且对所处环境也最为了解。CEO也应该负责，否则他可能会设定相互冲突的优先级或指令，而这些指令可能会被解读为凌驾于其他优先级之上（例如，如果CEO负责，他更有可能提醒所有人即使在生产冲刺以完成紧急订单时也要注意安全）。CEO和一线工人之间的所有人员也都应该负责，这既是为了消除责任漏洞，也是因为只有上级才拥有技术知识和权限来发现员工偷工减料的行为，从而避免损害长期目标（例如，CEO可能不知道员工何时以不安全的方式赶工，但他的直接主管应该知道）。

This idea seems at odds with the concept, taught in many management courses, that exactly one person should be accountable for any given task because otherwise, if two people are accountable for a failure, then they can blame each other and escape negative consequences. [6]

这种想法似乎与许多管理课程中教授的概念相矛盾，即任何一项任务都应该由一个人负责，否则，如果两个人对失败负责，他们就可以互相指责，从而逃避负面后果。[6]

The solution is to make it clear that, if two or more people are accountable for a given result, it means that they will all be affected positively if that result is achieved and negatively if it is failed, no matter whose fault or merit. Skin in the game for everyone. Once the possibility of excuses and blame is ruled out, the participants involved will be strongly incentivized to work together and ensure that the objective is achieved, no matter what.

解决方案在于明确指出，如果两个人或多人对某个结果负责，那么无论过错方是谁，结果达成后所有人都会受益，失败后所有人都会受损。这意味着每个人都与结果息息相关。一旦排除了推卸责任和互相指责的可能性，所有参与者就会更有动力齐心协力，确保目标达成，无论付出什么代价。

I’ve heard of excellent companies where, for example, every single employee had an objective on safety – theirs and of all their subordinates. For example, if a worker injured himself, he would miss part of his bonus for the year. His direct supervisor would miss part of his bonus, too. If enough employees in a plant would injure themselves, the plant manager would miss part of his bonus too. And so on. Full incentives alignment.

我听说过一些非常优秀的公司，例如，每个员工都设定了安全目标——既包括他们自己的安全，也包括所有下属的安全。举例来说，如果一名工人受伤，他将损失一部分年终奖金。他的直接主管也会损失一部分奖金。如果工厂里有足够多的员工受伤，工厂经理也会损失一部分奖金。以此类推。这才是真正的激励机制完全一致。

Good managers show what a good result looks like

优秀的管理者会展现出好的结果是什么样子。

Often, ineffective managers describe the result too blurrily or too narrowly. These descriptions are easily gameable. The employee might achieve the result using shortcuts which are formally correct but effectively terrible. For example, if a manager gives the task to “increase the output of the line to 90 pieces per minute”, a result which yields 90 pieces per minutes of which only 70 are of satisfactory quality is formally good but effectively terrible.

低效的管理者常常对结果描述得过于模糊或狭隘。这些描述很容易被钻空子。员工可能会使用一些形式上正确但实际上效果糟糕的捷径来达到目的。例如，如果管理者布置的任务是“将生产线的产量提高到每分钟90件”，那么最终每分钟能生产90件，但其中只有70件质量合格，这样的结果在形式上是好的，但在实际效果上却很糟糕。

Good managers paint visual, explicit, unambiguous and clear descriptions of what a good result looks like. They spend at least 20-30 seconds, perhaps even a minute or two. They use examples. They mention who will use the output of the task and how. They use adjectives. They ask their subordinates to repeat how a good result looks like. They ask them to verbally express examples of good results and of bad ones.

优秀的管理者会用形象、清晰、明确且毫不含糊的语言描述好的结果。他们至少会花20-30秒，甚至一两分钟的时间来解释。他们会举例说明，会说明谁会使用任务成果以及如何使用，还会使用形容词。他们会要求下属复述好的结果是什么样子，并让他们口头举例说明好的结果和坏的结果。

Good managers do not let any room for misunderstanding.

优秀的管理者不会给误解留下任何空间。

If you manage people who manage people themselves, I would urge you to set standards for how descriptive your subordinates should be in describing results when delegating them to their own subordinates.

如果你管理的是那些本身又管理下属的人，我强烈建议你制定标准，规定你的下属在向下属汇报工作时，应该如何描述工作成果。

What if the subordinate lacks know-how?

如果下属缺乏相关专业知识怎么办？

If the subordinate is new to his role, he might lack some of the know-how which is required to complete the task he has been assigned. In this case, his manager can provide such know-how directly, by showing him how he would solve the task at hand (or a similar enough one), or he might provide such know-how indirectly, by referring the subordinate to some colleague or book/manual where he can get the information he needs. In particular, during the first few days of a new employee, it can be effective to have him passively observe a colleague in the same role (a task called shadowing ).

如果下属是新上任的，他可能缺乏完成分配任务所需的一些专业知识。在这种情况下，他的经理可以直接提供这些专业知识，例如向他演示如何解决当前任务（或类似任务）；或者也可以间接提供，例如推荐下属向同事请教或查阅相关书籍/手册，以便他获取所需信息。尤其是在新员工入职的最初几天，让他被动地观察一位担任相同职务的同事（称为“影子学习”）会非常有效。

However, the manager must always make clear that, even if he is helping his subordinate to obtain some know-how, the objective is always to achieve some kind of result and never simply to collect the know-how. The know-how is a tool for completing an objective, never the objective itself.

然而，管理者必须始终明确，即便他是在帮助下属掌握某些技能，最终目标也始终是达成某种结果，而非仅仅收集这些技能。技能是实现目标的工具，而非目标本身。

If the subordinate lacks some know-how but has already spent at least a few months in his current role, then the manager should restrain himself from directly helping the subordinate (unless it is something which could be explained in just a few seconds) and should instead reconfirm that the subordinate has been given a task to complete, which includes proactively finding out how to solve it. The manager can give him some pointers, such as “why don’t you ask Mr. Whitestone who was in charge of something similar last year?”, but he should never take himself action instead of the subordinate. Doing so would teach the subordinate that he is not responsible for solving his own problems.

如果下属缺乏一些专业知识，但已经在目前的岗位上工作了至少几个月，那么经理应该克制自己，不要直接帮助下属（除非这个问题只需几秒钟就能解释清楚），而是应该再次确认下属的任务，包括主动寻找解决方案。经理可以给他一些建议，例如“你为什么不问问去年负责类似工作的惠特斯通先生呢？”，但绝不能代替下属采取行动。这样做会让下属觉得他无需为自己的问题负责。

There are three notable exceptions to the paragraphs above: the know-how related to regulations, to newly installed machines and to newly adopted processes. In these cases, the manager might be responsible for getting an expert (which could be himself, if appropriate) to teach his subordinates the related know-how.

以上段落有三个值得注意的例外情况：与规章制度相关的专业知识、新安装的机器以及新采用的流程。在这些情况下，经理可能需要负责聘请专家（如果合适，专家也可以是经理本人）来培训下属掌握相关的专业知识。

Local knowledge

本地知识

In general, a manager will have more knowledge regarding what results are needed by the company, whereas an experienced line worker will have more knowledge about how to achieve such results. This is because of the different kind of information each of them is exposed in their day-to-day work: the manager spends a sizable amount of his time participating to meetings and reading reports, whereas the line worker spends most of his time completing hands-on tasks.

一般来说，管理者更了解公司需要达成的目标，而经验丰富的基层员工则更了解如何实现这些目标。这是因为他们在日常工作中接触到的信息类型不同：管理者花费大量时间参加会议和阅读报告，而基层员工则将大部分时间用于实际操作。

This is not a problem when neither role oversteps the other one and everyone does what they know best. The manager, who is responsible for setting objectives, has a better overview of what the company needs; the line worker, who is responsible for completing objectives, has a better knowledge of what to practically do to achieve them.

如果两个角色互不越权，每个人都各司其职，那就不会有问题。负责制定目标的经理对公司的需求有更全面的了解；负责完成目标的基层员工则更清楚如何切实有效地实现目标。

However, in some cases, the manager might know better than the line worker how to achieve the objectives. This is the case of a newly hired line worker who is still undergoing training or of a newly promoted manager who used to do the work of the employees he now manages.

然而，在某些情况下，经理可能比一线员工更了解如何实现目标。例如，新入职的一线员工仍在接受培训，或者新晋升的经理曾经从事过他现在所管理员工的工作。

In such cases, the manager has to be careful not to use his superior knowledge to prescribe instruction, for two reasons.

在这种情况下，经理必须小心，不要利用自己的优越知识来制定指示，原因有二。

First, the more the manager exploits his superior knowledge to assign instructions together with objectives, the more restricted the perception of a role will his subordinates assume [7] .  The subordinates will come to believe that their role is to follow instructions rather than to achieve objectives. This will become a problem unless the job of the subordinates entirely consists in following a list of instructions with no chance for variations or incidents to take place (almost no job is like that).

首先，管理者越是利用其专业知识优势来下达指令并设定目标，下属对自身角色的认知就越会受到限制[7]。下属会逐渐认为他们的职责是执行指令，而不是完成目标。除非下属的工作完全由一系列指令组成，没有任何变通或意外发生的可能性（几乎没有工作是这样的），否则这将成为一个问题。

Second, it is very rare that the manager knows the environment in which his subordinates work. Most often, they know the environment in which they themselves used to work when they were in their subordinate’s position. In industries in which processes and technologies change very fast, a manager who thinks he knows the job of his subordinates quickly becomes a hindrance to the performance of his team, preventing its members to adopt new approaches and new tools. The faster the rate of change in an industry, the more the manager must assume he doesn’t know (anymore) how his subordinates should complete their tasks. [8]

其次，管理者很少真正了解下属的工作环境。他们通常只了解自己曾经担任下属职位时的工作环境。在流程和技术快速变化的行业中，如果管理者自以为了解下属的工作，很快就会成为团队绩效的阻碍，妨碍团队成员采用新的方法和工具。行业变化速度越快，管理者就越应该意识到自己（不再）了解下属应该如何完成任务。[8]

This does not mean that a manager should always let his subordinates figure out it entirely by themselves. He can figure it out with them, but he should never figure it out for them.

但这并不意味着管理者应该总是放任下属完全自行解决问题。他可以和下属一起解决问题，但绝不能替他们做决定。

If I had to summarize this chapter in a single sentence, it would be: do not do anything which might decrease the accountability of your subordinates.

如果让我用一句话来概括本章内容，那就是：不要做任何可能降低下属责任感的事情。

The lowest competent level

最低能力水平

Good companies acknowledge that, whereas objectives have to be set from some level of overview, the decisions related to how to complete them are complex and require specific, fast-changing, low-level local knowledge.

优秀的公司认识到，虽然目标必须从某种程度的概览层面来设定，但与如何完成这些目标相关的决策却很复杂，需要具体的、快速变化的、低层次的本地知识。

Therefore, great companies strive to have decisions taken at the lowest competent level.

因此，优秀的公司力求让能力最低的层级做出决策。

For example, they know that in supermarkets the local store manager should be the person who decides which products to shelf [9] . Not (only) because empowering him would motivate him and would make him grow, but because he is the best-placed person to take that decision. He is the one who best knows how his customers behave and how a change would affect the complex processes in which he spends his day-to-day. The person in the highest position might have access to more information, but this is a reason to give access to such information at a lower level, not to take decisions at the higher level.

例如，他们知道在超市里，应该由当地门店经理来决定哪些商品上架[9]。这不仅仅是因为赋予他权力会激励他、促进他成长，更是因为他是最适合做这个决定的人。他最了解顾客的行为，也最清楚任何改变都会如何影响他日常工作的复杂流程。职位最高的人或许掌握更多信息，但这恰恰是让较低层级的人也能获取这些信息的原因，而不是让高层来做决定。

This does not mean that the lowest competent level’s decision should not be vetted by higher levels before being executed; in some cases, this is necessary to prevent mistakes which might endanger the company.

但这并不意味着最低层级的决策在执行前不需要经过上层级的审查；在某些情况下，这样做是必要的，可以防止出现可能危及公司的错误。

Similarly, this does not mean that the lowest competent level necessarily coincides with the lowest level (regardless of competence). In the example above, the decision on which products to shelf can perhaps be taken by the local store manager, but not by the newly hired cashier.

同样，这并不意味着最低能力水平必然与最低级别（无论能力如何）相符。在上述例子中，决定哪些商品上架或许可以由当地门店经理做出，但新聘的收银员则无权决定。

Too often, companies take decisions at the highest competent level instead. Sometimes, this is due to the ego of the executives involved. Other times, it is due to a genuine yet incorrect belief that competence is correlated with rank for any kind of decision .

公司常常让能力最强的管理层来做决策。有时，这是因为相关高管的自负；有时，则是因为他们错误地认为，能力与职位高低在任何决策中都成正比。

In general, the rule of thumb is: decisions on what objectives to pursue should be set at the highest competent level and then trickled down. Decisions on how to fulfill the objectives, instead, should be taken at the lowest competent level.

一般来说，经验法则是：确定要追求的目标应该由最高层级的决策者制定，然后自上而下地传达。而如何实现这些目标的决策则应该由最低层级的决策者做出。

The 20% rule for knowing when to shut up

20%法则：何时闭嘴

Author Marshall Goldsmith proposes the “20% rule”: do not give a suggestion if it doesn’t improve the original situation by at least 20%. The rationale is that each suggestion decreases the ownership of the original idea or problem, therefore making the subordinate less motivated to take action. The amount of motivation lost per suggestions is usually constant (let’s say, 20%). Then, it makes sense to only propose suggestions which dramatically improve the outcome and to shut up otherwise, when the gain in effectiveness would not be enough to offset the loss in motivation.

作者马歇尔·戈德史密斯提出了“20%法则”：如果建议不能使原有情况改善至少20%，就不要提出。其逻辑在于，每提出一项建议，下属对原想法或问题的掌控力就会降低，从而降低其行动的积极性。每项建议造成的积极性损失通常是固定的（比如20%）。因此，只有当建议能够显著改善结果时，才应该提出建议；否则，如果效率的提升不足以弥补积极性的损失，就应该保持沉默。

That said, there is a situation in which the manager should always speak up: if he sees a subordinate committing the same mistake over and over. The risk is that the subordinate will end up frustrated and demotivated by his inability to overcome the recurring problem. In this case, the manager should be proactive in pointing out that the current approach is leading to nowhere and should suggest another one.

话虽如此，在某些情况下，经理必须挺身而出：如果他发现下属反复犯同样的错误。风险在于，下属会因为无法克服反复出现的问题而感到沮丧和失去动力。在这种情况下，经理应该主动指出目前的方法行不通，并提出其他建议。

What if the subordinate lacks motivation?

如果下属缺乏积极性怎么办？

Assigning accountability is not something that managers only do with already-motivated employees. Rather, it is how good managers make their employees motivated.

分配责任并非管理者只对那些本身就积极性很高的员工才做的事情。相反，优秀的管理者正是通过这种方式来激励员工。

If a manager does not assign accountability, he relies on his subordinates already being internally motivated. This is not a given. A good manager puts his subordinates in the condition to be effective regardless of whether they are internally motivated or not.

如果管理者不明确责任归属，就只能寄希望于下属的内在动力。但这并非必然。优秀的管理者会创造条件，让下属无论是否具备内在动力都能高效工作。

Accountability is not the result of motivation, but its cause. A certainty of good individual outcomes in case of good performance and of bad ones in case of bad performance is enough to motivate most employees.

问责制并非激励的结果，而是激励的原因。如果员工能够确定表现优异会获得良好的个人回报，表现不佳则会受到惩罚，那么这足以激励大多数员工。

Please note that the sentence above is not about a certainty of good individual outcomes in case of good performance or a certainty of bad ones in case of bad performance. Both are necessary. Experienced managers know that most employees are sensible to only one of the two. Ambitious employees chase rewards whereas unenthusiastic or insecure ones avoid punishments. A full spectrum of outcomes is necessary to cover all levels of motivation and of performance.

请注意，以上句子并非指表现好必然带来好的结果，也并非指表现差必然带来坏的结果。两者都不可或缺。经验丰富的管理者深知，大多数员工只对其中一种结果敏感。雄心勃勃的员工追求奖励，而缺乏热情或不自信的员工则避免惩罚。我们需要提供全方位的结果体系，才能涵盖所有激励水平和绩效水平。

Moreover, only ensuring good personal outcomes in case of good performance without also ensuring bad personal outcomes in case of bad performance invites some employees to take excessive risks in a gamble to grab rewards without suffering consequences if things go wrong. Hence the need to set both positive and negative consequences. [10]

此外，如果只确保表现良好时获得良好的个人回报，而不确保表现不佳时受到不良后果，就会诱使一些员工为了获得回报而冒险行事，却不愿承担失败的后果。因此，需要同时设定积极和消极的后果。[10]

Managers and motivation

管理者和激励

It is my belief that most individuals are born motivated. If a worker seems demotivated, chances are that he lost his motivation at some point of his career, for one of two reasons.

我认为大多数人天生都充满动力。如果一个员工看起来缺乏动力，很可能是因为他在职业生涯的某个阶段失去了动力，原因不外乎以下两点之一。

First reason: the worker has been deprived of ownership on his tasks. Someone – his boss or a colleague of his – keeps micromanaging him, providing him with suggestions or doing his work. His reaction has been to assume a fully passive role.

第一个原因：员工被剥夺了对工作的自主权。有人——可能是他的老板或同事——不断地对他进行微观管理，给他提建议，甚至替他做工作。他的反应是采取完全被动的角色。

Second reason: the worker has been deprived of accountability on his tasks. Perhaps, he completed some task exceptionally well (or, due to blurry objectives, he believes he did so) but did not enjoy a positive outcome out of it. Or perhaps, he failed some task but did not suffer a negative outcome. Either way, he learned the following lesson: no one cares. He might get taught to think: “If the results do not change, at least let’s spend the least amount of energy possible.”

第二个原因：员工的工作责任感缺失。或许他出色地完成了某项任务（或者，由于目标模糊，他自认为出色），却没有获得任何积极的结果。又或许他失败了某项任务，却没有遭受任何负面影响。无论哪种情况，他都从中吸取了这样的教训：没人关心他。他可能会被灌输这样的观念：“如果结果没有改变，至少我们应该尽可能少地付出精力。”

Regarding to motivation, I do not believe in the role of managers that is depicted in movies: inspiring speeches and charismatic personalities. I believe that managers do not have to motivate employees. Rather, they must prevent the conditions that might lead to them becoming demotivated. This consists in two practices: avoiding depriving them of the ownership of the tasks they have been assigned and keeping them accountable for the objectives they have been given. [11]

关于激励，我不认同电影中描绘的管理者角色：鼓舞人心的演讲和个人魅力。我认为管理者不必激励员工，而应该预防可能导致员工失去动力的情况。这包括两种做法：避免剥夺员工对所分配任务的所有权，并让他们对所设定的目标负责。[11]

Sometimes, a manager is given subordinates which are already demotivated, because of the actions of one of their previous bosses (or, in the case of freshly graduated employees, of one of their parents or teachers). In this case, the manager has an additional task: to show to the subordinate that he really owns the tasks he is assigned and that he really will be held accountable for his results, both good ones and bad ones and to try to catch as often as possible the demotivated subordinate doing something good and rewarding him for it – even just with a “thank you”. If the subordinate is so passive as not to do anything positive, then the manager should somehow find a way to have him doing something good, in order to then be able to reward him for it.

有时，经理会遇到一些士气低落的下属，这可能是由于他们之前的上司（或者，对于应届毕业生来说，可能是父母或老师）的影响。在这种情况下，经理需要额外承担一项任务：让下属明白，他确实要对自己的任务负责，并且无论结果好坏都要承担责任；同时，经理还要尽可能多地发现下属的积极表现并给予奖励——哪怕只是一句“谢谢”。如果下属消极被动，不愿做任何积极的事情，那么经理就需要想办法引导他去做一些有益的事情，以便给予奖励。

Negotiating objectives

谈判目标

One common problem I noticed afflicting most young project managers is a deep-rooted belief of efficiency being superior to efficacy. This is true for student life (often, students are constrained in their resources and try to “make the most of what they have”), but it is not always true for companies, for which “achieving results no matter the cost” is often more important.

我注意到，大多数年轻项目经理普遍存在一个问题，那就是他们根深蒂固地认为效率比效能更重要。这在学生时代或许如此（学生往往资源有限，会努力“充分利用现有资源”），但在公司里却并非总是如此，因为对公司而言，“不惜一切代价取得成果”往往更为重要。

Don’t get me wrong: efficiency is very important for companies too, but there are situations – such as winning a huge contract or satisfying a critical customer – where efficacy trumps efficiency, and Top Management would be much more satisfied with a “I achieved 100% of the objective spending120% of the budget” than with a “I achieved 80% of the objective with 50% of the budget”. In my experience, young employees are particularly susceptible to encounter difficulties in internalizing this.

别误会我的意思：效率对公司来说也很重要，但在某些情况下——比如赢得巨额合同或满足关键客户的需求——效能比效率更重要。高层管理人员更乐于听到“我用120%的预算完成了100%的目标”，而不是“我用50%的预算完成了80%的目标”。以我的经验来看，年轻员工尤其容易难以理解这一点。

To avoid situations like the one above, great managers teach their subordinates how to negotiate objectives. They explain to them that, if they have too much on their plate, they should be the one raising the hand and saying, “I have too much on my plate and cannot do everything well, what should I prioritize?”

为了避免出现上述情况，优秀的管理者会教导下属如何协商目标。他们会向下属解释，如果工作量过大，就应该主动举手说：“我的工作太多了，无法面面俱到，我应该优先处理哪些事情？”

Seasoned managers know that this is very preferable compared to trying to achieve everything and then failing, as the latter might catch everyone off-guard and start a chain of negative events. Young employees do not know this and must be taught it.

经验丰富的管理者明白，这远比试图面面俱到却最终失败要好得多，因为后者可能会让所有人措手不及，并引发一系列负面事件。年轻员工并不了解这一点，需要加以教导。

Similarly, objectives can be negotiated regarding budget, internal support, external support, training, etc. The only thing which cannot be negotiated, especially after it’s too late, is the desired outcome.

同样，关于预算、内部支持、外部支持、培训等方面的目标都可以协商。唯一不能协商的，尤其是在为时已晚之后，是预期结果。

there cannot be any misunderstanding about who is accountable for what

对于谁该为什么负责，不应该有任何误解。

Good managers understand the subtle difference between “it can be understood” and “it cannot be misunderstood”. The former assumes skill and motivation in the listener. The latter doesn’t assume anything; it simply works. Good managers strive for the latter.

优秀的管理者深谙“容易理解”和“绝对不会被误解”之间的微妙差别。前者假定听者具备一定的技巧和积极性，而后者则无需任何假设，它本身就能奏效。优秀的管理者力求做到后者。

Instead, bad managers are content with simply mentioning or implying accountability. When, inevitably, one of their subordinates misunderstands or forgets, they blame him. However, by blaming their subordinate for not having understood, they imply that not understanding is an option. This will have cascading consequences, as it is not that difficult to argue that an instruction was unclear. Earlier or later, someone will argue that, because instructions were not clear, he should be left out the hook. As discussed in the previous chapter, this is the beginning of a vicious circle which ends in mediocrity.

相反，糟糕的管理者满足于仅仅提及或暗示责任。当他们的下属不可避免地误解或遗忘时，他们便会责怪下属。然而，责怪下属没有理解，实际上是在暗示不理解也是一种选择。这将产生连锁反应，因为很容易就能找到理由证明指令不清晰。迟早会有人辩称，由于指令不清晰，他应该免责。正如前一章所述，这是一个恶性循环的开始，最终只会导致平庸。

To avoid this, good managers are so explicit in their communication with their subordinates that no one can possibly argue that there could have been a misunderstanding about them being accountable for the result of the task being delegated.

为了避免这种情况，优秀的管理者在与下属沟通时会非常明确，以至于没有人能够质疑他们是否对委派任务的结果负有责任。

In order to reach this unwavering level of explicitness and clarity, good managers are relentless in making the implicit explicit, even when doing so would seem an insult to the intelligence of their interlocutor. They do not let their politeness and their ego get in the way of the clear accountability assignment that is needed for their subordinates to perform at their best.

为了达到这种毫不妥协的清晰明确，优秀的管理者会坚持不懈地将隐含的信息明确化，即便这样做似乎是对对方智商的侮辱。他们不会让礼貌和自尊妨碍清晰的责任划分，而这对于下属发挥最佳水平至关重要。

Words are not enough; the attitude is important too. If a manager mentions to one of his subordinates that he will be held accountable for an objective but keeps micromanaging it, he is retaining accountability for himself. Just like the manager who would not release his grip on the pen in the opening paragraph of this chapter.

光说不做是不够的，态度也很重要。如果一位经理告诉下属他要对某个目标负责，但却仍然事无巨细地进行微观管理，那么他实际上是在为自己保留责任。就像本章开头提到的那位始终不肯松开笔的经理一样。

Good managers spend a lot of time with their subordinate during delegation time, but then let them relatively free. They do check-in regularly on whether the task is on track to achieve the desired results (unless the subordinate proved himself exceptionally reliable in the past), but even during those check-ins, they are always relaxed enough to let him know that he will be accountable for the result. They do not provide suggestions, unless asked or unless the subordinate is clearly off-track. Even in this case, they point out that the current methods might not achieve the desired result; they strive not to prescribe the new method to be used, in order not to steal ownership of the task. At no point good managers risk being ambiguous about who owns the results: it’s always the subordinate.

优秀的管理者会在授权期间花大量时间与下属交流，但之后会给予他们相对的自由。他们会定期检查任务进展是否符合预期（除非下属过去表现得非常可靠），但即使在这些检查中，他们也始终保持轻松的心态，让下属明白最终结果由他自己负责。除非被问及或下属明显偏离方向，否则他们不会主动提出建议。即使在这种情况下，他们也会指出当前的方法可能无法达到预期效果；他们尽量避免指定新的方法，以免抢走任务的主导权。优秀的管理者绝不会让下属对结果的归属产生任何疑问：最终的责任始终在下属身上。

Good managers never assume an attitude which signals that they own the tasks they delegate.

优秀的管理者绝不会摆出一副认为自己对委派的任务拥有所有权的态度。

…

Bad managers keep themselves accountable for the tasks their subordinates should be accountable for. Because they feel personally accountable for the tasks they delegated, they offer suggestions. They prescribe methods. They do not release their grip on the tools their subordinates will use. They do not let them feel accountable.

糟糕的管理者会把自己本应由下属负责的任务都揽在自己身上。因为他们觉得自己对委派的任务负有责任，所以他们会提出建议，规定方法，并且紧抓着下属使用的工具不放，不让下属承担责任。

Accountability cannot be shared. The more the manager feels accountable for the tasks he delegates, the less his subordinate will feel accountable.

责任不能分担。管理者越觉得自己对委派的任务负有责任，下属就越不会觉得自己有责任。

The less the subordinate feels accountable, the more likely he will be to use the prescribed tool in the wrong way. The more likely he will be to stop at the first bump. The more likely he will be to shut himself to innovation and collaboration. The more likely he will be to prioritize the short-term (executing the instructions he received and nothing else) and to neglect the long-term (the result to be achieved).

下属越缺乏责任感，就越有可能错误地使用既定工具；越有可能遇到第一个障碍就止步不前；越有可能封闭自己，拒绝创新和协作；越有可能只关注短期目标（执行指令，而忽略长期目标（最终结果））。

Accountability is the soul of the effective employee. By keeping accountability for himself, the bad manager transforms his subordinates into a group of mindless zombies who drag their limbs onto the workplace.

责任感是高效员工的灵魂。糟糕的管理者只顾自己，不负责任，只会把下属变成一群行尸走肉，拖着疲惫的身躯在工作场所苟延残喘。

Instead, the good manager shares the accountability with his subordinates. He gifts it to them. He makes them alive. He gives them brains. He might feel a little less alive himself, but he is rewarded by a vibrant entourage.

相反，优秀的管理者会与下属分担责任。他将责任赋予他们，让他们充满活力，激发他们的智慧。他自己或许会感到些许疲惫，但他会因团队的活力而受益匪浅。

Good managers are explicit about how results will be evaluated, when and by whom

优秀的管理者会明确说明如何评估结果、何时评估以及由谁评估。

A subordinate needs to know how the result of his task will be evaluated, when and by whom. Otherwise, he might get frustrated by an evaluation which does not conform to his expectations.

下属需要知道他的工作成果将如何被评估，何时评估以及由谁评估。否则，如果评估结果与他的预期不符，他可能会感到沮丧。

For example, a subordinate might be asked by his manager to complete a given task by Friday. The task takes a couple of hours to complete, so he schedules it for Thursday afternoon, expecting to be evaluated for the results not before the end of Friday. If the manager pops by on Wednesday and asks for a progress status, the employee will be frustrated. “The manager told me I have until Friday, and now he expects me have already began?”

例如，下属可能被经理要求在周五前完成某项任务。这项任务需要几个小时才能完成，所以他安排在周四下午，并期望在周五结束前收到结果评估。如果经理在周三突然来询问进度，员工就会感到沮丧。“经理明明告诉我周五之前可以完成，现在却希望我已经开始做了？”

Good managers are explicit about when results will be evaluated, including when progress updates will be asked. For example, they might say: “I expect you to finish this task by the end of the month, but I will check your progress every Monday, to ensure that you’ll be on track.”

优秀的管理者会明确说明何时评估结果，包括何时要求汇报进度。例如，他们可能会说：“我希望你在月底前完成这项任务，但我会在每周一检查你的进度，以确保你按计划进行。”

Similarly, good managers are explicit about how results will be evaluated and by whom. The reason is not only to make the goal clearer, but foremost to prevent surprises and frustration by subordinates who might think they have been unfairly judged. (“Unfairly” is often a synonym with “a rule not stated in advance”). The most effective way to prevent frustration during evaluations is by clarifying before the beginning of the task how the results will be evaluated, without leaving any wiggle room that might allow the subordinate to imagine a different way in which the results could be evaluated.

同样，优秀的管理者会明确说明如何评估结果以及由谁来评估。这样做不仅是为了使目标更清晰，更重要的是为了避免下属感到意外和沮丧，以免他们认为自己受到了不公平的评价（“不公平”通常等同于“事先未说明的规则”）。防止评估过程中出现不满情绪的最有效方法是在任务开始前就明确说明结果的评估方式，不留任何回旋余地，以免下属想象出其他评估方法。

The most difficult part about delegation

授权中最难的部分是什么？

Even if you completely internalized the contents of this chapter, chances are that you will still not delegate as much as you should.

即使你完全理解了本章的内容，你仍然很可能不会像应该的那样进行授权。

You will be effective at delegating the tasks you do not like. However, if you are like most managers I know, there is at least one task from one of your previous roles which you still enjoy doing. That task will be the hardest one to delegate.

你会很擅长委派自己不喜欢的任务。但是，如果你像我认识的大多数管理者一样，那么你以前的某个职位中至少有一项任务你仍然乐于去做。这项任务将是最难委派的。

When managers are promoted, often, releasing their grip on the tasks they used to perform but are not necessary anymore is just as big a challenge as grasping the new tasks which are required for their new role.

当经理晋升时，他们往往面临的挑战是，如何放手那些他们过去负责但现在已经不再需要的任务，与如何掌握新角色所需的新任务一样重要。

I once heard a manager calling this phenomenon “dopamine withdrawal”. I’m not sure about the neurological correctness of the term, but it does paint a clear idea of what’s going on here. Working on that task used to be pleasant or used to create a “rush”, something that made you feel alive. Managers that successfully delegate that task away begin feeling “withdrawal symptoms” from not being able to perform the task and feeling the “rush” again, and often relapse by grabbing control of that task or micromanaging the subordinates they delegated it to.

我曾听一位经理把这种现象称为“多巴胺戒断”。我不确定这个术语在神经学上是否准确，但它确实清晰地描绘了这里发生的事情。过去，完成这项任务会让人感到愉悦，或者带来一种“快感”，一种让你感觉充满活力的感觉。那些成功地将这项任务委派出去的经理，会因为无法亲自完成任务、无法再次感受到那种“快感”而开始出现“戒断症状”，他们往往会重新掌控这项任务，或者对被委派的下属进行微观管理，从而导致病情复发。

While I do understand the feeling – it probably used to be one of my major weaknesses, and sometimes it still is – this behavior is problematic for your team. They need to have operative control on the tasks that are of their competence. Release your grip on the tasks that used to be yours, and delegate them away. If you manage to do so for about 2-3 months, the “withdrawal symptoms” will disappear, as new tasks proper of your new role will begin taking the place of the old one as “rush providers”. You just need to trust that they have the potential to do so.

我理解你的感受——这或许曾经是我的一个主要弱点，有时现在依然如此——但这种行为对你的团队来说是个问题。他们需要对那些他们能力范围内的任务拥有实际的掌控权。放手那些曾经由你负责的任务，并将它们委派出去。如果你能坚持这样做两到三个月，“戒断反应”就会消失，因为你新角色中真正属于你的新任务会逐渐取代你之前那些“紧急任务”。你只需要相信他们有能力做到这一点。

Example of bad delegation

糟糕的授权示例

Bad managers tend to delegate as follows: “I need you to organize an event for potential B2B customers. Rent a meeting room at the Alps Hotel. Invite this list of people. Send them a letter and then call them after two weeks to make sure they received it. Tell our salesmen Blackman and Clear that they should prepare a presentation.”

糟糕的管理者往往会这样分配任务：“我需要你组织一场面向潜在B2B客户的活动。在阿尔卑斯酒店租一个会议室。邀请名单上的这些人。给他们发一封邀请函，两周后打电话确认他们是否收到。告诉我们的销售员布莱克曼和克莱尔，让他们准备一份演示文稿。”

This is bad delegation, for many reasons. It does not provide targets. How many attendees are a success? 5? 20? 50? Also, it does not provide a budget. Why does the meeting room have to be at the Alps Hotel? Does it have to be booked at any price? Could another hotel be used, especially if it would have better or cheaper facilities, or if it would be easier to reach by the attendees? How were the people in the list chosen? If the salespeople have other people to invite, can they? If the event is a failure, whose fault it is? (If the instructions provided during the delegation are followed and the event is a failure, it is the fault of whoever came up with the list of instructions: the manager.)

这份授权安排很糟糕，原因有很多。它没有设定目标。多少人参加才算成功？5人？20人？50人？此外，它也没有提供预算。为什么会议室一定要在阿尔卑斯酒店？难道一定要不惜一切代价预订吗？能否选择其他酒店，尤其是一些设施更好、价格更低，或者交通更便利的酒店？名单上的人员是如何选定的？如果销售人员还有其他人选，他们可以邀请吗？如果活动失败了，责任在谁？（如果按照授权期间提供的指示执行，但活动仍然失败，那么责任在于制定指示的人：经理。）

Example of good delegation

良好授权的例子

Good managers would delegate as follows: “You are responsible to organize by the end of June an event to extend our sales to potential B2B customers. You will also be the one inviting the leads. Here is a list of potential customers to begin with. Our salesmen Blackman and Clear might know more. You should call them, but feel free to ask other colleagues as well. I will consider the event a success if it will lead to at least 10 successful commercial proposals. Based on our experience, about 30 customers attending the event are needed because only a third of them converts into a proposal. Last year we organized a similar event at the Alps Hotel. Your colleague Bells ran it. You can call him to ask what we learned from that time. You will have a budget of $7000 to organize the event. If you manage to invite more than 30 leads, I can increase the budget by $2000. We need the sales. I can always increase the budget, but make sure you get enough solid prospects to attend. Get Blackman to deliver the presentation to the clients but also bring a few other salespeople to talk with the clients. I will hold you and the salespeople responsible for generating 10 proposals. Any questions?”

优秀的管理者会这样分配任务：“你负责在六月底前组织一场活动，以拓展我们面向潜在B2B客户的销售渠道。你还要负责邀请潜在客户。这里有一份潜在客户名单供你参考。我们的销售员布莱克曼和克莱尔可能掌握更多信息。你可以联系他们，也可以询问其他同事。如果活动能促成至少10份成功的商业提案，我就认为活动成功。根据我们的经验，大约需要30位客户参加，因为只有三分之一的客户最终会提交提案。去年我们在阿尔卑斯酒店组织了一场类似的活动，由你的同事贝尔斯负责。你可以联系他，了解我们从那次活动中学到了什么。你将有7000美元的活动预算。如果你能邀请到超过30位潜在客户，我可以增加2000美元的预算。我们需要销售业绩。我可以随时增加预算，但请确保你邀请到足够多的优质潜在客户参加。请布莱克曼向客户做演示，同时也要带上其他几位销售人员。”去和客户谈谈。我会要求你和销售人员负责准备10份提案。有什么问题吗？

This is an example of good delegation because it clearly states both the rationale behind the task and the metrics on which the subordinate will be held accountable. It provides options rather than prescriptions. The manager never tries to retain responsibility for the task. From the first sentence to the last one, it is clear that the task is delegated together with its results. No room for misunderstanding. Similarly, the objective is clear: 10 proposals. No room for wiggling. There is a clear deadline and a budget. Budgets are great because they allow the subordinate to make considerations and trade-offs. The priorities are explicit: getting the prospective customers to attend. This is shown through costly trade-offs: the manager makes it clear that an event which would cost one third of the budget but deliver half the proposals would be considered a failure. Effectiveness over efficiency. At the end of the conversation, the subordinate clearly knows what he is responsible for and what space he has to operate (budget, time, options). It is likely that he will achieve the objective.

这是一个优秀的授权案例，因为它清晰地阐明了任务背后的理由以及下属的考核指标。它提供的是多种选择，而非强制性规定。管理者从未试图保留对任务的责任。从第一句话到最后一句话，任务及其结果都已明确授权，没有任何误解的余地。同样，目标也很明确：10份提案，没有丝毫回旋余地。截止日期和预算都已设定。预算非常重要，因为它允许下属进行权衡取舍。优先事项也很明确：吸引潜在客户参与。这一点体现在高成本的权衡取舍上：管理者明确指出，如果活动花费了预算的三分之一，但最终只获得了一半的提案，则该活动将被视为失败。这里强调的是效果而非效率。谈话结束时，下属清楚地知道自己的职责以及可操作的空间（预算、时间、选择）。他很可能能够达成目标。

Summary

概括

When delegating, make sure your subordinates understand that they will be held accountable for their result on their objectives, no matter what might happen.

在授权时，务必让你的下属明白，无论发生什么，他们都要对完成目标的结果负责。

Avoid any behavior which might introduce ambiguity on whether they will be judged for their result on their objectives.

避免任何可能导致对其目标结果的评判产生歧义的行为。

# ↩

The 3rd Principle
of Operational Excellence:

Good managers demonstrate priorities with visible costly actions

卓越运营的第三项原则：优秀的管理者会通过可见的、代价高昂的行动来展现优先事项。

Most companies genuinely want their Core Values, such as sustainability, safety, or respect for people, to be a reality. However, too often, the day-to-day behavior of their employees fails to embody them.

大多数公司真心希望其核心价值观，例如可持续发展、安全或尊重员工，能够真正落地。然而，员工的日常行为往往未能体现这些价值观。

In this chapter, I will describe the one thing that great managers do to faultlessly get their subordinates to internalize the Core Values of their company.

在本章中，我将描述优秀管理者为了让下属完美地内化公司的核心价值观而所做的一件事。

Core Values are costly

核心价值观代价高昂

The reason why Core Values are so difficult to adopt in the day-to-day of Operations is that they represent short-term costs. “Sustainability” means that environmentally friendly products and machines have to be sourced, at a higher purchasing cost. “Safety” means that workers must wear their Personal Protective Equipment and respecting safety procedures (a time cost).

核心价值观之所以难以在日常运营中贯彻执行，是因为它们代表着短期成本。“可持续性”意味着需要采购环保产品和设备，这会增加采购成本。“安全”意味着员工必须佩戴个人防护装备并遵守安全规程（这需要时间成本）。

However, over the long-term, practicing Core Values has high returns. Sustainable companies improve their image, benefiting in sales and in a lowered risk of regulators imposing fines or removing their permit to operate. Safe companies tend to be better places to work in, with lower employee turnover and higher quality of output – safe environments are also more orderly and conducive to efficient work; moreover, the benefits of having learnt to follow safety procedures includes having become better at following any kind of procedure. Companies practicing “Respect for People” or “Diversity” find it easier to attract and maintain talent.

然而，从长远来看，践行核心价值观会带来丰厚的回报。可持续发展的公司能够提升自身形象，从而促进销售增长，并降低监管机构处以罚款或吊销营业执照的风险。安全的公司往往是更理想的工作场所，员工流动率更低，产出质量更高——安全的工作环境也更加有序，更有利于高效工作；此外，学习遵守安全规程的好处还包括能够更好地遵守任何类型的规程。践行“尊重员工”或“多元化”理念的公司更容易吸引和留住人才。

However, whereas the costs of practicing Core Values take place in the short-term, its returns only materialize in the long-term. This promotes two behaviors: workers acting lazily because the returns of practicing Core Values are distant in time and space (“ Will I ever gain anything out of it?” ) and managers caught into a production deadline or a costs-cutting initiative criticizing those workers who, by practicing Core Values, generate costs. This chapter talks about the second phenomenon: employees hesitating to embrace Core Values because of fear of being punished for generating costs before the returns arrive.

然而，践行核心价值观的成本虽然在短期内显现，但其回报却要到长期才能体现。这导致两种行为：一是员工因为践行核心价值观的回报在时间和空间上都显得遥远而变得懒惰（“我最终能从中得到什么好处吗？”）；二是管理者被生产截止日期或成本削减计划所束缚，批评那些践行核心价值观反而造成成本增加的员工。本章将探讨第二种现象：员工因为害怕在回报到来之前因造成成本增加而受到惩罚，而犹豫是否接受核心价值观。

Imagine a maintenance worker tasked with repairing a broken machine. He notices that, one meter away, there is another one, in function and with a lot of moving parts: an injury risk. He would ask the line supervisor to temporarily shut down the second machine so that he can safely perform the maintenance of the broken one. But he also knows that the supervisor would reply that it cannot be done, that it would be too expensive, that production must go on. Therefore, not to incur a certain short-term cost – being reprimanded – he decides to perform the maintenance without stopping the second machine, thereby incurring the risk of a possible personal injury.

想象一下，一名维修工奉命修理一台故障机器。他注意到一米开外还有另一台机器正在运转，而且有很多活动部件，存在受伤风险。他本可以请求生产线主管暂时关闭第二台机器，以便安全地维修故障机器。但他知道主管会拒绝，理由是成本太高，生产必须继续。因此，为了避免短期内受到训斥，他决定在不关闭第二台机器的情况下进行维修，从而冒着受伤的风险。

Of course, his managers wouldn’t want him to do that. They know that if Safety does become a practiced Core Value, good things will follow. Less injuries means higher morale and less need to have insufficiently trained workers replacing injured ones: both leading to better-maintained machines. However, these benefits only start to show after a few months or years. His managers, in their day-to-day, feel the pressure of production deadlines and temporarily forget these benefits. They only see the costs and benefits that materialize today. What matters to them today with a production deadline is that not stopping a machine to safely perform maintenance on the one nearby is a cost. Similarly, the maintenance worker, in his day-to-day, does not feel the benefits of Safety as a Core Value. For him, an injury is a distant possibility. Instead, getting scolded by the Line Supervisor if he takes too long to repair the broken machine is a close reality.

当然，他的经理们不会希望他这样做。他们知道，如果安全成为一项核心价值观并付诸实践，就会带来诸多益处。减少工伤意味着更高的士气，也意味着更少需要用训练不足的工人来顶替受伤的工人：这两点都有助于机器的维护保养。然而，这些好处往往需要几个月甚至几年才能显现。他的经理们在日常工作中承受着生产截止日期的压力，暂时忽略了这些好处。他们只关注眼前的成本和收益。在他们看来，在生产截止日期临近的情况下，不停机安全地维护附近的机器会造成损失。同样，维修工人在日常工作中也感受不到安全作为核心价值观带来的好处。对他来说，受伤似乎遥不可及。相反，如果他修理故障机器的时间过长，就会被生产线主管责骂，这才是迫在眉睫的现实。

In the paragraph above, I emphasized the word feel . The Line Supervisor and the maintenance worker in the example above are competent professionals who know that incidents are a possibility if maintenance is performed next to a machine in movement. However, they do not feel it. Or, to be more precise, they do not feel it respect to how much they feel the more immediate and certain cost of stopping production. Or, they feel it in some contexts only (perhaps, those in which a severe incident recently happened) but not in others. Or, they feel it enough to voice their concerns but not enough to do something about it.

在上文中，我强调了“感觉”这个词。上例中的生产线主管和维修工都是合格的专业人员，他们知道在运转中的机器旁进行维修可能会发生事故。然而，他们并没有切身感受到这种风险。或者更准确地说，他们感受到的风险远不及停产带来的直接且确定的损失。又或者，他们只在某些情况下（例如最近发生过严重事故的情况）感受到风险，而在其他情况下则感受不到。再或者，他们感受到的风险足以表达他们的担忧，但不足以促使他们采取行动。

In my experience, I’ve noticed that Core Values get adopted if and only if the managers go first and make visible tradeoffs that publicly show that the short-term costs of practicing the Core Values are a worthy investment which will bring future long-term benefits. For example, they are the first ones spending time to wear a helmet whenever they visit the factory floor, trading productive time for safety.

根据我的经验，我发现核心价值观只有在管理者率先行动，公开做出权衡取舍，表明践行核心价值观的短期成本是值得的投资，能够带来长远的收益时，才能被员工接受。例如，他们会率先佩戴安全帽，在每次巡视工厂时都这样做，牺牲一些生产时间来保障安全。

Managers making visible investments towards the future every day (practicing the Core Values) remind both themselves and their subordinates in a tangible and conspicuous form that Core Values are worth being stewarded every single time.

管理者每天对未来进行可见的投资（践行核心价值观），以切实可见的方式提醒自己和下属，核心价值观值得时刻践行。

Good managers know that one of the reasons employees do not practice Core Values is because they are fearful of potential punishments for not having been productive in the short-term.

优秀的管理者知道，员工不践行核心价值观的原因之一是他们害怕因短期内工作效率低下而受到惩罚。

Therefore, good managers personally take visible actions incurring these costs, to show that they are truly worth paying and that everyone is expected to do so.

因此，优秀的管理者会亲自采取可见的行动来承担这些成本，以表明这些成本确实值得付出，并且每个人都应该这样做。

A good manager who diligently spends some of his precious time to wear his safety shoes before walking in the plant sends a clear message: “Safety is a cost worth incurring. Safety is good for business.”

一位优秀的管理者，如果能认真抽出宝贵时间，在进入工厂前穿上安全鞋，就能传递一个明确的信息：“安全是一项值得投入的成本。安全对企业有利。”

Conversely, a bad manager who walks on the production line without his safety shoes sends an opposite though equally clear message: “Safety is a waste and has to be cut below what’s strictly necessary.”

相反，一个糟糕的经理如果不穿安全鞋就走上生产线，则会传递出截然相反但同样明确的信息：“安全是一种浪费，必须削减到低于绝对必要的程度。”

Plausibility

合理性

Not all workers think that Core Values are costs to minimize. Some genuinely believe in them. However, believing in a Core Value is not enough to practice it. A worker has to know that his manager practices it as well. In other words, he needs to know that he won’t be reprimanded by his manager for having incurred the short-term costs of having practiced the Core Value.

并非所有员工都认为核心价值观会增加成本，有些人真心相信它们。然而，仅仅相信核心价值观并不足以付诸实践。员工必须确信自己的经理也同样践行这些价值观。换句话说，员工需要知道，自己不会因为践行核心价值观而承担短期成本，从而受到经理的责备。

The only way to know this with certainty, is by seeing his superior incurring such costs himself. This provides the worker with the plausibility to say: “Yes, I’m costing the company by embracing Safety, but my superior is doing the same. I’m following his example.” He will not fear being held accountable for having incurred a cost.

唯一能确定这一点的方法，就是看到他的上级自己也承担了同样的成本。这样，员工就可以理直气壮地说：“没错，我因为注重安全而给公司增加了成本，但我的上级也在这样做。我是在效仿他。” 他不会害怕因为造成成本而被追究责任。

Words can be misinterpreted (“I didn’t really mean this”), actions cannot. Because they are visible and material, they are conspicuous. And, because they are conspicuous, they become norms.

言语可能会被误解（“我并非真心如此”），而行动则不会。因为行动是可见的、物质性的，所以它们引人注目。正因为它们引人注目，所以它们会成为规范。

A good manager who spends some of his precious time to follow safety procedures sends a clear message: “You won’t be punished for doing the same.”

一位优秀的管理者，如果能抽出一些宝贵的时间来遵守安全规程，就能传递一个明确的信息：“你如果也这样做，就不会受到惩罚。”

A bad manager who instead skips safety procedures sends another message, just as clear as the previous one: “I only allocate my precious time towards actions that contribute directly to the bottom line, and you are expected to do the same.”

糟糕的管理者如果忽视安全程序，就会传递出另一个同样明确的信息：“我只把宝贵的时间投入到能直接提高公司利润的事情上，你们也应该这样做。”

Cost as a signal

成本作为一种信号

The costlier an action, the stronger the signal it sends. Diamonds are an effective signal of commitment precisely because they are costly.

行动的代价越高，它所传递的信号就越强烈。钻石之所以能有效地象征承诺，正是因为它们价格昂贵。

Bad managers use words to communicate Core Values. Words are cheap, and their effect is limited.

糟糕的管理者只会用言语来传达核心价值观。言语廉价，效果有限。

Good managers use both words and actions. The costlier the action, the stronger its effect towards getting Core Values internalized.

优秀的管理者言行一致。行动成本越高，对核心价值观的内化效果就越好。

Costly actions are valuable for they change people.

代价高昂的行动之所以有价值，是因为它们能改变人。

In this context, by cost I intend time, money and emotion. Some examples: purchasing some good-quality Personal Protective Equipment is a financial cost; halting production for ten minutes to talk about Safety is both a time cost and a money cost (missed profits from missed production), and having the consistency to have a monthly Safety Meeting even when things are rushed is both a temporal and emotional cost.

在此语境下，我所说的成本指的是时间、金钱和情感成本。举例来说：购买高质量的个人防护装备是一项经济成本；停工十分钟讨论安全问题既是时间成本也是金钱成本（停工造成的利润损失）；即使在时间紧迫的情况下，坚持每月召开一次安全会议也是一项时间和情感成本。

Bad managers who did not internalize the importance of Core Values try to hide the costs of practicing them. They think that the lower the cost, the better. However, by hiding the cost of an action they also hide its importance. They miss an opportunity to positively influence their subordinates.

那些未能真正理解核心价值观重要性的糟糕管理者，试图掩盖践行这些价值观的成本。他们认为成本越低越好。然而，掩盖成本的同时，他们也掩盖了行动的重要性。他们错失了对下属产生积极影响的机会。

Good managers are not shy about these costs. They make them visible. Not in a transactional way – e.g., “We paid $15 each for the new safety gloves, you guys better use them now.” – but in a way which is humble yet transparent, e.g. “We paid $15 each for the new gloves, it’s a lot but we think this is well spent money, because Safety is just that important.”

优秀的管理者不会回避这些成本。他们会坦诚地说明。不是以交易式的方式——例如，“我们每副新安全手套花了15美元，你们最好现在就用上。”——而是以一种谦逊而透明的方式，例如，“我们每副新手套花了15美元，这笔钱不少，但我们认为这笔钱花得值，因为安全至关重要。”

The more visible the costs and the higher they are, the more they will demonstrate to the workers the importance of embracing Core Values.

成本越显而易见、成本越高，就越能向员工表明践行核心价值观的重要性。

Do not misread the above and think that artificially inflating costs is a good thing: it is not. If a pair of good-quality safety gloves costs $15, saying that they cost $30 to your subordinates or buying a more-expensive-yet-just-as-good pair will only pass the message that you are a poor purchaser. The point is not to overspend, but to be transparent with costs.

不要误解以上内容，认为人为抬高成本是件好事：事实并非如此。如果一副优质安全手套售价 15 美元，却告诉下属售价 30 美元，或者购买一副更贵但质量同样好的手套，只会让人觉得你是个不善于采购的人。关键不在于过度消费，而在于成本透明。

Examples of cost as a signal

成本作为信号的例子

A16Z’S fines. Silicon Valley Venture Capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (A16Z) charges its employees $10 per minute if they’re late at meetings with entrepreneurs (their “customers”). What a wonderful way to signal to everyone that not wasting time and caring about customers is a Core Value of the company!

A16Z的罚款。硅谷风险投资公司Andreessen Horowitz (A16Z)规定，如果员工在与创业者（他们的“客户”）的会议中迟到，将按每分钟10美元的标准收取罚款。这真是个绝妙的方式，向所有人表明，不浪费时间、重视客户是公司的核心价值观！

Amazon’s doors. During the first months of life of the retail giant, when cash was not abundant, CEO Jeff Bezos and the rest of the employees used to work on desks made of a wooden door horizontally placed over two stands. The practice of using doors as desks continued for several years, even as cash became more available. Why? So that, when a new employee would join the company and ask why he is supposed to work at a desk made with a door, his manager could reply something along the lines of “here at Amazon we look for every possible way to keep costs low and offer our customers the best price”. What a wonderful way to impress a Core Value in the memory of a newly hired employee!

亚马逊的门。在这家零售巨头成立之初，资金并不充裕，CEO杰夫·贝佐斯和其他员工都用一扇横放在两个支架上的木门做成办公桌。即使资金状况好转，这种用门做办公桌的做法也持续了好几年。为什么呢？这样，当新员工入职并询问为何要用门做办公桌时，他的经理就可以回答说：“在亚马逊，我们竭尽所能降低成本，为顾客提供最优惠的价格。” 这真是个绝妙的向新员工灌输核心价值观的方法！

DuPont’s phone-at-the-wheel ban. Industrial conglomerate DuPont banned its employees from using the phone while driving. This is another costly signal: these employees, especially if sales managers, could have used the phone to call customers or colleagues during long time-wasting journeys. Instead, the company would rather have them doing nothing productive rather than risking their safety. What a wonderful way to promote Safety as a Core Value!

杜邦公司禁止员工开车时使用手机。工业巨头杜邦公司禁止员工在驾驶时使用手机。这又是一个代价高昂的信号：这些员工，尤其是销售经理，本可以利用漫长的通勤时间用手机联系客户或同事。然而，公司宁愿让他们无所事事，也不愿让他们冒着安全风险。这真是推广“安全至上”理念的绝佳方式！

Culture is created by visible costly actions

文化是通过显而易见的、代价高昂的行动创造出来的。

Culture is not made of perks and terminology, but of time- and cost-expensive rituals which are conspicuously perceived as worth it.

文化不是由特权和术语构成的，而是由耗时耗力的仪式构成的，这些仪式被人们明显地认为是值得的。

What should be the uncompromisable Core Values of your company?

贵公司不可妥协的核心价值观是什么？

This is up to the Top Management to decide. Here are some options worth considering.

这最终由高层管理人员决定。以下是一些值得考虑的方案。

Safety is a great choice. Safe Operations are cost effective (less downtime, less employee turnover, less insurance fees, less legal costs, no need to substitute injured employees with less experienced ones, etc.). Moreover, in my experience, as soon as Safety is internalized in a company, improvements in related areas begin to appear: a safe warehouse is an orderly one, leading to improvements in logistics; a conscious worker who learnt to follow safety procedures also tends to follow other kind of procedures; the less injuries, the higher the morale; and so on.

安全是明智之选。安全运营能有效降低成本（减少停机时间、降低员工流动率、减少保险费用、减少法律成本、无需用经验不足的员工替代受伤员工等等）。此外，根据我的经验，一旦公司将安全理念内化，相关领域的改进就会开始显现：安全的仓库自然井然有序，从而提升物流效率；养成安全意识的员工也更倾向于遵守其他规章制度；工伤事故越少，员工士气越高；等等。

Ethics is another great choice for a Core Value. Being ethical has some upsides (candidates, suppliers and clients will trust you more, lowering your recruiting, sourcing and sales & marketing costs) but being unethical has huge costs. A single rogue employees can cost your company millions in litigation fees. An unethical decision might cost your company the right to operate.

道德是核心价值观的另一个绝佳选择。恪守道德有很多好处（候选人、供应商和客户会更加信任你，从而降低你的招聘、人才搜寻以及销售和市场营销成本），但不道德的行为则会带来巨大的代价。一个不守规矩的员工就可能让你的公司损失数百万美元的诉讼费用。一个不道德的决定甚至可能让你的公司失去经营权。

For companies with a heavy environmental impact, Sustainability is another great choice, for the same reasons as ethics.

对于对环境影响较大的公司而言，可持续性是另一个绝佳的选择，原因与道德相同。

Moreover, it is usually a good choice for a company to choose a Core Value which is part of their brand and of their competitive advantage. Some examples: customer experience, reliability, speed of response, quality, cost-savings, etc. It is important not to pick too many of these choices; ideally, only one. Core Values are never to be compromised. Therefore, they should be chosen so that they do not overlap. For example, it is possible to run great Operations without compromising on Safety and Ethics and Quality, but it is nearly impossible to run a company without compromising on Safety and Quality and Cost-Savings. It is likely that the latter two would somehow clash. You never want any employee of yours to have to decide which Core Value is more important, because doing so would open to the idea that Core Values are compromisable. They never are.

此外，对公司而言，选择一个能够体现其品牌和竞争优势的核心价值观通常是明智之举。例如：客户体验、可靠性、响应速度、质量、成本节约等等。重要的是不要选择太多核心价值观；理想情况下，最好只选择一个。核心价值观绝不能妥协。因此，选择核心价值观时应避免它们相互重叠。例如，在不牺牲安全、道德和质量的前提下，可以实现卓越的运营；但几乎不可能在不牺牲安全、质量和成本节约的前提下运营一家公司。后两者很可能存在某种冲突。您绝不希望任何员工被迫决定哪个核心价值观更重要，因为这样做会让他们误以为核心价值观是可以妥协的。而事实并非如此。

The need for uncompromisable priorities

需要制定不容妥协的优先事项

“Building a great company requires that great decisions are made at all levels; not just the top. As a company grows, the number of decisions and the number of people making them proliferates. What to do? […] the principles behind a decision are as important as the decision itself. I’ve observed that a sound decision is more likely when conversation and documentation is encouraged about the why and the what.” – Stripe’s Brie Wolfson

“打造一家伟大的公司需要各个层级做出明智的决策，而不仅仅是高层。随着公司的发展，决策的数量和决策者的人数都会激增。该怎么办呢？[…] 决策背后的原则与决策本身同样重要。我发现，如果鼓励就决策的‘为什么’和‘是什么’进行讨论和记录，就更有可能做出合理的决策。”——Stripe 的 Brie Wolfson

Hence the need for uncompromisable priorities: tools to enable employees at all levels to take decisions that are aligned with the organization’s long-term goals and to ensure that supervisors and managers evaluate the work of their subordinates in ways that grow the right principles in them.

因此，我们需要制定不容妥协的优先事项：提供工具，使各级员工能够做出与组织长期目标相一致的决策，并确保主管和经理以培养下属正确原则的方式评估其工作。

Whose role is it to demonstrate Uncompromisable Priorities?

谁应该负责展现不容妥协的优先事项？

Taking visible costly actions which demonstrate the importance of Core Values is part of the role of every manager and supervisor.

采取看得见摸得着的、代价高昂的行动来表明核心价值观的重要性，是每位经理和主管的职责之一。

Ideally, this should start from the CEO. The highest officer taking visible costly actions sets the example which demonstrates to the whole company that Core Values are to always be followed, even if costly.

理想情况下，这应该从首席执行官开始。最高领导人采取公开且代价高昂的行动，树立榜样，向全公司表明核心价值观必须始终贯彻执行，即使代价高昂。

Sometimes, in my consulting engagements, I do not get to work with the CEO. For example, if a company is American but I get hired to improve the Operational Excellence of the Italian manufacturing plant only. In such cases in which the scope of change is geographically limited, action should start from the highest resident manager at a given physical location. Most often, the Plant Manager.

有时，在我的咨询项目中，我可能无法直接与首席执行官合作。例如，如果一家公司是美国公司，但我受聘仅负责提升其意大利制造工厂的运营效率。在这种情况下，由于变革范围仅限于特定地域，行动应从该地域的最高负责人开始，通常是工厂经理。

If you read this book and are neither a CEO nor a Plant Manager, you can nevertheless begin demonstrating the Core Values of your company to your subordinates by taking visible costly actions, hoping to achieve a local change in how things are done here.

即使你读了这本书，但你既不是首席执行官也不是工厂经理，你仍然可以通过采取看得见的、代价高昂的行动，开始向你的下属展示公司的核心价值观，希望能够改变本地的做事方式。

This might or might not work, depending on your skills and on whether your own superiors are likely to personally interact with your subordinates, implicitly expecting them to compromise on Core Values to achieve short-term gains such as higher production this week and thus sabotaging your efforts to instill a strong respect for your company’s Core Values.

这或许有效，或许无效，取决于你的技能，以及你的上级是否可能亲自与你的下属互动，从而暗中期望他们为了获得短期利益（例如本周更高的产量）而在核心价值观上做出妥协，进而破坏你为灌输对公司核心价值观的强烈尊重所做的努力。

If this indeed happens, then you will have to get your superiors onboard. First, you can try explaining to them what you read in this chapter. If necessary, you can download a free excerpt of the relevant parts of this chapter at the following link www.luca-dellanna.com/third-principle and show it to them. If this is not enough, you will have to do the same with the highest resident manager at your location (for example, the Plant Manager).

如果这种情况真的发生，那么你需要向上级汇报。首先，你可以尝试向他们解释你在本章中读到的内容。如有必要，你可以从以下链接 www.luca-dellanna.com/third-principle 下载本章相关部分的免费摘录并展示给他们。如果这还不够，你还需要向你所在单位的最高级别管理人员（例如，工厂经理）进行同样的沟通。

In the unfortunate case that nothing of the above works, well, you will have to live with your superiors sabotaging your efforts. As bad as it seems, it doesn’t mean that it will not be possible to achieve Operational Excellence in your team. It just means that you will have to be extra consistent in explicitly requiring every subordinate of yours never to compromise on Core Values, even when it seems that a superior of yours would be okay with that.

如果以上方法都无效，那么你只能接受上级阻挠你努力的现实。虽然听起来很糟糕，但这并不意味着你的团队就无法实现卓越运营。这只是意味着你必须格外坚持，明确要求你的每一位下属都绝不能在核心价值观上妥协，即使你的上级似乎对此并不介意。

Managers spend most of their time at their office because it’s where the urgent tasks usually take place. However, ultimately, a company’s destiny is shaped by its employees’ performance at important tasks, not at urgent ones. And, regarding Operational Excellence, all important tasks take place in front of the workers, at their workplace. That’s why good managers spend a lot of their time there. In the second part of this book, Best Practices #1 and #2 will describe how managers should spend time at their subordinates’ workplace.

管理者大部分时间都待在办公室，因为紧急任务通常都在那里处理。然而，归根结底，决定公司命运的是员工在重要任务上的表现，而非紧急任务。就卓越运营而言，所有重要任务都发生在员工面前，在他们的工作场所。这就是为什么优秀的管理者会花大量时间在员工工作场所的原因。本书第二部分“最佳实践#1”和“最佳实践#2”将阐述管理者应该如何花时间在下属的工作场所。

CEOs (and Plant Managers) have a superpower: they are the most visible person in the company (or in the plant). Therefore, they are the ones whose example gets followed the most. By hiding in their office or in conference rooms, they waste their superpower.

首席执行官（以及工厂经理）拥有一项超能力：他们是公司（或工厂）中最受瞩目的人。因此，他们的榜样最容易被效仿。如果他们躲在办公室或会议室里，就浪费了这项超能力。

Summary

概括

Core Values are difficult to implement because they are costly. Core Values have short-term costs and long-term benefits. Even though the short-term costs are outweighed by the long-term benefits, employees must be confident that they won’t be punished in the time frame between the costs and the benefit materializing by a manager who would only consider the former.

核心价值观难以推行，因为成本较高。核心价值观既有短期成本，也有长期收益。尽管短期成本远不及长期收益，但员工必须确信，在成本显现到收益实现的这段时间内，他们不会因为管理者只关注短期收益而受到惩罚。

Core Values succeed when it is conspicuously admissible to pay their costs. Visible costly actions are the only way that a manager can pass both of the following messages: “there are long-term benefits that justify paying the short-term costs of practicing our Core Values” and “you will not be punished for incurring a short-term cost because you will always be able to point a finger at me and saying ‘I was doing like him’”.

核心价值观只有在人们可以公开承认并接受为此付出代价的情况下才能成功。只有通过显而易见的、代价高昂的行动，管理者才能传递以下两个信息：“长期的收益足以弥补践行核心价值观所带来的短期成本”以及“你不会因为承担短期成本而受到惩罚，因为你总可以指责我，说‘我当时也像他那样做了’”。

Cost as a signal. Words are cheap; actions are costly. Bad managers hide the costs of their actions; good managers show them, without transactionality.

成本是一种信号。言语廉价，行动代价高昂。糟糕的管理者会掩盖其行为的成本；优秀的管理者则会坦诚地展示这些成本，而不掺杂任何交易成分。

Conspicuous actions. Words can be misinterpreted (“I didn’t really mean this”), actions cannot. Because they are visible and material, they are conspicuous and likely to become norms.

引人注目的行动。言语容易被误解（“我并非真心如此”），而行动则不会。因为行动是可见的、物质性的，所以它们引人注目，并有可能成为规范。

Culture is created by visible costly actions, not by perks and terminology. Culture is made of time- and cost-expensive rituals which are conspicuously perceived as worthy.

文化是由看得见的、耗费成本的行动创造出来的，而不是由特权和术语创造出来的。文化是由耗时耗力、且被公认为有价值的仪式构成的。

# ↩

The 4th Principle
of Operational Excellence:

Good managers are obsessively consistent in holding their subordinates accountable

卓越运营的第四原则：优秀的管理者会始终如一地要求下属承担责任。

In this chapter, I will talk about reward and punishment, praise and reprimand: how to apply individual outcomes to the performance of your subordinates. When I mention rewards and punishments, I do not limit myself to raises, promotions, awards and disciplinary rulings. I include them, but also consider nice words, assignments to desirable or undesirable projects, letters of merit, opportunities for personal growth, and so on. Similarly, when I mention praises and reprimands, I do not only intend public exhibits of appreciation or disapproval, but also 1-on-1 conversations. Managers have a whole range of tools at their disposal to apply individual outcomes to the actions of their subordinates, and they should always choose the most appropriate one, as explained further below.

在本章中，我将探讨奖惩、表扬与批评：如何将个人绩效结果应用于下属的表现。我所说的奖惩，并非仅限于加薪、晋升、奖励和纪律处分。这些固然重要，但也包括赞扬、分配到理想或不理想的项目、表扬信、个人发展机会等等。同样，我所说的表扬与批评，不仅指公开的表扬或批评，也包括一对一的谈话。管理者拥有多种工具来将个人绩效结果应用于下属的行为，他们应该始终选择最合适的工具，下文将对此进行详细阐述。

Let me make clear one thing: applying individual outcomes to the performance of your subordinates against their objectives as consistently as possible is not about squeezing every single bit of productivity out of them. It is about treating them fairly and giving them the opportunity to work in a place where good work is useful and rewarded, where they will never have to feel bad because their manager didn’t notice their work or where a colleague who is slacking is treated just the same as them.

让我澄清一点：尽可能始终如一地将个人绩效与下属的目标挂钩，并非是为了榨干他们的每一分生产力，而是为了公平对待他们，让他们有机会在一个优秀的工作得到认可和奖励的环境中工作，让他们不必因为经理没有注意到他们的工作而感到难过，也不必担心偷懒的同事会受到同样的对待。

The objective of performance management is not compliance or short-term productivity. Performance management is about avoiding motivational losses, so that long-term productivity can become a worthy goal, for the employees too.

绩效管理的目标并非合规或短期生产力。绩效管理旨在避免员工积极性下降，从而使长期生产力成为员工自身也值得追求的目标。

The difference between squeezing every single bit of productivity and treating employees fairly is in setting humane objectives, which are ambitious yet attainable and do not require workers to go in self-destruction mode to complete them.

榨取每一分生产力与公平对待员工之间的区别在于设定人性化的目标，这些目标既要有挑战性，又要切实可行，并且不需要员工为了完成目标而自我毁灭。

This point will be further explored in the next chapter, “The Role of The Manager”.

这一点将在下一章“经理的角色”中进一步探讨。

Good managers are consistent

优秀的管理者始终如一。

Once a good manager communicates a standard to his team, he consistently measures the performance of its subordinates against that standard. He never applies double standards nor he makes exceptions. He understands that if he did, he would compromise the integrity of the standard, which would then become pointless, just like a single hole can compromise the usefulness of a whole boat.

一位优秀的管理者一旦向团队传达了标准，就会始终如一地以此标准衡量下属的绩效。他从不搞双重标准，也从不破例。他明白，如果他这么做，就会损害标准的完整性，使之失去意义，就像一个小洞就能让整艘船失去作用一样。

Bad managers are volatile in the application of the standards they set. They believe that workers respond to the average application of the standard. Instead, workers remember the extremes. If a bad manager holds accountable his subordinates only nine out of the ten times they failed the standard, they will remember that one time. They will remind him: “but boss, Jack did the same last month and you didn’t care”. Failing to hold workers accountable to the standard even just once opens the door to a hundred new transgressions.

糟糕的管理者在执行他们设定的标准时往往摇摆不定。他们认为员工会对标准的平均执行情况做出反应。然而，员工记住的往往是极端情况。如果一个糟糕的管理者只在下属十次未能达到标准的情况下追究九次的责任，那么员工就会记住那一次。他们会提醒管理者：“但是老板，杰克上个月也犯了同样的错误，你却不管。” 即使只一次没有追究员工的责任，也会为之后一百次新的违规行为打开方便之门。

Good managers are consistent in rewarding good work

优秀的管理者会始终如一地奖励优秀的工作。

Good managers try to catch their subordinates meeting the operational standards. When they see one of them doing a good job, they do not fail letting him know.

优秀的管理者会努力发现下属符合运营标准的情况。当他们看到有下属表现出色时，一定会及时表扬。

They do not need to praise their employees every day, but when they do, they make sure it is clear that they noticed it all. “Thank you, John, for doing such a good job, it’s been a few days you’ve been excellent!”.

他们不需要每天都表扬员工，但当他们表扬时，会确保员工清楚地感受到他们注意到了所有细节。“约翰，谢谢你做得这么好，你这几天表现都非常出色！”

Managers know that an employee who gets praised every single day might grow complacent. Bad managers react by praising inconsistently. This leads to confusion and frustration in their subordinates. “Doesn’t he care anymore?”, they might think, “is good work not important anymore?”

管理者都知道，如果员工每天都受到表扬，可能会变得自满。糟糕的管理者会采取不规律的表扬方式，这会导致下属感到困惑和沮丧。“他是不是已经不在乎了？”他们可能会想，“难道做好工作不再重要了吗？”

Instead, good managers fight complacency in well-performing subordinates by setting larger timeframes for evaluation (“So far I’ve measured your work daily but since you’ve been consistently excellent, I will measure it on a weekly basis now”) or by raising standards. The point is to never compromise on consistency, even when fighting complacency.

相反，优秀的管理者会通过延长评估周期（“之前我都是每天评估你的工作，但你一直表现出色，所以现在我会每周评估一次”）或提高标准来对抗表现优异的下属的自满情绪。关键在于，即使在对抗自满情绪时，也绝不能降低评估的一致性。

Once a standard for performance and a protocol for evaluation are set, subordinates must be hold accountable accordingly and consistently.

一旦制定了绩效标准和评估规程，就必须对下属进行相应的、一致的问责。

Consistent judgement is well perceived

一致的判断力会受到好评。
