Best Practice #3:

Weekly meetings

最佳实践#3：每周例会

To understand the impact Weekly Meetings and their role in shaping how things are done in the company, let’s see them from the point of view of its attendees.

为了了解每周例会的影响及其在塑造公司运作方式中的作用，让我们从与会者的角度来看待它们。

- Whether the meeting starts on time and what is the treatment reserved to the attendees who are late will inform the attendees upon whether time is considered an important resource in this organization.

会议是否准时开始，以及对迟到参会者的待遇如何，将让参会者了解时间是否被视为该组织的重要资源。

- The first item on the agenda will inform the attendees on what should be kept in mind at all times during the rest of the week.

- 议程上的第一项内容将告知与会者在本周剩余时间里应该始终牢记哪些事项。

- Whether the organization’s Core Values are mentioned during the Weekly Meeting will inform the attendees on whether they are still relevant.

- 组织的核心价值观是否在每周例会上被提及，可以让与会者了解这些价值观是否仍然适用。

- Which tradeoffs are explicitly mentioned by the manager during the decisions (or communication of previously taken decisions) will inform the attendees about the tradeoffs they can make during their day-to-day work. In particular, what will be mentioned as non-compromisable by the manager (and demonstrated through his choices) will be considered as non-compromisable by the attendees too.

- 管理者在决策过程中（或沟通先前已做出的决策时）明确提及的权衡取舍，将使与会者了解他们在日常工作中可以做出的权衡取舍。特别是，管理者明确指出（并通过其选择体现）哪些事项是不可妥协的，与会者也会将其视为不可妥协的。

- Conversely, if some Core Value or standard has been compromised during the Weekly Meeting (for example, a decision showing that the Core Value or standard is not absolute), the attendees will deduce that it can be compromised by them too. Not taking the time to talk about a Core Value during the meeting counts as having compromised it.

反之，如果在周会期间某些核心价值观或标准遭到破坏（例如，某项决定表明该核心价值观或标准并非绝对），与会者就会推断他们自己也可能违反这些价值观或标准。在会议上不花时间讨论某个核心价值观，也等同于违反了该价值观。

Weekly Meetings are opportunities for reinforcement

每周例会是强化沟通的机会。

The main function of Weekly Meetings is to reinforce the Core Values and Operational Culture of the organization.

每周例会的主要功能是强化组织的核心价值观和运营文化。

If something is talked about during the meeting, it probably is important. If something is not talked about, it probably isn’t. Or, at least, this is what the attendees will conclude.

如果会议期间讨论了某件事，那它很可能很重要。如果会议没有讨论某件事，那它很可能不重要。或者至少，与会者会得出这样的结论。

Good managers know that organizational culture is subject to erosion, and that repeating the importance of some metric or Core Value does not imply putting into discussion the intelligence of their subordinates. People need to be repeated the importance of whatever is not the default state, for they progressively revert back to it otherwise.

优秀的管理者深知组织文化会受到侵蚀，反复强调某些指标或核心价值观的重要性并不意味着要质疑下属的智力。人们需要不断被灌输非默认状态的重要性，否则他们就会逐渐回归默认状态。

If a decision is to be taken during the meeting, whatever criteria is compromised in eventual trade-offs, its attendees will feel like they are expected to take the same compromise during the following week. For example, if a decision is made in which the manager considers appropriate to sacrifice quality in order to rush and meet a deadline, then the attendees will internalize the message “it is okay to sacrifice quality in order to meet targets”, and they will compromise quality in their future decisions.

如果会议期间必须做出决定，无论最终权衡取舍的依据是什么，与会者都会觉得他们在接下来的一周里也需要做出同样的妥协。例如，如果经理认为为了赶工完成任务而牺牲质量是合适的，那么与会者就会内化“为了达成目标可以牺牲质量”的信息，并在未来的决策中做出类似的妥协。

Weekly Meetings are tools to disperse doubts

每周例会是消除疑虑的工具。

Even if the manager and the company have been embracing Core Values over and over, chances are that its employees will always doubt whether they can embody these values when doing so would mean compromising their short-term output, especially if in the past they have worked for a boss or company which never accepted short-term results to be compromised.

即使经理和公司一直奉行核心价值观，员工们也常常会怀疑，如果践行这些价值观意味着牺牲短期业绩，他们是否能够做到，尤其是在过去，他们曾为一位从不接受牺牲短期业绩的老板或公司工作过。

Good managers disperse those doubts by using Weekly Meetings to confirm, each week, that the company’s and the team’s Core Values are still the same, and that its employees are still expected never to compromise on them.

优秀的管理者会通过每周例会来消除这些疑虑，每周确认公司和团队的核心价值观仍然相同，并且仍然期望员工永远不要在这些价值观上妥协。

Good managers know that, no matter how many times Core Values have been mentioned during Weekly Meetings, if during a single Weekly Meeting they are not mentioned, doubt will rise again in its attendees. They might think: “Why did the manager didn’t mention the Core Values while he was telling us what we should do this week? Does it mean we can or should compromise the Core Values, if doing so would help to complete this week’s orders?”

优秀的管理者明白，无论在周会上核心价值观被提及多少次，如果某次周会上没有提及，与会者的疑虑就会再次产生。他们可能会想：“为什么经理在告诉我们这周应该做什么的时候没有提到核心价值观？这是否意味着，如果为了完成这周的任务，我们可以或应该违背核心价值观？”

Weekly Meetings are tools for conspicuousness

每周例会是提高知名度的工具

Weekly meetings are exceptional tools for communication because the manager has the opportunity to talk to his whole team at the same time. Each attendee will know that whatever expectation has been set during the meeting, all the other attendees heard it as well.

每周例会是绝佳的沟通工具，因为管理者有机会同时与全体团队成员交流。每位参会者都会知道，会议期间设定的任何目标，其他参会者也都听到了。

For example, if the manager said that John has to complete a key task this week and everyone else in the team is supposed to provide him with whatever he asks for, then John will feel more confident asking for help.

例如，如果经理说约翰本周必须完成一项关键任务，团队中的其他所有人应该为他提供他提出的任何要求，那么约翰就会更有信心去寻求帮助。

Conspicuousness – setting expectations in a way which is visible to everyone – is a great way to effectively influence the actions of others. Compare two workers: one who understand what has to be done and thinks his colleagues know it too, and one who understands what has to be done but thinks others do now know or do not embrace it. The former will be more likely to ask others for help and to hold them to the operational standards, regardless of whether his colleagues do know and embrace what has to be done.

明确传达——以人人都能看到的方式设定预期——是有效影响他人行为的绝佳途径。不妨比较两位员工：一位明白工作内容，并且认为同事们也明白；另一位明白工作内容，但认为同事们要么不明白，要么不接受。前者更有可能寻求他人帮助，并要求他们遵守操作规范，无论同事们是否明白或接受。

Good managers do not only communicate to get their subordinates to know and embrace what has to be done; they also communicate to make sure that every subordinate knows that everyone else in the team knows and embraces what has to be done. Weekly meetings are a great channel to do that.

优秀的管理者不仅通过沟通让下属了解并接受需要完成的任务，还会确保每位下属都明白团队中的其他成员也了解并接受这些任务。每周例会是实现这一目标的绝佳途径。

The focus of Weekly Meetings is communication. First and foremost, of operational culture; and secondly, of whatever the manager might need to communicate to his subordinates this week.

每周例会的重点是沟通。首先是沟通运营文化；其次是沟通经理本周需要向下属传达的任何信息。

Weekly Meetings are not about taking decisions

每周例会并非旨在做出决定。

In an ideal world, no major decision is taken during Weekly Meetings. Instead, they are taken into ad-hoc meetings, where only people whose input is required are invited.

理想情况下，每周例会上不会做出任何重大决定。相反，这些决定会在临时会议上讨论，只有那些需要参与讨论的人员才会被邀请参加。

However, for some teams, it makes sense to take decisions during Weekly Meetings, if most decisions require input from most team members and if it is logistically very advantageous to hold a single meeting (e.g., if the manager is located in a different office and only visits the team once per week).

然而，对于某些团队来说，如果大多数决策需要大多数团队成员的意见，并且在后勤方面举行一次会议非常有利（例如，如果经理在不同的办公室，每周只访问团队一次），那么在每周例会上做出决策是有意义的。

In this case, it is necessary that Weekly Meetings are divided into two phases, communication and decisions making, and that they take place in this order. Otherwise, decision making will take most of the time available and whatever message passed during the communication phase will be rushed and half-listened. Moreover, the order chosen sends an implicit message: whatever is talked about first is the real priority.

在这种情况下，每周例会必须分为沟通和决策两个阶段，并且必须按此顺序进行。否则，决策阶段将占用大部分时间，而沟通阶段传递的信息将显得仓促且缺乏深入理解。此外，选择的顺序也传递了一个隐含的信息：先讨论的内容才是真正的优先事项。

What happens during an effective weekly MEETING?

一次高效的每周例会期间会发生什么？

At the beginning

一开始

The manager thanks the attendees for having arrived in time, explaining it is a sign of respect for each other’s time and work. This action achieves multiple results: it makes people feel it was worth to arrive on time, it makes people want to arrive on time not to feel like an outsider who doesn’t respect the other members of the teams, and it clarifies that people are required to be on time not because the manager is rigid, but because he is respectful of his subordinates’ time.

经理感谢与会者准时到达，并解释说这是对彼此时间和工作的尊重。这一举动产生了多重效果：它让大家觉得准时到达是值得的；它让大家更愿意准时到达，以免觉得自己像个不尊重团队其他成员的局外人；它也明确表明，要求大家准时并非因为经理固执己见，而是因为他尊重下属的时间。

The agenda

议程

The first topic on the agenda should be an update related to one or more of the organization’s Core Values. For example, the manager could open the Weekly Meeting asking if anyone in the team has observed any unsafe behavior or condition (if safety is a Core Value), or if there has been any exceptionally satisfied customer (if customer satisfaction is a Core Value). I call this a “Core Value Review”.

议程上的第一个议题应该是与组织一项或多项核心价值观相关的最新进展。例如，经理可以在周会上询问团队成员是否有人观察到任何不安全行为或状况（如果安全是核心价值观之一），或者是否有任何客户特别满意（如果客户满意度是核心价值观之一）。我称之为“核心价值观回顾”。

Most of the meeting should be about communication, mostly from the manager to the team. The manager communicates whatever piece of information he might need to communicate to his team and uses any opportunity he can find to reinforce Core Values and standards.

会议的大部分时间应该用于沟通，主要是经理与团队之间的沟通。经理会传达他需要与团队沟通的所有信息，并利用一切机会强化核心价值观和标准。

If there is any decision to be made, these should happen after all communication has taken place.

如果需要做出任何决定，都应该在所有沟通进行完毕之后再做决定。

Handling discussions

处理讨论

It is possible that during the meeting, participants enter into heated discussions. This is okay as long as they are about issues and not about personalities. If any comment is made upon someone’s personality, the manager should immediately refocus it on someone’s behavior. For example, if an employee says that “John is lazy” because it takes multiple emails to get him to handle some request, the manager should reply along the lines of “You mean that John is slow to respond to internal requests?”. This achieves multiple results: it makes John more likely to comment constructively rather than defensively and it makes the feedback more precise, allowing to pinpoint what could be improved.

会议期间，与会者可能会展开激烈的讨论。只要讨论的是问题本身，而不是针对个人，这都是可以接受的。如果有人评论某人的性格，经理应该立即将话题引回其行为上。例如，如果一位员工说“约翰很懒”，因为需要发好几封邮件才能让他处理某个请求，经理应该这样回应：“你是说约翰对内部请求的反应很慢吗？”。这样做有多重好处：它能促使约翰提出建设性的意见，而不是进行辩解；同时，它还能使反馈更加精准，从而指出哪些方面需要改进。

If the manager is consistent in reminding his subordinates that “here, we only discuss issues, not personalities” every time that someone critiques a colleague as a whole (rather than critiquing one of his behaviors), then in a few weeks his subordinates should have learned to formulate their comments appropriately. It is extremely important that the manager does not let a personal comment pass even once without reminding the team that they are not allowed. If he does, all his good work will be destroyed and in no time the team will be back to commenting on each other with nonconstructive feedback.

如果经理每次在有人对同事进行整体评价（而非针对其具体行为）时，都坚持提醒下属“我们这里只讨论问题，不讨论人身攻击”，那么几周后，下属应该就能学会如何恰当地表达自己的意见。经理务必确保即使出现一次人身攻击，也要及时提醒团队成员这是不允许的。否则，他之前所做的一切努力都将付诸东流，团队很快就会恢复到互相进行毫无建设性批评的状态。

Handling decisions

处理决策

If, at any point during the meeting, two participants have a disagreement, the manager should let them work it out; possibly, outside of the meeting, in order not to waste everyone’s time.

如果在会议期间，两名参会人员发生分歧，经理应该让他们自行解决；最好在会外解决，以免浪费大家的时间。

If multiple participants have a prolonged disagreement on a decision which is of interest for the whole team, then the manager is supposed to step in and take the decision himself, as the final arbiter.

如果多个参与者对一个关乎整个团队利益的决定存在长期分歧，那么经理应该作为最终仲裁者介入并亲自做出决定。

Some managers might be hesitant to do it, not to displease anyone. They should remember that usually people do not get angry if someone took a decision they do not like, but they get angry if someone took a decision without hearing them out. As long as the manager collects the input of everyone who has an opinion and makes sure these people trust that they have been heard, then he can confidently take a decision and know that his subordinates will not be angry with him. They might have other emotions – such as frustration – but they won’t be personally angry with him.

有些管理者可能因为害怕得罪人而犹豫不决。他们应该记住，通常情况下，人们不会因为别人做了自己不喜欢的决定而生气，但如果决策者没有听取他们的意见就贸然做出决定，他们就会生气。只要管理者收集了所有有意见的人的想法，并确保他们相信自己的意见得到了重视，那么他就可以自信地做出决定，并且知道下属不会对他生气。他们可能会有其他情绪——比如沮丧——但他们不会对他个人生气。

While listening to the opinions of their team members, managers should be careful not to use their own assumptions to interpret the words they hear. In order to truly listen, one should listen not only to the interlocutor’s words, but most importantly to the interlocutor’s assumptions.

管理者在倾听团队成员的意见时，应注意避免将自身的假设强加于他们所听到的内容之上。真正做到倾听，不仅要关注对方的言语，更重要的是要关注对方的假设。

At the end: getting commitment

最后：获得承诺

Before the meeting ends, the manager has to make sure that every single participant will walk out the door committed to do whatever task has been assigned to him during the meeting, even if he did not agree about it.

在会议结束前，经理必须确保每一位参会者都能带着完成会议期间分配给他的任何任务的决心离开会议室，即使他并不同意这项任务。

Ideally, meetings should follow the “disagree and commit” model: during the meeting, every participant should voice its concerns about any of the topics discussed, and the manager should make sure he really listens to them, ensuring that each participant feels like his concerns have been understood. However, at the end of the meeting, every participant should be committed to support whatever has been decided, even if they still disagree with it.

理想情况下，会议应遵循“求同存异”模式：会议期间，每位参与者都应就讨论的任何议题表达自己的担忧，管理者应确保认真倾听，让每位参与者都感到自己的担忧得到了理解。然而，会议结束时，每位参与者都应承诺支持已做出的决定，即使他们仍然不同意该决定。

If the reader does not believe that the “disagree and commit” model can be applied in reality, it is because, in the meetings he has attended so far, the leader did not do a proper job in really listening to the concerns voiced. In general, subordinates are okay with their managers’ decision if they feel they have been listened to. Whenever a subordinate disagrees with his manager, it is because he does not really believe that the manager understood his concerns.

如果读者不相信“异议并承诺”模式在现实中可行，那是因为在他迄今为止参加的会议中，领导者并没有真正倾听下属提出的意见和建议。一般来说，如果下属感到自己的意见被认真听取，他们就会接受管理者的决定。每当下属与管理者意见相左时，往往是因为他们并不真正相信管理者理解了他们的顾虑。

It can take time to reall y listen to everyone’s concerns during a meeting. For this reason, it is recommended that only people whose presence is required to the meeting are invited (to keep the number of participants low) and that the manager talks before the meeting with the participants more likely to have concerns with the topics to be discussed, in order to have some time to properly listen to them.

在会议中真正倾听每个人的意见和建议可能需要一些时间。因此，建议只邀请必须出席会议的人员（以减少参会人数），并且管理者应在会前与那些可能对讨论主题有疑虑的参会者进行沟通，以便有时间认真倾听他们的意见。

It is critical that each participant in the meeting walks out the door with the commitment to communicate to their own subordinates what has been decided in the right way. A supervisor that walks out of the meeting and does not communicate a decision to his team because he does not agree with it can create problems down the road, when his team will somehow learn about the decision and complain they were kept in the dark.

至关重要的是，每位参会者都应承诺在会后以正确的方式将会议决定传达给各自的下属。如果一位主管因为不认同某个决定而离开会场，却不将其传达给团队，那么日后他的团队成员一旦得知该决定，就会抱怨自己被蒙在鼓里，从而引发问题。

Moreover, it is critical that an attendee that walks out the meeting communicates to his team the right things in the right way . A supervisor that says something along the lines of “Management decided X and we have to live with that” nourishes discontent in his team. Instead, supervisors should walk out of the meeting and communicate demonstrating commitment and supporting whatever has been decided. For example: “We decided X; this is not good for our team because of this and that concern, which I communicated during the meeting; nevertheless, for this and that reason we anyway decided that X would be in the best interests of everyone involved.”

此外，至关重要的是，与会者在会后要以恰当的方式向团队传达正确的信息。如果主管说类似“管理层决定了X，我们只能接受”这样的话，只会加剧团队的不满。相反，主管应该在会后与团队沟通，展现出对已决定的承诺和支持。例如：“我们决定了X；由于种种原因，这对我们的团队不利，我在会上已经提到过；但是，出于这些原因，我们最终还是决定X符合所有相关人员的最佳利益。”

One of the worst things that can happen during the meeting is that the attendees walk out passively committed. They didn’t disagree but didn’t agree either. As a result, they will carry out whatever action has been decided, but not committedly enough so that it results in a success. This is the worst outcome, because the fact that the action has been carried out but not committedly enough makes it hard for managers to hold their subordinates accountable. After all, they did what was asked of them, just not committedly enough. The line is blurry and the manager will have a hard time applying any individual outcome.

会议期间最糟糕的情况之一就是与会者带着消极态度离开。他们既没有反对也没有同意。结果，他们会执行已决定的行动，但不够投入，因此无法取得成功。这是最糟糕的结果，因为行动虽然执行了，但投入不足，使得管理者很难追究下属的责任。毕竟，他们完成了被要求做的事情，只是不够投入。界限模糊不清，管理者很难对任何个人绩效进行评估。

Passive commitment is equal to passive sabotage.

消极承诺等同于消极破坏。

To prevent this, great managers require active commitment from every single participant to their meetings. They do so by asking each of them “What will you do after this meeting to carry out the tasks which have been assigned to you?”. This is a great question, because answering it requires active commitment.

为了避免这种情况，优秀的管理者要求每位参会者都积极参与会议。他们会问每个人：“会后，你将如何完成分配给你的任务？” 这是一个很好的问题，因为回答这个问题需要积极的承诺。

Bad managers, instead, ask the following question: “Will you do this?”. This is a bad question, for answering it only requires passive commitment.

糟糕的管理者反而会问这样的问题：“你会做这件事吗？”。这是一个糟糕的问题，因为回答这个问题只需要被动的承诺。

Great managers demand conflict (by asking everyone to voice their concerns), then demand commitment (by asking everyone to promise what they will do) and finally demand results (by letting everyone know that they will be held accountable for achieving whatever objective the team decided). It is necessary that every participant voices his active commitment during the meeting. This way, everyone’s commitment is conspicuous. Each participant will feel more committed because he sees that everyone else is committed too. Conversely, if no one voices his active commitment during the meeting, each participant will be left wondering whether the others are actually committed.

优秀的管理者会先引发冲突（鼓励每个人表达自己的顾虑），然后要求承诺（要求每个人做出行动承诺），最后要求结果（让每个人明白，他们将对团队共同制定的目标的实现负责）。每位参与者都必须在会议期间积极表达自己的承诺。这样，每个人的承诺都会清晰可见。每位参与者都会因为看到其他人的投入而感到更有动力。反之，如果会议期间没有人积极表达承诺，每位参与者都会怀疑其他人是否真的投入其中。

Action points

行动要点

1) If you do not have regular Weekly Meetings with your subordinates, schedule one immediately.

1）如果你没有与下属定期举行每周例会，请立即安排一次。

2) Book a 15-minutes slot in your calendar immediately after each of the first three meetings, in which you will re-read this chapter and think on what went well and what can be improved.

2）在前三次会议结束后，立即在日历上预留 15 分钟的时间，重新阅读本章，思考哪些方面做得好，哪些方面可以改进。

# ↩

Best Practice #4:

One-on-one Meetings

最佳实践#4：一对一会议

“People who think one-on-one meetings are a bad idea have been victim of poorly-designed ones.” – Silicon Valley entrepreneur Ben Horowitz

“那些认为一对一会议不好的人，都是被设计糟糕的会议所害过。”——硅谷企业家本·霍洛维茨

One-on-one Meetings are a powerful tool to gather intelligence, reinforce priorities, assign accountability and review performance, all in an intimate setting.

一对一会议是一种强大的工具，可以在私密的环境中收集信息、强化优先事项、明确责任和审查绩效。

They are such a powerful tool that every manager should have at least one a week with every single one of his subordinates. For some industries such as software development, where subordinates benefit from long uninterrupted stretches of work, One-on-one Meetings can happen once every two weeks. Most industries instead benefit from weekly ones.

一对一会议是一种非常有效的工具，每位管理者都应该每周至少与每位下属进行一次。对于某些行业，例如软件开发，下属需要长时间不间断地工作，一对一会议可以每两周进行一次。但大多数行业每周进行一次会议效果更佳。

One-on-one Meetings should last at least half an hour, even if there is nothing to discuss, especially if there is nothing to discuss. This because there is never nothing to discuss. If it looks like there is nothing to discuss, it means that the manager should get better at asking questions, or better at handling silence.

一对一会议至少应持续半小时，即使没有什么可讨论的，尤其是没有什么可讨论的时候。因为实际上总会有可讨论的。如果看起来好像没什么可讨论的，那就意味着经理应该提高提问技巧，或者更好地应对沉默。

The most useful pieces of information come out after a long, awkward silence: often, that’s the moment when the subordinate will voice what he would not voice before – that’s usually the most important piece of information.

最有用的信息往往在漫长而尴尬的沉默之后才会出现：通常，在这个时候，下属会说出他以前不会说的话——而这通常是最重要的信息。

Conducting One-on-one Meetings

进行一对一会谈

The first time that the manager has a one-on-one meeting with a new subordinate, he should take some time to explain to him what the meeting is about. The manager should clarify that the One-on-one Meetings will happen on a weekly basis but they are not an instance of micromanagement. The opposite: ideally, they will be the only management-initiated contact during the week, with the exception of Weekly Team Meetings and Management Walks. Because the manager uses the weekly One-on-one Meeting to ensure that the subordinate is aligned with him on priorities, the manager can let him free to behave on his own during the rest of the week. Of course, there might be more contact between the manager and the subordinate, for example during project-specific meetings or subordinate-initiated conversations.

经理第一次与新下属进行一对一会谈时，应该花些时间向他解释会谈的目的。经理应该明确说明，一对一会谈每周举行一次，但这并非微观管理。恰恰相反，理想情况下，除了每周团队会议和管理巡视之外，一对一会谈应该是管理层每周唯一主动与下属进行的沟通。由于经理利用每周的一对一会谈来确保下属在工作重点上与自己保持一致，因此在一周的其他时间里，经理可以放手让下属自主工作。当然，经理和下属之间可能还有其他沟通，例如在项目相关的会议或下属主动发起的对话中。

The manager must then fulfill his promise that weekly One-on-one Meetings are not instances of micromanagement. The manager should use this time to assign objectives and review progress towards them while at the same time restraining himself from delving in the details of how the subordinate is fulfilling them – unless a how question comes from the subordinate himself or if the how was a recent problem or if the subordinate previously lied on progress or omitted relevant issues. Even then, the manager should give tips, hints and references and not detailed instructions list, unless necessary.

经理必须履行承诺，确保每周的一对一会议不是微观管理。经理应该利用这段时间设定目标并审查进展情况，同时克制自己不要过问下属如何完成目标的细节——除非是下属主动询问，或者问题出在最近，又或者下属之前隐瞒了进展情况或遗漏了相关问题。即便如此，经理也应该提供建议、提示和参考资料，而不是详细的指示清单，除非必要。

A good manager understands that weekly One-on-one Meetings are tools to gather intelligence and to reinforce priorities, Core Values and accountability; not a tool for micromanagement. As long as he leads the meeting with this in mind, there is no fixed structure for the One-on-ones.

一位优秀的管理者明白，每周的一对一会议是收集信息、强化工作重点、核心价值观和责任感的工具，而不是微观管理的工具。只要他始终牢记这一点，一对一会议就没有固定的模式。

The following is an example of structure for One-on-one Meetings.

以下是一对一会议的结构示例。

First, the manager thanks the subordinate for having come and asks him if there is any urgent issue to talk about. It is good to ask this question at the beginning of the meeting in order to clear any concern which might occupy the mental space of the participant. However, the manager must not allow such urgent issues to take more than half of the time dedicated to the one-on-one meeting. If any single issue is taking too long, an ad-hoc meeting can be scheduled in the next days.

首先，经理感谢下属的到来，并询问是否有紧急事项需要讨论。在会议开始时提出这个问题很好，以便消除参与者可能存在的任何疑虑。但是，经理不应让此类紧急事项占用超过一对一会议时间一半的时间。如果某个事项耗时过长，可以安排在接下来的几天内另行召开一次会议。

Second, the manager should ask the subordinate for some high-level progress update towards the tasks and projects he has been assigned. Such progress updates should not delve into detail; their purpose is to ascertain whether the subordinate is stuck or proceeding in the wrong direction.

其次，经理应该询问下属对其负责的任务和项目进行一些总体进展情况的汇报。这类进展汇报无需深入细节，其目的是了解下属是否遇到困难或方向错误。

During the progress updates, the manager should be firm in not letting any excuse pass. There is a difference between “this came up, so I am doing that to take care of it” (good) and “this came up, so the project will be delayed” (bad). The first progress update came with ownership of the problem and with a solution; the second one came with passiveness and a missed objective.

在进度汇报中，经理应该态度坚决，不容忍任何借口。 “出现了这个问题，所以我正在处理”（好的）和“出现了这个问题，所以项目将会延期”（坏的）之间是有区别的。第一次进度汇报体现了对问题的责任感和解决方案；第二次汇报则体现了消极态度和未能达成目标。

At all times, ensuring that the objectives will be fulfilled on schedule and on specification should be the priority of both the manager and the subordinate. If the subordinate is not fully focused on this, it is the manager’s job to repristinate such lack of alignment.

始终确保按时按质完成目标应该是管理者和下属的首要任务。如果下属未能全心投入，管理者有责任纠正这种目标不一致的情况。

During the progress updates, the manager should encourage the discovery of possible upcoming problems, by asking questions such as “If the project will fall behind schedule, what do you think would have been the cause?” (This is called a pre-mortem , as opposed to post-mortems, which are project reviews held after the project ended.)

在进度汇报过程中，经理应该鼓励大家发现可能出现的问题，例如提出“如果项目进度落后，你认为原因可能是什么？”之类的问题。（这被称为项目前分析，与项目后分析（即项目结束后进行的项目回顾）相对。）

Please note that this is a different question from “Why do you think the project might fall behind schedule?”. Presenting the subordinate with an imaginary already-happened delay will focus him on addressing problems he might be uncomfortable with; instead, asking the subordinate to imagine the possible causes of a generic delay which didn’t even materialize in his head will result in him not taking the possibility seriously or to restrict the range of problems he will consider to the ones he is comfortable addressing.

请注意，这与“你认为项目为什么可能会延期？”这个问题不同。向下属展示一个已经发生的假想延期案例，会让他专注于解决他可能不擅长处理的问题；相反，如果让他想象一个他自己都还没意识到的、普遍存在的延期可能的原因，他要么不会认真对待这种可能性，要么只会考虑那些他觉得可以轻松解决的问题。

A great follow-up question to increase the comprehensiveness of this analysis is: “so, if we do X and Y, there is no way that the project will be delayed?”

为了进一步完善分析，可以提出这样一个后续问题：“那么，如果我们做 X 和 Y，项目就不会延误吗？”

Once the progress update is completed, there should still be time remaining in the meeting. If not, either the manager planned too little time, or he let the discussion delve into unnecessary details.

进度汇报结束后，会议应该还有剩余时间。如果没有，要么是经理安排的时间太少，要么是他让讨论陷入了不必要的细节。

The rest of the meeting should be spent gathering intelligence from the subordinate. What problems might the team face in the near future? What personal issues are ruining the atmosphere? Does anyone need something from the manager? What is important and yet not talked about?

会议剩余时间应该用来收集下属的信息。团队近期可能会面临哪些问题？哪些个人问题正在破坏团队氛围？有人需要经理帮忙吗？还有哪些重要但尚未被提及的问题？

One of the most effective ways to gather such information is the manager reacting to a non-informational answer by shutting up and letting an awkward silence follow. The subordinate will likely feel compelled to fill the silence by saying something – often, what he would not have said otherwise. Of course, the manager has to ensure that the silence is not filled with small talk, with unnecessary details, or with the subordinate checking his mobile phone. If the manager decides to use this tactic, he should let the silence last for at least 30 seconds. If, after one minute, the subordinate did not speak yet, the manager might nudge him to do so by asking “Is there anything else I need to know about the team?”

收集此类信息最有效的方法之一是，当下属的回答缺乏实质性内容时，管理者保持沉默，让尴尬的沉默持续一段时间。下属很可能会感到有必要打破沉默，说些什么——通常是一些他原本不会说的话。当然，管理者必须确保沉默不会被闲聊、无关细节或下属查看手机等行为所打破。如果管理者决定采用这种策略，他应该让沉默至少持续30秒。如果一分钟后下属仍然没有说话，管理者可以尝试引导他开口，例如问：“关于团队，还有什么我需要了解的吗？”

If the manager is doing his job properly – gathering intelligence and reinforcing priorities rather than micromanaging – within a few weeks his subordinates will begin to look forward for the weekly One-on-one Meetings.

如果经理尽职尽责——收集情报、强化优先事项，而不是事无巨细地管理——那么几周之内，他的下属就会开始期待每周的一对一会议。

Good questions to ask

问得好的问题

In my experience, I found the following questions very effective in surfacing important information: “On what pending issues there is no progress?”, “What are you scared of?”, “What are we scared of, as a team or as a company?”, “What should be on my to-do list as a manager, but isn’t?”, “What should be on our to-do list as a company, but isn’t?”

根据我的经验，以下问题对于挖掘重要信息非常有效：“哪些悬而未决的问题没有进展？”、“你害怕什么？”、“作为一个团队或公司，我们害怕什么？”、“作为一名经理，我的待办事项清单上应该有哪些事情，但却没有？”、“作为一个公司，我们的待办事项清单上应该有哪些事情，但却没有？”

The point of such questions is not to collect advice, but in collecting intelligence.

这类问题的目的不是为了征求意见，而是为了收集情报。

In his book “The Hard Thing About Hard Things”, Silicon Valley executive Ben Horowitz proposes the following questions for One-on-one Meetings: “If we could improve in any way, how would we do it? What’s the number one problem with our organization? Why? What’s not fun about working here? Who is really kicking ass in the company? Whom do you admire? If you were me, what changes would you make? What don’t you like about the product? What’s the biggest opportunity that we’re missing out on? What are we not doing that we should be doing? Are you happy working here?”

在《创业维艰》一书中，硅谷高管本·霍洛维茨提出了以下一对一会议问题：“如果我们能在任何方面进行改进，我们会怎么做？我们组织面临的最大问题是什么？为什么？在这里工作有什么不好的地方？公司里谁最出色？你最欣赏谁？如果你是我，你会做出哪些改变？你对产品有什么不满？我们错失的最大机会是什么？我们应该做但没做的事情有哪些？你在这里工作开心吗？”

It is critical that, after the question is asked, the manager lets the subordinate answer it freely without interrupting or criticizing him. [14] Otherwise, that will be the last time he will collect useful intelligence from that subordinate.

至关重要的是，在提出问题后，经理应该让下属自由地回答，不要打断他或批评他。[14] 否则，这将是他最后一次从该下属那里收集有用的信息。

Action points

行动要点

1) Schedule a single 1-hour one-on-one meeting with all of your direct subordinates, this week or next week. Do not schedule multiple meetings with the same subordinate: at the end of the meeting, you will schedule the next one.

1）安排与所有直接下属进行一次1小时的单独会议，时间在本周或下周。不要与同一位下属安排多次会议：会议结束后，安排下一次会议。

2) After the first round of meetings is finished, read this chapter again to see what went well and what can be improved.

2）第一轮会议结束后，再读一遍本章，看看哪些方面做得好，哪些方面可以改进。

Best Practice #5:

Bright Spot Analysis

最佳实践#5：亮点分析

Bright Spot Analysis [15] is a powerful tool to find ideas to improve your Operations that work.

亮点分析[15]是一个强大的工具，可以找到改进运营的有效方法。

Bright Spot Analysis is a simple Best Practice consisting of 3 steps: looking at who’s the best performer in your area, understanding what he does differently, and figuring out whether it’s something which could be replicated by the rest of the employees.

亮点分析是一种简单的最佳实践，包括 3 个步骤：找出你所在领域表现最好的员工，了解他与众不同的地方，并弄清楚其他员工是否可以复制这种做法。

First step: identifying the Bring Spot

第一步：确定搬运点

Good managers routinely ask themselves one of the following questions:

优秀的管理者通常会问自己以下问题之一：

- “Who is the best performing person in my team?”

“我的团队里谁表现最好？”

- “Which is the best performing team in my unit?”

- “我们单位里表现最好的团队是哪个？”

- “Which is the best performing line in my factory?”

- “我厂里哪条生产线性能最好？”

- “Which is the best performing factory in my corporation?”

- “我公司旗下哪家工厂业绩最好？”

- “Which is the best performing company in my industry?”

- “我所在行业中表现最好的公司是哪家？”

The questions above might refer to overall performance or to performance at specific tasks (e.g.: “Who is the best person in my team at ensuring that projects are completed on time?”).

以上问题可能指的是整体表现，也可能指的是特定任务的表现（例如：“我的团队中谁最擅长确保项目按时完成？”）。

Second step: understanding the Bright Spot

第二步：理解亮点

Once the Bright Spot has been identified (an employee, a team, a line, a plant, or a competitor), the manager studies its behavior to understand if there is some trait, procedure or environmental condition which can be replicated to every area the manager controls.

一旦确定了亮点（一名员工、一个团队、一条生产线、一家工厂或竞争对手），管理者就会研究其行为，以了解是否存在某些特征、程序或环境条件可以复制到管理者控制的每个领域。

Good managers routinely ask themselves the following two questions:

优秀的管理者通常会问自己以下两个问题：

- Is there anything the Bright Spot does , which makes it exceptionally effective and which can be replicated elsewhere in the organization?

- “亮点”项目有哪些特别有效且可以在组织内其他地方复制的特点？

- Is there anything about the environment the Bright Spot operates in, which makes it exceptionally effective and which can be replicated elsewhere in the organization?

- Bright Spot 所处的环境中有哪些因素使其运作格外高效，而这些因素又可以在组织内的其他地方复制？

The latter question is often overlooked, as people tend to attribute exceptional behaviors to the personalities of the people involved. Instead, most behavior is determined by the environment in which people operate, including the incentive systems, management, and culture of their team and organization. These are largely replicable, though doing so will take time and effort.

后一个问题常常被忽略，因为人们倾向于将一些特殊行为归因于当事人的个性。然而，大多数行为是由人们所处的环境决定的，包括激励机制、管理方式以及团队和组织的文化。这些因素在很大程度上是可以复制的，尽管这需要时间和精力。

For example, once a team has been identified as the Bright Spot, the manager performing the analysis should examine what goals, what incentives, what managers and what culture the team has. Could any be the cause for their exceptional performance?

例如，一旦确定某个团队为“亮点团队”，进行分析的经理就应该考察该团队的目标、激励机制、管理人员以及团队文化。这些因素中是否有任何一项是其卓越表现的原因？

Third step: replicating the Bright Spot

第三步：复制亮点

Once the cause for the Bright Spot has been identified, the manager should attempt to replicate it across his organization, where appropriate.

一旦确定了亮点的原因，管理者就应该酌情尝试在组织内复制这一亮点。

For example, if the Bright Spot was a team following a procedure which no other team is following, and it makes sense for other teams to follow that procedure as well, then the manager should try to roll-out the procedure across the other teams.

例如，如果“亮点”团队遵循着其他团队都没有遵循的流程，并且其他团队也应该遵循该流程，那么经理就应该尝试将该流程推广到其他团队。

How to roll-out new procedures is described in the third part of this book.

本书第三部分介绍了如何推行新流程。

No cherry-picking

不进行选择性引用

Cherry-picking is the process of making one’s opinion of a person or of a group of people based on one single aspect of their performance, rather than on their overall one.

选择性评价是指根据一个人或一群人表现的某一方面，而不是根据他们的整体表现来形成对他们的看法。

For example, a rule for personal life is never to envy anyone you wouldn’t fully swap your life with. Envying someone for a single aspect of their life is pointless, for he probably made trade-offs which would not be good for you.

例如，个人生活中的一条原则是：永远不要羡慕你不想和他/她完全交换生活的人。羡慕别人生活的某一方面毫无意义，因为他/她很可能做出了对你不利的取舍。

Similarly, when performing Bright Spot Analysis, managers should be careful not to cherry-pick performance data points and instead focus on overall performance only. If a team or individual is the best one at a single aspect of their job (for example, production output) but has subpar overall performance (for example, they lack in quality of output), do you really want to replicate the procedures they use to produce at higher speeds?

同样，在进行亮点分析时，管理者应注意不要选择性地挑选绩效数据点，而应只关注整体绩效。如果一个团队或个人在工作的某个方面（例如，产量）表现最佳，但整体绩效却不尽如人意（例如，产品质量欠佳），你真的想复制他们提高生产速度的流程吗？

Side effects

副作用

Every intervention and every new practice or procedure comes with side-effects: the time, energy and money needed for its implementation and the eventual loss of morale and motivation incurring in everyone who gets told that “the way he was working before was wrong”.

每一次干预和每一项新做法或程序都会产生副作用：实施过程中需要时间、精力和金钱，以及最终导致每个人被告知“他以前的工作方式是错误的”而造成的士气和动力下降。

It is important that managers using Bright Spot Analysis (or Dark Spot Analysis) consider, before the third step, whether any new practice or procedure they would implement would bring enough benefits to compensate all its side effects – leaving some margin of safety for the possible presence of hidden ones.

使用亮点分析（或暗点分析）的管理者在进行第三步之前，必须考虑他们将要实施的任何新做法或程序是否会带来足够的收益来弥补其所有副作用——为可能存在的隐藏副作用留出一些安全余量。

Choose something that works, not something that makes sense

选择有效的方法，而不是合乎逻辑的方法。

When picking a procedure or a factor to replicate, it is extremely important that you limit yourself to things that proved to work, without including ideas that make sense but have not been proven to work in practice.

在选择要复制的程序或因素时，务必将自己限制在已被证明有效的方法或因素范围内，而不要包括那些听起来有道理但尚未在实践中证明有效的想法。

Copying things that already work somewhere else is called bottom-up adaptation and has a high success rate. Implementing ideas that make sense but have not been tested yet is called top-down adaptation and has an abysmally low success rate.

照搬其他地方行之有效的方法称为自下而上的适应，成功率很高。而实施那些合情合理但未经检验的想法称为自上而下的适应，成功率极低。

Two reasons: first, usually ideas have to be refined times and times over; copying something that works means copying something which has already been refined, whereas copying something which has not been tested yet will likely result in the revelation that it still has to be refined before working.

原因有二：首先，想法通常需要反复完善；复制行之有效的东西意味着复制已经完善的东西，而复制未经测试的东西很可能会导致人们发现它还需要完善才能奏效。

Second: most initiatives and interventions have hidden side effects, which are often bigger than the evident benefits. If you copy something which works and has been in use for a long time, most of its side effects will have been revealed already, whereas if you attempt to implement something which has not been tested yet, you might have a bad surprise once side-effects begin to emerge.

第二：大多数举措和干预措施都存在隐性副作用，而且这些副作用往往比显而易见的益处更大。如果你照搬一个行之有效且长期使用的方法，那么它的大部分副作用可能早已显现；而如果你试图实施一个未经检验的方法，一旦副作用开始显现，你可能会措手不及。

# ↩


Dark Spots

黑斑

The sister Best Practice of Bright Spot Analysis is Dark Spot Analysis.

与亮点分析类似的最佳实践是暗点分析。

It works similarly:

其工作原理类似：

1) First, the manager looks for an individual / team / line under his management which is particularly underperforming.

1）首先，经理会寻找他管理下表现特别差的个人/团队/部门。

2) Then, the manager tries to look for the root cause for the underperformance and attempts to address it.

2）然后，经理会尝试找出业绩不佳的根本原因，并努力解决它。

3) Finally, in case of success during the second step, the manager tries to replicate the learnings to ensure that never again will any individual or team under his management underperform for the same reason.

3）最后，如果第二步取得成功，经理会尝试复制这些经验，以确保他管理的任何个人或团队不会再因为同样的原因而表现不佳。

4) Eventually, the learnings of step three can also be distributed across the company, if appropriate.

4）最终，如果合适，第三步中学到的经验也可以在公司内部推广。

Action points

行动要点

1) Schedule in your calendar a 30-minutes slot in which you will perform the Bright Spot Analysis. (This is a low-priority task; the Action Points of the previous Best Practices have a higher priority.)

1）请在日历中安排 30 分钟的时间段进行亮点分析。（这是一项优先级较低的任务；之前最佳实践中的行动要点优先级更高。）

2) When the time for the Bright Spot Analysis comes, re-read this chapter and then try to apply its contents.

2）当需要进行亮点分析时，请重新阅读本章，然后尝试应用本章内容。

3) Schedule in your calendar a follow-up 30-minutes session in which you will perform another Bright Spot Analysis.

3）在你的日历中安排一个后续的 30 分钟会议，你将在其中进行另一次亮点分析。

Best Practice #6:
最佳实践#6：

Standard Operating Procedures
标准操作程序

“When companies choose chat first, they revert into an almost oral tradition.” – David H. Hansson (DHH)

“当公司优先选择聊天工具时，他们实际上又回到了口头沟通的传统模式。”——大卫·H·汉森（DHH）

In all kind of organizations, writing down procedures, rules, standards and Core Values is important for three reasons. First, it makes them permanently available. Anyone can check them at any time and know how he is supposed to act. Second, it makes them conspicuous. If you act according to written tradition, you don’t have to think about justifying your actions to others (or risking being wrong). Third, it allows for fair application of individual outcomes.

在各种组织中，将流程、规则、标准和核心价值观书面化至关重要，原因有三。首先，它使这些内容永久可用。任何人都可以随时查阅，了解自己的行为准则。其次，它使这些内容更加醒目。如果按照书面惯例行事，就无需考虑向他人解释自己的行为（或承担犯错的风险）。第三，它有助于公平地评估个人绩效。

A company that only relies on oral tradition will find itself with many problems. Between others, employees not knowing what to do, receiving contrasting input about which tradeoff to make, and employees being able to justify selfish behavior saying, “what he said wasn’t clear” or “but I was told otherwise.”

一家只依赖口头传统的公司会发现自己面临诸多问题。其中包括员工不知道该做什么，对如何权衡利弊会收到相互矛盾的说法，以及员工会以“他说的不清楚”或“但我听到的说法不一样”为由，为自己的自私行为辩解。

In companies, a big part of written tradition is constituted by Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs).

在公司里，书面传统很大一部分是由标准操作程序（SOP）构成的。

SOPs are sheets detailing the most critical procedures employees might encounter in their work, regularly reviewed and stored somewhere easy to be accessed by anyone who might need them.

标准操作程序 (SOP) 是详细说明员工在工作中可能遇到的最关键程序的表格，定期审查并存储在任何需要的人都容易访问的地方。

Standard Operating Procedures fulfill three purposes. First, they ensure that any worker who might need to perform a business-critical task has a reference to use. Second, they ensure that if anything goes wrong, there is an objective reference to use to verify whether anyone did anything wrong. Third, they ensure that when a change is applied to the current operations (for example, a new piece of hardware is added or a procedure is changed), it is possible to check all other procedures for possible collateral effects.

标准操作规程 (SOP) 具有三个目的。首先，它们确保任何可能需要执行关键业务任务的员工都有可供参考的准则。其次，它们确保一旦出现任何问题，都有客观的参考依据来核实是否存在操作失误。第三，它们确保当对现有操作进行更改时（例如，添加新的硬件或更改某个流程），可以检查所有其他流程是否存在潜在的附带影响。

The structure of SOPs

标准操作程序的结构

Standard Operating Procedures are bundles of sheets of paper (or their digital equivalent) which consist of at least the following written elements.

标准操作规程是一叠纸质文件（或其电子版本），其中至少包含以下书面要素。

A title identifying the procedure.

用于识别手术过程的标题。

A unique identifier used to reference the procedure and to find it more easily, usually a number or a string of letter and numbers, sometimes containing punctuation such as dots, slashes and dashes. For example, “procedure 3-54”.

用于引用流程并方便查找的唯一标识符，通常是一个数字或字母和数字的组合，有时包含标点符号，例如点、斜杠和破折号。例如，“流程 3-54”。

A list of steps which constitute the instructions that must be followed by the workers performing the procedure. They usually include all necessary information and requirements, so that any worker should at least know whether he can safely perform the operation.

操作步骤清单，列出了执行该操作的工人必须遵循的步骤。清单通常包含所有必要的信息和要求，以便任何工人至少能够知道自己是否可以安全地执行该操作。

A date , which identifies the last time that the procedure has been reviewed or modified.

一个日期，用于标识该程序上次被审查或修改的时间。

An expiration date , which identifies the time at which the procedure will have to be reviewed. This is critical because the environment in which the procedure is to be used constantly changes. For example, a new machine might have been installed, a new supply might have been procured, or an experienced employee might have been fired. In all these cases, the procedure might have become obsolete and might require changes. Setting an expiration date (usually 6 or 12 months after the last review or edit) ensures that the procedure is constantly checked against the need for changes.

有效期是指流程需要进行审查的时间点。这一点至关重要，因为流程的使用环境会不断变化。例如，可能安装了新机器、采购了新的耗材，或者经验丰富的员工被解雇。在所有这些情况下，流程都可能过时，需要进行修改。设定有效期（通常在上次审查或编辑后的 6 个月或 12 个月）可以确保流程始终受到检查，以确定是否需要进行修改。

A purpose , to be used during the procedure review. If the purpose of the procedure is not clear, “zombie procedures” might keep existing long after their need was gone. A purpose ensures that whoever is tasked with using or reviewing the procedure can judge its obsoleteness.

目的，将在流程审查过程中使用。如果流程的目的不明确，“僵尸流程”可能会在不再需要后继续存在很长时间。明确目的可以确保负责使用或审查流程的人员能够判断其是否过时。

A single role responsible for writing and reviewing the procedure , to ensure that a competent person will be reviewing the procedure when needed.

设立一个专门负责编写和审核流程的职位，以确保在需要时由合格人员审核流程。

A signature of the person who wrote the procedure or last reviewed it, to ensure that the point above was met.

编写该程序或最后审核该程序的人员的签名，以确保满足上述要求。

A list of roles which should be informed if the procedure is to be modified, if any. Whereas each procedure should have a single person responsible for reviewing and editing it, it might be the case that other people might have to be notified of changes, if any. This because procedures do not exist in a vacuum but live in a complex environment. It is unlikely that a single person is aware of all the variables involved. For example, a procedure involving how to operate a given machine might require the team responsible for its maintenance to vet any change to it.

如果流程需要修改，则需要通知以下人员：虽然每个流程都应指定专人负责审核和编辑，但实际操作中，如有任何变更，可能还需要通知其他人员。这是因为流程并非孤立存在，而是处于复杂的环境中。一个人不太可能了解所有相关变量。例如，涉及特定机器操作的流程，任何变更都可能需要负责维护该机器的团队进行审核。

Management of change

变革管理

In companies which are far from achieving Operational Excellence, procedures only contain a title, a list of steps and perhaps a signature. They neglect Management of Change (MoC): the checks which are needed to ensure that whenever something changes in the environment in which the procedure takes place, the procedure is adapted as well; and to ensure that whenever the procedure is about to be changed, it has been checked whether any change in its environment is needed.

在那些距离卓越运营还很远的公司里，流程通常只有标题、步骤列表，或许还有签名。它们忽略了变更管理（MoC）：变更管理是指在流程所处的环境发生变化时，确保流程本身也随之调整；以及在流程即将变更时，确保已检查其环境是否需要进行相应调整。

Therefore, all SOPs should contain the additional components listed above. Otherwise, they will work until they inevitably don’t.

因此，所有标准操作规程都应包含上述附加内容。否则，它们虽然能用，但终究会失效。

Contractors

承包商

Written SOPs are especially useful to manage contractors. Make sure you include them in the list of procedures to write, and involve them while writing them.

书面标准操作程序 (SOP) 对管理承包商尤其有用。务必将承包商纳入待编写的程序清单中，并在编写过程中让他们参与其中。

The storage of SOPs

标准操作规程的存储

Standard Operating Procedures must be stored somewhere easily accessible by anyone required to use them. Usually, this is a binder with transparent sleeves, each containing a single SOP. Apart from the smallest premises, multiple copies of such binder exist, to ensure that workers do not have to walk miles to check the procedures they need. If multiple copies of the binder exist, some system has to be in place to ensure that whenever a SOP is changed, the change is replicated to all binders.

标准操作规程必须存放在方便所有需要使用人员取阅的地方。通常情况下，这种存放方式是在一个带有透明封套的活页夹中，每个封套内装一份标准操作规程。除了极少数小型场所外，通常会准备多份这样的活页夹，以确保员工无需长途跋涉即可查阅所需的规程。如果存在多份活页夹，则必须建立相应的系统，确保每当标准操作规程发生变更时，所有活页夹中的规程都会自动更新。

SOPs are often maintained also as a digital file, to facilitate edits and re-prints, but they should be maintained in paper version too, unless each worker of the company always has a device with him from which he can access the latest version of the procedure. Paper might seem inefficient, but it has advantages and it is often more likely to be accessed; think about the fact that most books sold are still in paper form, even now that eBooks are available to everyone.

标准操作程序 (SOP) 通常也会以电子文件的形式保存，以便于编辑和重印，但除非公司每位员工都随身携带可以访问最新版本程序的设备，否则也应该保留纸质版本。纸质文件看似效率不高，但它也有其优势，而且更容易查阅；想想看，即使现在电子书唾手可得，市面上销售的大部分书籍仍然是纸质版。

Job descriptions

职位描述

Job descriptions are a particular case of SOP. In a broad sense, the requirements for a position and its task describe part of the procedures that Human Resources and managers will have to follow to hire or promote someone to that position.

职位描述是标准操作程序 (SOP) 的一个特例。广义上讲，职位要求及其任务描述了人力资源部门和管理人员在招聘或晋升该职位人员时必须遵循的部分程序。

For example, if a position requires some specific piece of knowledge, a job description that clarifies this need will be useful to ensure that any candidate for that position is screened for that knowledge and that any person promoted to that position is trained on that knowledge.

例如，如果某个职位需要一些特定的知识，那么一份明确说明这一需求的职位描述将有助于确保该职位的任何候选人都接受过相关知识的筛选，并且任何晋升到该职位的人都接受过相关知识的培训。

Job descriptions are the task of the manager who manages the role being described. In large organizations, HR should support with the task, but the manager’s input is required.

职位描述是管理该职位的经理的职责。在大型组织中，人力资源部门应协助完成这项工作，但经理的意见也必不可少。

Every single position in the company should have a job description. This should be a written document fulfilling all requirements for Standard Operating Procedure (such as an expiration date, a signature, a purpose, etc.).

公司的每个职位都应该有职位描述。这份文件应该是书面的，符合标准操作程序的所有要求（例如有效期、签名、用途等）。

In particular, job descriptions should contain both the know-how requirements for the position and the list of tasks the position is responsible for.

具体来说，职位描述应该包含该职位所需的技能要求以及该职位负责的任务清单。

Some of the best managers I know prepare documents with a list of behaviors expected from the position (and of behaviors which are expected not to take place), and circulate that document internally, privately (with those in that position) or publicly (by hanging that document somewhere visible in the office or in the plant).

我认识的一些最优秀的经理会准备一份文件，列出该职位应有的行为（以及不应发生的行为），并将该文件在内部私下（与该职位的人员）或公开（将该文件张贴在办公室或工厂的显眼位置）传阅。

Meta-procedures

元程序

There should also be procedures regarding procedures: a procedure to create SOPs, one to update them, and one to review them, at least.

此外，还应该有关于程序的程序：至少应该有一个制定标准操作规程的程序，一个更新标准操作规程的程序，以及一个审查标准操作规程的程序。

Action points

行动要点

If you have the authority to write procedures, do the following.

如果您有权编写程序，请执行以下操作。

1) Write the three meta-procedures described just above, according to the content of this chapter. Make sure that in the procedure for creating SOPs, you clarify which areas of competence should contain procedures and who is responsible for writing each.

1）根据本章内容，编写上文所述的三个元程序。确保在制定标准操作规程 (SOP) 的过程中，明确哪些能力领域应包含程序，以及每个程序的编写负责人。

2) Schedule a 30-minutes meeting with each of the people responsible for writing procedures and go through the contents of this chapter with them, assigning them the objective of writing the procedures for which they are responsible within a reasonable time frame. Most probably, your company already has some written SOPs. In this case, make sure that both the following are done: old SOPs are checked and rewritten if necessary, and the need for additional new SOPs is evaluated.

2) 安排与每位负责编写流程的人员进行30分钟的会议，与他们一起学习本章内容，并设定目标，要求他们在合理的时间范围内完成各自负责的流程编写工作。贵公司很可能已经有一些书面的标准操作程序 (SOP)。在这种情况下，请确保完成以下两项工作：检查现有的SOP，并在必要时进行修订；评估是否需要制定新的SOP。

3) Schedule some follow-up meeting to check the progress against writing procedures.

3）安排一些后续会议，检查编写程序的进展情况。

4) Once the procedures are written, make sure that the appropriate people review them (HSE, Line Supervisors, etc. – anyone directly involved in using them or in managing people using them should be informed and be given the chance to review them, with the addition of relevant technical specialists, if any).

4) 一旦程序编写完成，确保相关人员对其进行审查（健康、安全与环境 (HSE)、生产线主管等——任何直接参与使用程序或管理使用程序人员的人员都应被告知并有机会对其进行审查，如有相关技术专家，也应加入）。

5) Delegate the task of printing and distributing the SOPs.

5）委派打印和分发标准操作规程的任务。

6) Make sure that each Manager and Supervisor is assigned the task of going through each procedure with each of his subordinates who would be affected by them.

6）确保每个经理和主管都负责向其下属讲解每个流程，这些流程会受到这些流程的影响。

The topic of SOPs is highly complex and the action list above is likely non-exhaustive. Please use your best judgement, follow the Four Principles of Operational Excellence and contact an industry expert if appropriate.

标准操作规程 (SOP) 是一个非常复杂的主题，以上列出的行动清单可能并不详尽。请运用您的最佳判断，遵循卓越运营的四大原则，并在必要时联系行业专家。

This is likely the most difficult and lengthy Best Practice to implement – and yet, a very important one.

这可能是实施起来最困难、耗时最长的最佳实践——然而，也是非常重要的最佳实践。

# ↩

Best Practice #7:
最佳实践#7：

Surfacing Problems
发现问题

Just in time

恰逢其时

In business school, many would describe Just In Time as the concept of having components arriving directly at the production line the moment they are needed, in order to reduce the financial costs and handling time associated with having them delivered to a warehouse first.

在商学院里，许多人会将准时生产描述为这样一种概念：让零部件在需要时直接到达生产线，从而减少因先将零部件运送到仓库而产生的财务成本和处理时间。

This is only partially correct.

这种说法只部分正确。

While it is true that having components handled twice (once to go from the delivery truck to the warehouse, and once from the warehouse to the production line) and renting space just to have components sit there are two unnecessary costs which do not provide any value to the customer, that is not the most important advantage of Just In Time.

虽然零部件需要两次搬运（一次是从送货卡车到仓库，一次是从仓库到生产线），以及仅仅为了让零部件存放在那里而租用空间，这两项都是不必要的成本，并没有为客户带来任何价值，但这并不是准时生产最重要的优势。

Warehouses are buffers, and buffers protect against supply volatility. For example, if you have a warehouse with enough components, you will be able to continue production even if the truck delivering components to your production line is late.

仓库是缓冲地带，缓冲地带可以抵御供应波动。例如，如果您的仓库储备了足够的零部件，即使运送零部件到生产线的卡车晚点，您也能保证生产不中断。

A company with a buffer (such as a warehouse with enough components to last a week) will not consider a truck being one day late as a problem. This means that no one in the company will take any steps to ensure that the truck comes on time. If one day, eventually, the truck is one week late, then production will have to stop and the company will be unprepared on how to react.

拥有缓冲库存（例如，仓库里备有足够一周使用的零部件）的公司不会把货车晚点一天视为问题。这意味着公司里没有人会采取任何措施来确保货车准时到达。如果最终货车晚点一周，那么生产就不得不停止，而公司将不知所措，不知道该如何应对。

Conversely, a company without a buffer (no large warehouse for components) will consider even a one-hour delay of the delivery truck as a problem and will take immediate action to ensure that the truck comes on time, every time. As a consequence, its operations will become much more robust and efficient.

相反，一家没有缓冲库存（没有大型零部件仓库）的公司，即使送货卡车晚点一小时也会被视为问题，并会立即采取措施确保卡车每次都能准时到达。因此，其运营将更加稳健高效。

Buffers prevent problems from surfacing, until it’s too late. Just In Time (and other techniques which reduce buffers) allow problems to surface so that they can be solved before it’s too late.

缓冲机制会阻止问题显现，直到为时已晚。而即时交付（以及其他减少缓冲机制的技术）则允许问题显现，以便在为时过晚之前得到解决。

Just In Time is about removing buffers to surface problems.

即时生产是指消除缓冲，尽快发现问题。

The red rope

红绳

Toyota production lines used to have a red rope hanging from the roof (“Andon Cord”). Workers of any level were instructed to pull on the rope every time they would notice a problem in the production process, such as a defect. Pulling on the rope would immediately stop production.

丰田的生产线过去会在屋顶悬挂一根红绳（“安灯绳”）。所有级别的工人都被告知，一旦发现生产过程中出现问题，例如产品缺陷，就必须拉动这根绳子。拉动绳子会立即停止生产。

Everyone who ever worked in a plant knows how costly it is to stop production. And in Toyota, that would happen every time a worker – any worker! – would notice a problem and pull the red rope. What a way to ensure that problems are solved immediately rather than being lost in a suggestion form!

凡是在工厂工作过的人都知道停产的代价有多高。而在丰田，只要任何一个工人——任何一个工人！——发现问题并拉动红绳，就会立即停产。这真是确保问题能够立即得到解决，而不是被束之高阁，最终不了了之！

Not only the red rope is a brilliant implementation of the 3rd Principle of Operational Excellence (demonstrate priorities by taking costly actions), but it is also a wonderful way to align incentives towards solving problems now .

红绳不仅是对卓越运营第三原则（通过采取代价高昂的行动来表明优先事项）的出色实践，而且也是将激励机制调整为立即解决问题的绝佳方式。

Incentives to solve problems

解决问题的激励措施

In Toyota, reportedly, managers have personal objectives on their own individual results, on their division’s and on development of their subordinates.

据报道，丰田的经理们对自己的个人业绩、部门业绩以及下属的发展都有个人目标。

A manager who fulfills his own objectives but whose subordinates do not grow is considered a bad manager, and his career will not progress.

如果一位经理实现了自己的目标，但下属却没有成长，那么他就会被认为是一位糟糕的经理，他的职业生涯也不会有进步。

This is a costly signal (it might lead to managers quitting the company as they look for other career opportunities) which demonstrates a priority of the organization: growing its employees. The message is simple: unless you make the development of your subordinates one of your priorities, you will not have a career in this company.

这是一个代价高昂的信号（可能会导致管理人员离职，另谋高就），但也表明了公司的一项优先事项：员工发展。信息很简单：除非你把下属的培养作为你的工作重点之一，否则你将无法在这家公司获得职业发展。

Problem solving

问题解决

The two examples above, Just in Time and the Red Rope, are good introductions for the topic of this chapter: how to implement problem solving techniques and how to implement incentives to make sure that those techniques are used proactively (before serious problems take place) rather than reactively.

以上两个例子，即“及时”和“红绳”，很好地引出了本章的主题：如何实施问题解决技巧以及如何实施激励措施，以确保这些技巧得到积极主动的使用（在严重问题发生之前），而不是被动地使用。

Escalating problems to upper management or to experts is an extremely slow approach, for two reasons. First, it takes time for an escalated issue to reach the person who will solve it, and for her to act. And second, it takes time to even begin the escalation, as line workers are wary of being seen “creating problems” and would often wait a few hours, days or weeks before getting themselves to escalating the issue.

将问题上报给高层管理人员或专家是一种极其缓慢的方法，原因有二。首先，问题需要时间才能传达给最终解决问题的人，并由其采取行动。其次，即使只是启动上报程序也需要时间，因为一线员工担心被视为“制造问题”，往往会等待数小时、数天甚至数周才会主动上报问题。

Of course, this is not good. Problems grow the size they need in order to be acknowledged. An organization that is slow in acknowledging problems will find itself with big problems.

当然，这并非好事。问题只有发展到一定程度才会被人重视。一个组织如果迟迟不肯正视问题，最终只会陷入更大的麻烦。

The alternative is to set in place systems to tackle problems immediately as their first symptoms appear, or even before that.

另一种方法是建立相应的系统，以便在问题出现最初症状时，甚至在此之前，立即解决问题。

There are two complementary approaches for doing so: decentralized problem solving and measuring leading indicators.

实现这一目标有两种互补的方法：分散式问题解决和衡量领先指标。

Decentralized problem solving

去中心化问题解决

Decentralized problem solving consists in deploying tools and expectations to allow line workers to fulfill the principle that problems should be solved at the lowest competent level.

分散式问题解决是指运用各种工具和方法，让一线员工能够遵循“问题应该在最低能力层级解决”的原则。

Tools

工具

There is an abundance of problem-solving tools and techniques to be used by line workers and line management to solve operational problems.

一线员工和一线管理人员可以使用大量的解决问题的工具和技巧来解决运营问题。

The most famous one is perhaps Six Sigma. Whereas Six Sigma cannot be used for all problems – most of its tools only apply to contexts whose characteristic distributions are Gaussian [16] – it is useful to provide line workers and line management with tools to solve problems by themselves and in a structured way.

其中最著名的或许是六西格玛。虽然六西格玛不能用于所有问题——它的大多数工具只适用于特征分布为高斯分布的情况[16]——但它对于为一线员工和一线管理人员提供以结构化方式自行解决问题的工具是有用的。

Another well-known tool is the “5 Whys”, in which the worker interrogates himself on the cause of a defect for a few times, typically five, with each answer becoming the basis for the next question. (For example: “Why did my teammate injure himself?” “Because he tripped on a cable.” “Why was the cable on the floor?” “Because it connected a tool to the plug on the other side of the room.” “Why wasn’t the tool plugged to the closest side of the room?” “Because there was no plug there.” The solution: to ask an electrician to install a plug on that wall). In my experience, the right number of iterations to stop at is not 5, nor any other precise number. It is when taking care of that problem would ensure that no similar incident will ever happen again.

另一个广为人知的工具是“5个为什么”，即员工反复追问自己缺陷的原因，通常是五次，每次的答案都成为下一个问题的基础。（例如：“我的同事为什么会受伤？”“因为他被电线绊倒了。”“为什么电线会在地上？”“因为它连接着房间另一侧的工具插座。”“为什么工具没有插在离房间最近的插座上？”“因为那里没有插座。”解决方案：请电工在那面墙上安装一个插座）。根据我的经验，合适的迭代次数并非5次，也不是任何其他精确的数字。而是当解决问题能够确保类似事件不再发生时，迭代次数才算合适。

In general, problems are solved only when the action addressing them answers positively the question “will doing this prevent the same problem from occurring ever again?”

一般来说，只有当解决问题的行动能够肯定地回答“这样做能否防止同样的问题再次发生？”这个问题时，问题才能得到解决。

Bright Spot Analysis and Dark Spot Analysis (Best Practice #5) are great tools to solve problems proactively.

亮点分析和暗点分析（最佳实践#5）是主动解决问题的绝佳工具。

Expectations

期望

Whereas many organizations understand the need for decentralized problem solving and deploy tools for line workers to solve problems, only a few set the expectations that line workers are to actually use them.

虽然许多组织都理解分散式问题解决的必要性，并部署工具供一线员工解决问题，但只有少数组织期望一线员工真正使用这些工具。

To some managers this might seem puzzling – if we gave them the tools, of course they are expected to use them –, but the reality is that unless the expectations are explicit and linked to personal outcomes, tools will not be used.

对于一些管理者来说，这可能令人费解——如果我们给了他们工具，当然希望他们使用这些工具——但现实是，除非期望明确且与个人结果挂钩，否则工具就不会被使用。

Moreover, if any manager explicitly communicates the expectations that line workers are supposed to solve their problems by themselves, but at any point he punishes one of the workers for having done so, the message that will pass to the team is: you are not really supposed to solve problems by yourselves (“punish” is used here in the broadest way possible – even just a bad look or rolling eyes “punish” the worker having tried to solve a problem).

此外，如果任何经理明确传达了对一线工人的期望，即工人应该自己解决问题，但他在任何时候惩罚了这样做的工人，那么传递给团队的信息就是：你们实际上不应该自己解决问题（这里的“惩罚”一词含义非常广泛——即使只是一个糟糕的眼神或翻白眼也是在“惩罚”试图解决问题的工人）。

Of course, there might be circumstances in which line workers are expected to escalate problems. Procedures or rules-of-thumb must be put in place to clarify whether an issue is expected to be escalated or to be solved locally.

当然，在某些情况下，一线员工可能需要上报问题。必须制定相应的程序或经验法则，以明确某个问题应该上报还是在内部解决。

It is critical that managers both deploy problem-solving tools and constantly reinforce the expectations that workers are supposed to use them autonomously. The efficacity of decentralized problem solving in your organization will be the lowest of the two.

管理者必须既部署问题解决工具，又不断强调员工应该自主使用这些工具，这一点至关重要。在你们组织中，分散式问题解决的效率将是这两种方式中最低的。

Leading indicators

领先指标

Leading indicators are a great tool to recognize problems before they take place. Let’s see a practical example, related to workplace safety.

先行指标是识别潜在问题的绝佳工具。让我们来看一个与工作场所安全相关的实际例子。

In 1931, US safety manager Herbert Heinrich noticed a relationship between incidents in factories. For each accident causing a serious injury, there would be about 29 accidents causing a minor injury and 300 accidents causing no injury. These exact coefficients got later disproved, but Heinrich was onto something: for each death there are indeed many serious injuries, for each serious injury there are many minor injuries, for each minor injury there are several accidents causing no injury (also known as “near misses”, for example, a brick falling from the roof but hitting no one), and for each accident causing no injury, there are many unsafe behaviors (such as a worker walking in the plant with no safety helmet) and unsafe conditions (such as a sharp edge near a walkway). These relationships can be displayed as a pyramid, as in the image below.

1931年，美国安全经理赫伯特·海因里希注意到工厂事故之间存在某种关联。每发生一起造成严重伤害的事故，大约就会有29起造成轻微伤害的事故和300起未造成伤害的事故。虽然这些具体的系数后来被推翻，但海因里希的发现确实具有一定的意义：每一起死亡事故背后确实存在多起严重伤害事故，每起严重伤害事故背后又存在多起轻微伤害事故，每起轻微伤害事故背后又存在数起未造成伤害的事故（也称为“险些受伤”事故，例如，砖块从屋顶掉落但未砸到人），而每起未造成伤害的事故背后又存在许多不安全行为（例如，工人在厂区内行走时未佩戴安全帽）和不安全状况（例如，走道附近存在锋利的边缘）。这些关联可以用金字塔图来表示，如下图所示。

Now, let’s make a thought experiment. Imagine that, in a fictional company, there has been one workplace death four years ago, one three years ago, one two years ago, and zero deaths last year. Can we say that the company became safer?

现在，我们来做一个思想实验。假设在一家虚构的公司里，四年前发生过一起工伤死亡事故，三年前发生过一起，两年前发生过一起，而去年没有发生死亡事故。我们能说这家公司变得更安全了吗？

No, we cannot. Perhaps the plant’s current safety level warrants 0.75 deaths per year, and last year the employees of the company just got lucky. Maybe, next year there will be another death (or two). The sample is too small, and the results too volatile.

不，我们不能这么说。或许这家工厂目前的安全水平允许每年0.75人死亡，而去年该公司的员工只是侥幸逃过一劫。也许明年还会出现另一起（或两起）死亡事故。样本量太小，结果波动性太大。

Trends measured at the top of the pyramid are too volatile to have any predictive value.

金字塔顶端的趋势波动太大，不具有任何预测价值。

Now, let’s imagine that in the same company, 25 employees recorded an injury four years ago, 30 three years ago, 15 two years ago and 5 last year.

现在，假设在同一家公司，四年前有 25 名员工记录了工伤事故，三年前有 30 名员工记录了工伤事故，两年前有 15 名员工记录了工伤事故，去年有 5 名员工记录了工伤事故。
