Can we say that the company got safer?

我们能说公司变得更安全了吗？

Perhaps; we cannot be certain. Though the sample is now large enough to enable us to spot more reliable trends, other possibilities might invalidate the results. It is possible that, starting two years ago, the management covertly warned the employees and asked them not to report injuries. Also, there is the possibility that operations that produce light injuries did get safer, but that the operations that cause no light injuries but might kill employees (such as electrical maintenance operations) did not get safer. Finally, trends measured in the top half of the pyramid lack data on improvements relative to rare threats. For example, employees may have now a lowered probability of injury from common sources of accidents but are perhaps still a high risk of injury from infrequent ones, such as a fire.

或许如此；我们无法确定。虽然样本量已足够大，能够让我们发现更可靠的趋势，但其他可能性也可能使结果无效。例如，管理层可能从两年前就开始暗中警告员工，要求他们不要报告工伤。此外，也可能是那些造成轻微伤害的操作确实变得更安全了，但那些不会造成轻微伤害但可能导致员工死亡的操作（例如电气维修操作）并没有变得更安全。最后，金字塔上半部分衡量的趋势缺乏关于罕见威胁下安全改善的数据。例如，员工现在可能因常见事故而受伤的概率降低了，但可能仍然面临因火灾等罕见事故而受伤的高风险。

Now, let’s imagine that in the same company, random observations showed that four years ago 50% of the employees were wearing a safety helmet in the areas where their use is required; three years ago, 80% of the employees; two years ago, 90% of the employees and last year, almost 100% of the employees.

现在，假设在同一家公司，随机观察显示，四年前，50% 的员工在需要佩戴安全帽的区域佩戴安全帽；三年前，80% 的员工佩戴安全帽；两年前，90% 的员工佩戴安全帽；去年，几乎 100% 的员工佩戴安全帽。

Can we say that the company got safer? Yes, most probably. There is a correlation between the consistency of safe behaviors and how safe it is to work at a plant. Given that most incidents take place because of unsafe behaviors, the workers are safer now.

我们能说公司变得更安全了吗？是的，很有可能。安全行为的持续性与工厂的工作安全程度之间存在关联。鉴于大多数事故都是由不安全行为造成的，工人们现在更安全了。

Trends measured at the basis of the pyramid of risk are more reliable, both because of a larger sample and because of a lower number of assumptions needed.

在风险金字塔底部衡量的趋势更加可靠，这既是因为样本量更大，也是因为所需的假设数量更少。

Moreover, indicators at the top of the pyramid have a disgraceful property: they measure events that already happened. For this reason, they are called lagging indicators. Companies and individuals which measure lagging indicators tend to be reactive: they only act when the lagging indicator shows a problem: after the negative event took place, when it’s too late. Conversely, the indicators at the bottom of the pyramid can tell us whether negative events will occur, before they happen. They are leading indicators. Companies and individuals which measure leading indicators tend to be proactive and usually act to avoid the negative event before it happens.

此外，金字塔顶端的指标有一个令人遗憾的特性：它们衡量的是已经发生的事件。因此，它们被称为滞后指标。衡量滞后指标的公司和个人往往是被动的：他们只有在滞后指标显示问题时才会采取行动，那时负面事件已经发生，为时已晚。相反，金字塔底端的指标可以预测负面事件是否会发生，甚至在它们发生之前就告知我们。它们是先行指标。衡量先行指标的公司和个人往往是积极主动的，通常会在负面事件发生之前就采取行动来避免它。

If a company only increases the frequency of safety trainings after a workplace death occurs, it is bound to have at least one workplace death. If, instead, a company increases the frequency of safety trainings the moment it notices that not all employees are following the safety guidelines, then it will probably be able to prevent the deaths.

如果一家公司只在发生工伤死亡事故后才增加安全培训的频率，那么它必然还会发生至少一起工伤死亡事故。相反，如果一家公司在发现并非所有员工都遵守安全准则时就立即增加安全培训的频率，那么它很可能就能预防这些死亡事故的发生。

Measuring trends at the bottom of the pyramid allows to be proactive and to prevent negative events; measuring trends at the top causes to be reactive and to suffer from negative events.

衡量金字塔底部的趋势可以让我们积极主动地预防负面事件；而衡量金字塔顶部的趋势则会导致我们被动应对，从而遭受负面事件的打击。

Using leading indicators

使用领先指标

In order to use leading indicators, managers have to tie at least partially performance rewards to leading indicators, rather than to lagging ones.

为了使用领先指标，管理者必须将绩效奖励至少部分地与领先指标挂钩，而不是与滞后指标挂钩。

(I remind the reader that there are various types of performance rewards, including financial rewards, rewards of recognition and noticing the good, as well as disciplinary punishments or punishments in the form of admonishment. It doesn’t only have to be promotions and bonuses, or their absence.)

（我在此提醒读者，绩效奖励有多种类型，包括金钱奖励、表扬奖励和对优秀表现的认可，以及纪律处分或训诫等惩罚。它不一定非得是晋升和奖金，或者说，不一定非得是晋升和奖金的缺失。）

When harmful negative events are less frequent than positive ones, there is a risk of overoptimization : maladaptation to a temporary lack of harm. For example, a few lucky months with no injury might make the workers complacent and take unnecessary risks. Hence the importance to reward leading indicators (such as the number of people wearing the safety helmet) in addition to lagging indicators (such as the number of injuries) to prevent people from optimizing for other metrics (for example, not wearing the helmets in order to save a few seconds).

当有害的负面事件发生频率低于正面事件时，就存在过度优化的风险：即对暂时没有伤害而产生的适应不良。例如，几个月没有发生任何工伤事故可能会使工人变得自满，从而承担不必要的风险。因此，除了滞后指标（例如工伤事故数量）之外，奖励领先指标（例如佩戴安全帽的人数）也至关重要，以防止人们为了追求其他指标而进行优化（例如，为了节省几秒钟而不佩戴安全帽）。

By tying consequences (rewards and punishments) to leading indicators in addition to lagging ones, the frequency of negative events increases, causing the incentive to optimize for the frequent small profits to disappear. Let’s explore this phenomenon using an example.

通过将后果（奖励和惩罚）与领先指标（而非滞后指标）挂钩，负面事件的发生频率会增加，从而导致追求频繁小额利润的动机消失。让我们通过一个例子来探讨这种现象。

A sales manager whose compensation is tied to his sales (a lagging indicator) will focus all his energy and time on making the numbers for the current quarter. If he has an additional hour, he will spend it on making one more phone call or on sending one more proposal. He will favor small unprofitable clients who have a faster purchasing process over bigger ones to which a sale might take quarters. He will try to squeeze every dime out of every deal, getting some short-term profits but damaging the long-term relationship with the client. He might even be tempted to sell defective products, or products he knows would offer no benefit to that particular customer.

如果销售经理的薪酬与销售额（一种滞后指标）挂钩，他就会把所有精力和时间都投入到完成本季度的业绩目标上。如果多出一个小时，他就会用来多打一个电话或多发一份提案。他会更倾向于那些采购流程快捷、利润微薄的小客户，而不是那些可能需要几个季度才能完成销售的大客户。他会想方设法从每笔交易中榨取每一分钱，虽然能获得一些短期利润，但却会损害与客户的长期关系。他甚至可能会忍不住推销有缺陷的产品，或者明知对特定客户毫无益处的产品。

Conversely, a sales manager whose compensation is tied to leading indicators (such as client satisfaction, which is a predictor of repeated sales [17] , sales trainings attended, which are supposed to improve future sales, and customer research and qualification, which are supposed to improve the quality and profitability of customers) is more likely to bring great long-term results.

相反，如果销售经理的薪酬与领先指标（例如客户满意度，它是重复销售的预测指标[17]；参加的销售培训，旨在提高未来的销售额；以及客户研究和资格审查，旨在提高客户的质量和盈利能力）挂钩，那么销售经理更有可能带来良好的长期业绩。

When I present the concept of the pyramid of risk and of leading indicators, people tend to understand it rather easily. However, while putting it into practice, very often they make a key mistake. They do pay attention to leading indicators and they do measure them, but they fail to tie them to individual outcomes. If a bad performance on a lagging indicator does not impact the employee in any way, then he will not change his behavior.

当我讲解风险金字塔和领先指标的概念时，人们通常很容易理解。然而，在实践中，他们常常犯一个关键错误。他们确实关注并衡量了领先指标，但却未能将其与个人结果联系起来。如果滞后指标的糟糕表现对员工没有任何影响，那么他就不会改变自己的行为。

As illustrated in the chart below, only the top half of the pyramid is inherently linked to physical harm; consequences such as emotional or career rewards must be actively tied to the indicators at the basis of the pyramid to ensure that employees change their behavior to improve them.

如下图所示，只有金字塔的上半部分与身体伤害有内在联系；情感或职业回报等后果必须与金字塔底部的指标积极联系起来，以确保员工改变他们的行为以改善这些指标。

Solving problems without using shortcuts

不使用捷径解决问题

Problems disappear only when their root cause is addressed. Otherwise, if the problem is solved but not its root cause, the latter will act as a source of new problems.

只有解决根本原因，问题才能真正消失。否则，即使问题本身得到了解决，但其根本原因却没有被消除，那么根源问题反而会成为新问题的根源。

Shortcuts are the shortest way to another instance of the same problem.

走捷径是导致再次出现相同问题的最短途径。

Good managers insist that root causes are solved; not superficial problems. [18]

优秀的管理者坚持解决根本原因，而不是表面问题。[18]

Therefore, they do not reward those who solved the former without taking care of the latter.

因此，他们不会奖励那些只解决前者而不解决后者的人。

Incident investigations

事件调查

A particularly effective problem-solving tool is incident investigations: a procedure that is triggered by safety incidents, quality incidents and ethics incidents and whose aim is to find their root causes.

事故调查是一种特别有效的解决问题的工具：它是由安全事故、质量事故和道德事故触发的程序，其目的是找出事故的根本原因。

Incident investigations are a necessary but not sufficient tool: they are great to address problems which already manifested but cannot take care of problems which still have to manifest. Therefore, they are to be implemented together with the other tools described in this chapter.

事件调查是必要的，但并非充分条件：它能有效解决已经出现的问题，但无法预防尚未出现的问题。因此，事件调查必须与本章所述的其他工具结合使用。

Incident investigations are performed by a committee created ad-hoc immediately after the incident.

事故调查由事故发生后立即成立的临时委员会进行。

Incident investigations are as effective as the level of the highest person involved . Therefore, it is advised that the CEO or the highest manager resident at a geographical location (e.g., the Plant Manager) are part of the committee, if the incident is consequential enough (a severe injury, a quality concern which led to a recall, a rogue employee which did or could have caused harm to the company, etc.). Their time is limited so they are not expected to actively conduct the investigation; however, they should at least order the investigation and be informed of its results. Because their time is limited, their participation to the investigation is a costly (thus effective) signal of its importance. If a high manager is part of the investigating committee, the committee will find it easier to collect the information it might need or to implement any corrective action aimed at avoiding the occurrence of similar incidents in the future.

事故调查的有效性取决于最高负责人的级别。因此，如果事故后果严重（例如严重人身伤害、导致产品召回的质量问题、员工不当行为已经或可能对公司造成损害等），建议由首席执行官或驻地最高管理人员（例如工厂经理）参与调查委员会。由于他们的时间有限，因此无需主动开展调查；但他们至少应该下令进行调查并了解调查结果。鉴于他们的时间有限，他们参与调查本身就是一种高昂的成本（因此也是有效的）信号，表明了调查的重要性。如果调查委员会中有高层管理人员，委员会将更容易收集所需信息，或实施旨在避免未来发生类似事件的纠正措施。

The purpose of the incident investigation committee is to ascertain what happened, investigate the root causes of the incident, and propose recommendations so that no incident with the same root cause will ever take place again.

事故调查委员会的目的是查明发生了什么，调查事故的根本原因，并提出建议，以防止再次发生由相同根本原因引起的事故。

The committee should conclude its investigation with a written report answering the three following questions: what happened, what was the root cause, what should we do about it. In case of a quality incident, the report should be sent to the area manager, to the QA manager, and, if appropriate, to the global QA manager and/or to other area managers whose operations are similar enough to be likely to benefit from the learnings of the investigation. In case of a safety incident, the report should be sent to the area manager, the local HSE manager, the global HSE manager, the Operations Manager and the Plant Manager. These five roles are responsible for both taking immediate action based on the recommendations and to evaluate whether other geographical locations of the company could benefit from implementing the same measures (and, in this case, contacting them; members of the Top Management should be contacted as appropriate).

委员会应以书面报告的形式完成调查，回答以下三个问题：发生了什么？根本原因是什么？我们应该如何应对？如果是质量事故，报告应发送给区域经理、质量保证经理，并在适当情况下发送给全球质量保证经理和/或其他运营模式相似、可能从调查经验中受益的区域经理。如果是安全事故，报告应发送给区域经理、当地健康、安全与环境（HSE）经理、全球HSE经理、运营经理和工厂经理。这五位负责人负责根据建议立即采取行动，并评估公司其他地区是否也能从实施相同措施中受益（在这种情况下，应联系相关人员；必要时应联系高层管理人员）。

The paragraph above is provided as a simple guideline; each company should choose the list of people to be informed as it works best. However, such list should be written in a procedure itself, so that everyone knows who the results of the investigation should be sent to.

以上段落仅供参考；各公司应根据实际情况选择最合适的通知对象名单。但是，该名单应写入相关流程文件中，以便所有人都清楚调查结果应发送给哪些人。

It might happen that the investigation committee lacks the technical resources to interpret what happened during the incident, to find its root causes or to propose corrective measures. In such case, they should involve a technical expert (internal or external to the company) as appropriate.

调查委员会可能缺乏必要的技术资源来解读事件经过、找出根本原因或提出纠正措施。在这种情况下，他们应酌情聘请技术专家（公司内部或外部）。

Incident investigations are not about blaming the person responsible for the incident (though he must be hold accountable in case of negligence). They are about finding the root cause of the incident and preventing its reoccurrence in the future.

事故调查的目的并非在于追究事故责任人的责任（尽管在存在疏忽的情况下，他必须承担责任），而在于找出事故的根本原因，并防止其再次发生。

Summary

概括

Companies with Excellent Operations implement a variety of problem-solving tools, most of them decentralized, and constantly reinforce expectations about who is supposed to use them.

运营卓越的公司会实施各种问题解决工具，其中大多数是分散式的，并且不断强化关于谁应该使用这些工具的预期。

Such companies act on both incidents and declining leading indicators; they have systems in place to tackle the root causes of the problems that materialized in the past and of those which didn’t happen yet.

这类公司既会根据已发生的事件采取行动，也会根据下降的领先指标采取行动；他们已经建立了相应的系统，以解决过去出现的问题和尚未出现的问题的根本原因。

Action points

行动要点

1) Schedule a meeting with either your HSE manager or your QA manager and implement an incident investigation procedure. Make sure that a Standard Operating Procedure is also written.

1）安排与您的 HSE 经理或 QA 经理召开会议，并实施事故调查程序。同时确保制定标准操作规程。

2) Think about some leading indicators which are relevant to the areas you manage. Assign to someone in your team (it might be yourself) the task to measure and improve them.

2）思考一些与你管理领域相关的领先指标。指派团队成员（可以是你自己）负责衡量和改进这些指标。

3) The next time decisions are made or problems are addressed, make sure that it is done at the lowest competent level.

3）下次做决定或解决问题时，务必在最低的、有能力的层级上进行。

# ↩

Best Practice #8:

Visual Aids

最佳实践#8：视觉辅助

Best practices are tools to practically apply the 4 Principles of Operational Excellence. Whereas the seven previous Best Practices required at some point the physical presence of the manager, the eight one does not.

最佳实践是将卓越运营的四大原则付诸实践的工具。前七项最佳实践在某些环节需要管理者亲临现场，而第八项最佳实践则不需要。

Visual aids comprise posters hanged on walls, labels describing hardware, barriers limiting action and any other form of visual communication meant to remind or guide the actions of whoever sees it.

视觉辅助工具包括挂在墙上的海报、描述硬件的标签、限制行动的障碍物以及任何其他形式的视觉交流，旨在提醒或引导看到它的人的行动。

Visual aids serve two purposes. First, to provide visible tangible reminders of what is important, even when the manager is not there. And second, to provide an uncontestable objective reference for the standards and objectives: if it’s been hanging on the wall for a month, no one can say it hadn’t been possible for them to know.

视觉辅助工具有两个用途。首先，即使经理不在场，也能提供清晰可见、触手可及的重要事项提醒。其次，为标准和目标提供无可争议的客观参考：如果它已经在墙上挂了一个月，那么任何人都不可能说自己之前不知道。

If I had to choose a sentence to summarize the first three Principles of Operational Excellence, it would be: “make sure that the important cannot be misunderstood”. Visual aids are a key Best Practice to ensure this, together with Observation Walks and Audits (which provides on-hands feedback), Weekly and One-on-one Meetings (which are occasions to re-state the important), and Standard Operating Procedures (which are another form of objective reference, though it has to be “pulled” and can hardly be “pushed” in front of the people who need to see it, when they need to see it).

如果要我用一句话来概括卓越运营的前三项原则，那就是：“确保重要事项不会被误解”。视觉辅助工具是确保这一点的关键最佳实践，此外还包括观察巡视和审核（提供现场反馈）、每周例会和一对一会议（重申重要事项的机会）以及标准操作程序（这是另一种客观参考形式，但它必须“主动”推送，而很难在需要的时候“强行”推送给需要看到它的人）。

The most common four forms of visual aids are: posters, poster charts, labels and barriers.

最常见的四种视觉辅助工具是：海报、海报图表、标签和屏障。

# ↩


Posters

海报

Posters are large prints hanged on the walls of offices, walkways, factories and warehouses. They usually depict or describe rules, standards, priorities and Core Values. For example, a poster hanged on the wall of the warehouse might remind the workers of the safety rules they must observe while in there, or a poster hanged on the walls of an office might remind its workers that “Environmental Sustainability” is a Core Value of the company.

海报是悬挂在办公室、走廊、工厂和仓库墙壁上的大幅印刷品。它们通常描绘或描述规则、标准、优先事项和核心价值观。例如，悬挂在仓库墙上的海报可能会提醒工人他们在仓库内必须遵守的安全规则，或者悬挂在办公室墙上的海报可能会提醒员工“环境可持续性”是公司的核心价值观。

Some managers dismiss the importance of posters saying that their subordinates already know what’s written on them. These managers forget that Communication doesn’t happen when a message is first said; it happens when it cannot be mistaken anymore.

有些管理者轻视海报的重要性，认为下属都知道上面写的内容。这些管理者忘记了，沟通并非发生在信息被说出的那一刻，而是发生在信息不再被误解的那一刻。

A message has never been communicated enough unless the manager feels it had been way overcommunicated. No message is clear enough to justify not putting it on posters.

除非管理者觉得信息已经过度传达，否则就不能说信息传达得足够好。任何信息都不能清晰到不张贴出来。

Moreover, posters are a conspicuous reference; therefore, they provide a function that the spoken word alone cannot provide. Any worker can tell the manager “You didn’t say that!”, but no worker can do so if the message has also been hanged on the wall.

此外，海报是一种醒目的指示物；因此，它们发挥了口头语言无法实现的作用。任何员工都可以对经理说“你没说过这话！”，但如果信息也张贴在墙上，任何员工都无法这样做。

As a rule of thumb, if no Core Value and Standard is hanged at least once in every office floor, factory floor, canteen and warehouse, then your company needs more posters. (Multiple Core Values or standards can share the same poster, though.)

一般来说，如果公司每个办公楼层、工厂车间、食堂和仓库都没有张贴核心价值观和标准，那么贵公司就需要更多海报。（不过，多个核心价值观或标准可以共用一张海报。）

Poster charts

海报图表

Poster charts are posters which show a chart tracking the evolution of one or more key metrics over time.

海报图表是一种展示图表的海报，该图表跟踪一个或多个关键指标随时间的变化情况。

Poster charts differ from normal charts in two ways: they are hanged somewhere visible to all workers in a given area, and they are clear enough that the message they convey can be read by someone passing by without him having to stop and wear his glasses. Hence: not too much text on them.

海报图表与普通图表有两个不同之处：一是它们张贴在特定区域内所有员工都能看到的地方；二是它们足够清晰，路人无需停下来戴眼镜就能阅读其传达的信息。因此，海报图表上的文字不会太多。

Their function is not (only) to inform the workers of the trend of some key metric. Rather, their main function is to remind the workers of some key output of their job which they should keep at the top of their mind at all times.

它们的功能并非（仅仅）是告知员工某些关键指标的趋势。相反，它们的主要功能是提醒员工工作中一些关键的产出，让他们始终牢记于心。

The best poster charts contain a title large enough that it can be spotted from 2-3 meters away. This way, workers passing by the room will be reminded of what matters without having to stop by the chart. Also, workers will be more confident that other workers saw it too.

最好的海报图表标题要足够大，以便在2-3米外也能清晰可见。这样，路过房间的员工无需驻足查看图表就能记住重点内容。此外，员工也会更加确信其他员工也看到了图表。

As a rule of thumb, every factory or office worker should either be working in front of a poster chart or passing in front of one while walking from his workstation to the toilets.

一般来说，每个工厂或办公室的工人要么应该在海报图表前工作，要么应该在从工作台走到洗手间的路上经过海报图表。

Labels

标签

Labels are small pieces of paper, fabric, plastic or similar material next or attached to a critical piece of hardware. For example, a label might be a sticker next to a button which explains what happens if pressed, or it could be a piece of plastic connected to a key that explains what the key is for.

标签是指贴在关键硬件旁边或附着在其上的小块纸片、布料、塑料或其他类似材料。例如，标签可以是按钮旁边的贴纸，用来说明按下按钮后会发生什么；也可以是连接在钥匙上的塑料片，用来说明这把钥匙的用途。

Labels could also be writings next to critical pieces of hardware. For example, a bottle might be labeled with its contents or with the risks associated with its contents (e.g., “inflammable”).

标签也可以是贴在关键硬件旁边的文字。例如，瓶子上可能会贴有标签，标明其内容物或与其内容物相关的风险（例如，“易燃”）。

Finally, labels could also be panels indicating a direction. For example, an arrow indicating where the emergency exit is.

最后，标签也可以是指示方向的面板。例如，箭头指示紧急出口的位置。

Great companies use labels extensively. Every critical button, tool, container, shelf, pathway, lever, valve and indicator is clearly labeled.

优秀的公司会广泛使用标签。每一个关键按钮、工具、容器、货架、通道、控制杆、阀门和指示器都清晰地标明了位置。

Great companies do not assume that, because their workers have undergone training, they do not need labels. Labels (and visual aids in general) are not there to protect against inexperience. They are there to protect against fatigue, rushing, and other mental conditions which might cause an otherwise competent operator to commit a mistake.

优秀的公司不会因为员工接受过培训就认为不需要标签。标签（以及其他视觉辅助工具）并非为了弥补经验不足，而是为了防止疲劳、匆忙以及其他可能导致原本胜任的操作人员犯错的精神状态。

Some labels, in addition to preventing mistakes, also make operations faster or more efficient. For example, some factory workers attach stickers of different colors (blue, yellow, pink and so on) to their tools and then attach stickers of the same colors to the table they work on. This way, they know where each tool is supposed to rest on their table. Having each tool at the same place translates into faster working speed, if a high number of tools is involved.

除了防止出错，一些标签还能提高操作速度和效率。例如，一些工厂工人会在工具上贴上不同颜色的标签（蓝色、黄色、粉色等等），然后在工作台上也贴上相同颜色的标签。这样，他们就能知道每件工具应该放在工作台上的哪个位置。如果工具数量较多，每件工具都放在固定位置就能提高工作效率。

A particular form of label are signs on the floor which indicate walkways or separate areas. For example, most factories have the areas where workers are supposed to walk delimitated with long clear stickers. These labels serve three functions. First, they keep workers outside areas where they’re not supposed to be (such as forklift passageways). Second, they guide the movements of workers, making it easier for them to get safely where they want to go. Third, they delimit the areas where parts and equipment can be stored, ensuring that they are accumulated there rather than on the walkways where they can slow movement or cause injuries.

一种特殊的标签形式是地面上的标志，用于指示通道或独立区域。例如，大多数工厂都会用长条状的透明贴纸标明工人应该行走的区域。这些标签有三个作用。首先，它们可以防止工人进入不应该进入的区域（例如叉车通道）。其次，它们可以引导工人的移动，使他们更容易安全地到达目的地。第三，它们可以划定零件和设备的存放区域，确保这些物品堆放在指定区域，而不是堆放在通道上，以免阻碍通行或造成人身伤害。

Barriers

障碍

Barriers are pieces of hardware which limit movement, preventing workers from accidentally walking or moving parts of their bodies where they’re not supposed to. For example, a grid might prevent workers from entering by mistake within the range of motion of a robot which might cause injuries.

防护栏是一种限制人员移动的硬件装置，可以防止工人意外地走到或将身体部位移动到不该去的地方。例如，网格可以防止工人误入机器人的活动范围，从而避免受伤。

As a rule of thumb, if you have an area which is routinely accessed by unqualified workers or which contains moving hardware which might cause injuries (such as robots), then the access to the dangerous zones must be limited by some form of barrier.

一般来说，如果某个区域经常有不合格的工人进入，或者该区域内有可能造成伤害的移动硬件（例如机器人），那么必须用某种形式的屏障来限制进入危险区域。

# ↩


Whose responsibility it is to use visual aids?

使用视觉辅助工具的责任应该由谁承担？

In companies with low Operational Excellence, visual aids are usually installed under the orders of the HSE manager and are usually limited to HSE matters.

在运营卓越性较低的公司中，视觉辅助工具通常是在 HSE 经理的命令下安装的，并且通常仅限于 HSE 事项。

In companies with medium Operational Excellence, visual aids are additionally installed by the area manager, to drive attention towards the organizational priorities.

在运营卓越程度中等的公司中，区域经理还会安装视觉辅助工具，以引导员工关注组织优先事项。

In companies with great Operational Excellence , visual aids are additionally installed by each worker, in his or her own area of competence. Workers use these aids both for themselves and for others, both to prevent injuries, to drive attention towards what’s important and to improve the efficiency and efficacy of their own work.

在运营卓越性极高的公司中，每位员工都会在其职责范围内安装视觉辅助工具。员工使用这些工具既是为了自己，也是为了帮助他人，其目的在于预防工伤、集中注意力于重要事项，并提高自身工作的效率和效能。

If you are reading this, feel free to request to your area manager or HSE manager any visual aid you think the workers in your area of competence might need, as appropriate. Do not wait for them to be set in place; if they haven’t been set so far, chances are that they won’t be set in the near future either, unless you take the situation in your own hands.

如果您正在阅读此文，请随时向您的区域经理或健康、安全与环境 (HSE) 经理提出您认为您职责范围内的员工可能需要的任何视觉辅助工具。不要坐等这些工具到位；如果至今尚未到位，除非您主动采取行动，否则很可能在不久的将来也不会到位。

Summary

概括

Great companies make extensive use of visual aids to remind their workers about the important things.

优秀的公司会广泛使用视觉辅助工具来提醒员工重要的事情。

They do not only use visual aids for things that are hard to remember; they use them for things which are important to remember, regardless of whether they’re obvious or not.

他们不仅用视觉辅助工具来帮助记忆难以记住的事情，而且还用它们来帮助记忆那些重要的事情，无论这些事情是否显而易见。

Great companies make use of all types of visual aids: posters, poster charts, labels and barriers.

优秀的公司会利用各种视觉辅助工具：海报、海报图表、标签和屏障。

Action points

行动要点

1) Is there any tool, bottle, box or shelf space which is unlabeled? Label them (or ask the area manager or area owner to do so, as appropriate).

1）是否有任何工具、瓶子、盒子或货架空间未贴标签？请贴上标签（或酌情请区域经理或区域负责人贴标签）。

2) If your subordinates’ workplace does not contain enough posters on Core Values (“enough” as defined above), add some.

2) 如果你的下属工作场所没有足够多的核心价值观海报（“足够”的定义如上所述），请添加一些。

3) Which poster charts would benefit your subordinates? Create them.

3）哪些海报图表对你的下属有益？把它们做出来。

4) Is any area under your management in need for barriers?

4）您管理的任何区域是否需要设置屏障？

# ↩

Paradigm shifts

范式转变

The First Best Practice (Management Walks) introduced a paradigm shift from “ a manager’s most important work takes place in his office ” to “a manager’s most important work takes place on his subordinates’ workplace.”

第一个最佳实践（管理巡视）引入了一种范式转变，从“经理最重要的工作是在他的办公室里进行的”转变为“经理最重要的工作是在他的下属的工作场所进行的”。

The Second Best Practice (Audits) introduced a paradigm shift from “inspections are to correct behaviors and conditions” to “inspections are to reinforce Core Values and standards .”

第二项最佳实践（审核）引入了一种范式转变，从“检查是为了纠正行为和状况”转变为“检查是为了强化核心价值观和标准”。

The Third Best Practice (Weekly Meetings) introduced a paradigm shift from “weekly meetings are to communicate new information” to “weekly meetings are to communicate old information (Core V alues and standards).”

第三项最佳实践（每周例会）引入了一种范式转变，从“每周例会是为了传达新信息”转变为“每周例会是为了传达旧信息（核心价值观和标准）”。

The Fourth Best Practice (One-on-one Meetings) introduced a paradigm shift from “ information during one-on-ones flows from the manager to the employee ” to “information during one-on-ones flows from the employee to the manager.”

第四个最佳实践（一对一会议）引入了一种范式转变，从“一对一会议期间的信息从经理流向员工”转变为“一对一会议期间的信息从员工流向经理”。

The Fifth Best Practice (Bright Spot Analysis) introduced a paradigm shift from “innovation is about applying new ideas” to “innovation is about applying old practices.”

第五个最佳实践（亮点分析）引入了一种范式转变，从“创新是应用新想法”转变为“创新是应用旧做法”。

The Sixth Best Practice (Standard Operating Procedures) introduced a paradigm shift from “SOPs are about compliance” to “SOPs are about managing change (hires, promotions, purchases, innovation, etc.).”

第六项最佳实践（标准操作程序）引入了一种范式转变，从“标准操作程序是关于合规性的”转变为“标准操作程序是关于管理变革（招聘、晋升、采购、创新等）的”。

The Seventh Best Practice (Surfacing Problems) introduced a paradigm shift from “problem solving is about taking care of already-occurred problems” to “problem solving is about preventing future problems.”

第七项最佳实践（发现问题）引入了一种范式转变，从“解决问题就是处理已经出现的问题”转变为“解决问题就是预防未来出现的问题”。

The Eight Best Practice (Visual Aids) introduced a paradigm shift from “visual aids are about compliance in perfect circumstances” to “Visual Aids are about avoiding mistakes in imperfect circumstances (e.g. when employees are rushed, tired, etc.).”

八项最佳实践（视觉辅助）引入了一种范式转变，从“视觉辅助是为了在完美情况下遵守规定”转变为“视觉辅助是为了在不完美情况下避免错误（例如，当员工匆忙、疲惫等时）。”

# ↩

What to do now

现在该怎么办

In the third part of this book, you will find a Roadmap to change the Operational Culture of your organization. However, you might want to start small first, limiting the scope of change to your direct reports. The following points will help you prioritize what to do over the next few days.

本书第三部分提供了一份改变组织运营文化的路线图。不过，您不妨先从小处着手，将变革范围限定在您的直接下属身上。以下几点将帮助您确定未来几天的工作重点。

From now on:

今后：

  • Practice the Four Principles in every interaction with your subordinates. Be unmistakably clear, assign unambiguous individual rewardable objectives, delegate accountability, take visible costly actions and be obsessively consistent in holding them accountable.
    在与下属的每一次互动中都要践行这四项原则：表达要清晰明确，设定明确的个人奖励目标，授权责任，采取显而易见的、代价高昂的措施，并始终如一地追究他们的责任。

Today:

今天：

  • Schedule a one-on-one meeting with each of your subordinates to be held over the next few days. Book a 0ne-hour slot in their calendar. During the meeting, clarify their individual objectives. Do not forget to add individual objectives on Core Values. Take a blank sheet of paper to the meeting and write down any agreed objective. The act of writing will force clarity. Also write down how you will evaluate their progress against their objectives. At the end of each individual meeting, schedule with the attendee the next meeting, in one-week time.
    在接下来的几天里，安排与每位下属进行一对一会谈。在他们的日程表中预留一个小时的时间段。会谈期间，明确他们的个人目标。不要忘记将个人目标与核心价值观相结合。带一张白纸去开会，写下所有已达成共识的目标。书写的过程有助于理清思路。同时，也要写下你将如何评估他们实现目标的进展情况。每次单独会谈结束后，与参会人员约定一周后的下次会议时间。
  • Schedule in your calendar a 30-minutes slot for your Management Walks, as described at the end of the relative chapter.
    按照相关章节末尾的描述，在您的日历中安排 30 分钟的管理巡视时间。
  • One month from now, schedule in your calendar a 60-minutes slot in which you will take the actions under the paragraph title “one month from now”, which you will find below.
    一个月后，在你的日历中安排一个 60 分钟的时间段，用于执行标题为“一个月后”的段落中的操作，这些操作将在下面找到。

One week from now:

一周后：

  • After you finished the first round of One-on-one Meetings, review the sheets in which you wrote the individual objectives of your subordinates. Write down in your calendar or agenda any follow-up action which is needed, if any.
    第一轮一对一会议结束后，请回顾您记录下属个人目标的表格。如有任何后续行动需要跟进，请记入您的日历或议程中。
  • During the second round of One-on-one Meetings, and in every following round, make sure you review progress against the individual objectives of your subordinates and hold them accountable accordingly to what was agreed. If any issue arises because of you not having been clear in the past, own your mistakes and bring the required clarity.
    在第二轮一对一会议以及之后的每一轮会议中，务必检查下属个人目标的完成进度，并根据既定目标追究他们的责任。如果由于你之前沟通不畅而导致出现任何问题，请勇于承认错误并及时澄清。

One month from now:

一个月后：

  • Review the second part of this book, “Best Practices”, and see if your actions during the last months were aligned with them. Make any required adjustment.
    请回顾本书第二部分“最佳实践”，看看你过去几个月的行动是否与这些实践相符。如有需要，请做出相应调整。

Onwards:

继续：

  • Keep implementing the Eight Best Practices of Operational Culture and eventually ask your subordinates to do the same, if appropriate.
    持续推行运营文化的八项最佳实践，并在适当的时候要求你的下属也这样做。
  • Never compromise on Core Values. Never. No matter what. It is not worth it.
    绝不妥协核心价值观。绝不。无论如何。不值得。
  • Behave as per your words, and if impossible, own your mistakes and take immediate action to ensure that you will never have to disrespect your words again for the same reason.
    言出必行，如果做不到，就勇于承认错误，并立即采取行动，确保以后不会再因为同样的原因而违背自己的诺言。
  • Set weekly or monthly 15-minutes slots in your agenda for “Operational Culture Reviews”, in which you will meditate on whether during the past week you lived the Operational Culture you desire to build in your team, and on what has to be done differently next week.
    在您的日程安排中，每周或每月留出 15 分钟的时间进行“运营文化回顾”，思考在过去的一周里，您是否践行了您希望在团队中建立的运营文化，以及下周需要做出哪些改变。
  • Schedule half-yearly 2-hours slots in your calendar in which you will review this book.
    在你的日历中安排每半年一次、每次 2 小时的时间来阅读这本书。

Notes – The list above is non-comprehensive. It has been written with the sole purpose of giving you some quick tips on what to begin working on as you internalize the concepts read so far. The third part of this book will provide you with more information on rolling-out change in your organization.

注：以上列表并不完整。其目的仅在于为您提供一些快速入门技巧，帮助您理解目前为止所读到的概念。本书第三部分将为您提供更多关于如何在组织中推行变革的信息。

# ↩

Part III:
The Roadmap to Change

第三部分：变革路线图

In the first part of this book, you learnt the Four Principles of Operational Excellence:

本书第一部分介绍了卓越运营的四大原则：

1) Good managers set unambiguous, individual and rewardable objectives.

1）优秀的管理者会设定明确、个人化且可奖励的目标。

2) Good managers always explicitly assign full accountability together with objectives.

2）优秀的管理者总是明确地将全部责任与目标结合起来。

3) Good managers demonstrate priorities with visible costly actions.

3) 优秀的管理者会通过看得见的、代价高昂的行动来表明优先事项。

4) Good managers are obsessively consistent in holding their subordinates accountable.

4）优秀的管理者会坚持不懈地要求下属承担责任。

In the second part of this book, you learnt the Eight Best Practices that transform the Four Principles into visible action:

本书第二部分介绍了将四大原则转化为可见行动的八项最佳实践：

1) Management Walks

1）管理层巡视

2) Audits

2）审计

3) Weekly Meetings

3）每周例会

4) One-on-one Meetings

4）一对一会议

5) Bright Spot Analysis

5）亮点分析

6) Standard Operating Procedures

6）标准操作程序

7) Surfacing Problems

7）表面问题

8) Visual Aids

8）视觉辅助工具

The third part of this book is about implementing the content you’ve seen so far.

本书第三部分是关于如何运用你目前所学的内容。

It will guide you to plan an initiative to change the operational culture of your team, plant or company, to get Top Management buy-in, to roll-out the initiative and to sustain it over time.

它将指导您制定一项改变团队、工厂或公司运营文化的计划，以获得高层管理人员的支持，推出该计划并使其长期持续下去。

# ↩

Getting Buy-In

获得支持

If you are a member of Top Management, you are probably already familiar with the contents of this chapter and can skip to the next one. The following paragraphs have been written for people less experienced with getting the buy-in to roll-out initiatives aimed at changing the operational culture of the team, plant or company they work in.

如果您是高层管理人员，您可能已经熟悉本章内容，可以直接跳到下一章。以下段落是为那些在推动旨在改变团队、工厂或公司运营文化的举措方面经验较少的人员撰写的，旨在帮助他们获得支持。

The need for past evidence

对过往证据的需求

You do not want to ask immediately Top Management for support if you do not have past evidence supporting the effectiveness of the initiative you are proposing.

如果你没有过去的证据来证明你所提出的方案的有效性，就不要立即向高层管理人员寻求支持。

Such evidence can be of three types:

此类证据可分为三种类型：

  • Successful pilot: you already successfully implemented the initiative in your current company on a smaller scale (for example, on a single production line).
    试点成功：您已在目前的公司中小规模成功实施了该举措（例如，在一条生产线上）。
  • Previous experience: you already successfully implemented the initiative in your previous company, at a scale at least comparable to the one of your current company.
    以往经验：您已在之前的公司成功实施了该项举措，其规模至少与您目前所在的公司相当。
  • External experience: the initiative will be rolled-out by external experts, such as a consulting company (the author of this book could help you; don’t hesitate to contact him), or by yourself assisted by such external experts.
    外部经验：该计划将由外部专家（例如咨询公司）推出（本书作者可以为您提供帮助；请随时与他联系），或者由您自己在外部专家的协助下推出。

Do not bother asking Top Management for support if you do not have at least one of the three types of evidence, unless you are working for a small startup with limited headcount. Instead, work on getting that evidence. The easiest way is to start with a pilot. Begin with rolling out the initiative within your own team.

如果你没有至少三种证据中的一种，就不要费力向高层管理人员寻求支持，除非你是在人手有限的小型创业公司工作。相反，你应该努力获取这些证据。最简单的方法是从试点开始。首先在你自己的团队内部推广这项举措。

Presenting evidence

提供证据

When you request support from Top Management, you should not only have past evidence of the effectiveness of the initiative you are proposing, but you should also be able to present it in a way that is relevant to them.

当你请求高层管理人员支持时，你不仅应该有过去证据证明你所提出的计划是有效的，而且还应该能够以与他们相关的方式进行陈述。

Do not focus too much on the technical details of the initiative: they will be useful and important for you, but not for them. Instead, focus on ensuring that your letter / presentation / request for support covers the two following points.

不要过分关注项目的技术细节：这些细节对你来说固然重要，但对他们而言却并非如此。相反，你应该着重确保你的信函/演示文稿/支持请求涵盖以下两点。

Past evidence that it will work. As mentioned in the previous section, make sure that you have past evidence that your project will work, and make sure to mention it in your request.

过往经验证明其可行性。如前所述，请确保您有过往经验证明您的项目可行，并在申请中提及。

Bottom-line impact. Every project – every single one – will be checked against its impact on the bottom line: is it an allocation of people and money that will bring more profits than competing alternatives?

最终影响。每个项目——每一个项目——都会根据其对最终收益的影响进行评估：这项人力和资金投入是否比其他替代方案更能带来利润？

You need to answer this question – even if it is not asked, because the people evaluating your proposal will make the computation anyway, so you might as well be the one making it for them.

你需要回答这个问题——即使没人问，因为评估你方案的人无论如何都会进行计算，所以你最好替他们计算出来。

To calculate the bottom-line impact of your initiative, consider both the benefits of it being implemented and the costs of it not being implemented. For example, how much will it cost your company to keep producing components with the current defect rate?

要计算您的举措对最终收益的影响，请同时考虑实施该举措带来的收益和不实施该举措的成本。例如，如果贵公司继续以目前的缺陷率生产零部件，将会损失多少成本？

When you calculate the costs of continuing operating with the current problems, do not forget to also include hidden costs. They are often much larger than visible ones. Let’s say, for example, that due to the current lack of Operational Excellence, your company has a high injury rate. The visible costs are the costs of non-production (if the line has to stop due to incidents) and the costs of managing the recovery of the employee. The hidden costs are the cost of finding a replacement for the injured employee (or of maintaining extra staff for redundancy purposes), the cost of lower quality (as the temporary replacement for the injured employee will likely be less experienced or proficient), the higher cost of health and safety insurance (companies with lot of injuries are more expensive to insure), the morale and turnover cost of injuries (employees in companies with a lot of injuries are more likely to quit, increasing hiring and training costs), and so on.

在计算继续应对当前问题的成本时，切勿忘记将隐性成本也考虑在内。这些隐性成本通常远高于显性成本。例如，假设由于目前缺乏卓越运营，贵公司工伤率居高不下。显性成本包括停产成本（例如生产线因事故停工）和员工康复管理成本。隐性成本则包括：寻找受伤员工的替代人选（或出于冗余目的而维持额外员工）的成本、质量下降的成本（因为临时替代人选可能经验不足或技能欠佳）、更高的健康与安全保险成本（工伤事故多的公司保险费用更高）、工伤事故造成的士气和人员流动成本（工伤事故多的公司员工离职的可能性更高，从而增加了招聘和培训成本）等等。

Get commitment

获得承诺

I know of consulting companies that do not work unless the CEO (or, if engaged by a subsidiary, the Managing Director or Plant Manager) commits to be both a participant to the initiative and a promoter of it. I personally do the same for my consulting practice, except very particular cases.

我知道有些咨询公司，如果首席执行官（或者，如果是受聘于子公司，则是总经理或工厂经理）没有承诺既参与又推动项目，那么项目就无法顺利开展。我个人在咨询业务中也遵循同样的原则，除非遇到非常特殊的情况。

This is so important. Unless the CEO is the first person to participate to the trainings and to set the expectations for all the other employees, your project will not be considered a priority. As soon as the CEO talks about another matter, that matter will become the new priority and your project will fall into oblivion (because the CEO talked about that matter but not about your project , and this places your project on a lower level).

这一点至关重要。除非CEO亲自参加培训并为其他员工设定目标，否则你的项目不会被优先考虑。一旦CEO谈论其他事情，那件事就会成为新的优先事项，而你的项目就会被遗忘（因为CEO谈论的是那件事，而不是你的项目，这会让你的项目优先级降低）。

Do not begin your initiative until you got written commitment of personal support from the CEO (or, if your initiative is limited to a single location within your company, from the highest role resident there). This might be a hassle, and it might delay the start of the initiative, but it will make everything easier.

在获得首席执行官（或，如果你的项目仅限于公司内部的某个特定地点，则需获得该地点最高领导层的书面支持）的书面承诺之前，切勿启动你的项目。这可能会比较麻烦，也可能延迟项目的启动，但会让一切变得更加容易。

Insist

坚持

Your role – as a professional – is not (only) to propose the initiatives you believe will be good for your company. It is to fight for their implementation.

作为一名专业人士，你的职责不仅仅是提出你认为对公司有利的方案，还要争取让这些方案得以实施。

If Top Management refuses your proposal, do not take it as the death of your initiative. Instead, take it as a sign that you didn’t prepare your proposal well enough. Perhaps, you didn’t understand Top Management’s point of view well enough. Or maybe, you were not able to present your case in a way that resonated with them. Either way, it is your responsibility to try again.

如果高层管理人员拒绝了你的提案，不要就此放弃你的计划。相反，这说明你准备的提案还不够充分。或许，你没有充分理解高层管理人员的观点。又或许，你没能用他们能理解的方式阐述你的理由。无论如何，你都有责任再次尝试。

Acquire the skills you might need (presenting? Writing? Finance?), make the connections you might need, ask for the help you might need, and then submit your proposal again.

掌握你可能需要的技能（演讲？写作？财务？），建立你可能需要的人脉，寻求你可能需要的帮助，然后再次提交你的提案。

# ↩

Rolling out

推出

Achieving critical mass

达到临界质量

While rolling out an initiative, the most important thing you should care about is not how many people are adopting the desired new behaviors, but how geographically concentrated these people are. For example, if you manage to get 20 people in your 200-employees plant to adopt a new habit, but those people are scattered across teams, the change will be short lived. Those 20 people will see that those around them are not changing and will quickly revert to their previous habits. Instead, if those 20 people are part of the same team, they will see that the people around them (those they spend the most time with) are exhibiting the new behavior. This will have a self-sustaining effect.

在推行一项举措时，你最应该关注的不是有多少人采纳了期望的新行为，而是这些人的地域分布是否集中。例如，如果你成功地让一家拥有 200 名员工的工厂里的 20 人养成了一种新习惯，但这些人分散在不同的团队中，那么这种改变将难以持久。这 20 个人会发现周围的人并没有改变，很快就会恢复到以前的习惯。相反，如果这 20 个人属于同一个团队，他们就会看到身边的人（也就是他们相处时间最长的人）都在践行这种新行为。这将产生一种自我维持的效应。

In my experience, the main predictor for whether an initiative will succeed is whether it achieved critical mass : whether, in at least one location (a team, a production line, a plant, an office floor, etc.), at least 80-90% of the people are exhibiting the desired behaviors.

根据我的经验，一项举措能否成功的主要预测因素是它是否达到了临界规模：至少在一个地方（一个团队、一条生产线、一个工厂、一个办公楼层等），至少 80-90% 的人是否表现出了期望的行为。

Managers have a limited amount of time to properly implement the 8 Best Practices of Operational Excellence. They can only apply them with 100% effectiveness over a limited area. If they try to change too many people, or too many teams at once, they will have to scatter their attention between them. This approach will perhaps yield more impressive results during the first couple of weeks, but these results will quickly fizzle out as the critical mass fails to be achieved. Instead, good managers focus on changing one location at a time.

管理者只有有限的时间来有效实施卓越运营的八项最佳实践。他们只能在有限的范围内才能百分之百地发挥这些实践的效用。如果他们试图一次性改变太多人或太多团队，就不得不分散精力。这种方法或许在最初几周内能取得更显著的效果，但随着未能达到临界规模，这些效果很快就会消失。因此，优秀的管理者会专注于一次只改变一个地点。

The 3 rd Principle of Operational Excellence states the importance of obsessive consistency: never let pass even once an undesired behavior. If you manage to correct 90% of the undesired behaviors across two teams, the members of these teams will still remember the 10% of times you let it pass. Instead, it is much more effective to focus on a single team for one month, and to move your focus to the second team only during the following month, after the first team will have internalized the change.

卓越运营的第三原则强调了坚持不懈的重要性：绝不容许任何不良行为发生。即使你成功地纠正了两个团队中90%的不良行为，团队成员仍然会记住你放任不管的那10%。因此，更有效的做法是，先集中精力在一个团队上进行一个月的培训，等第一个团队完全适应了新的方法后，再在下个月将精力转移到第二个团队。

Similarly, the scope of the initiative should be limited also on the amount of behaviors it aims to change. An initiative that aims to introduce ten new procedures is likely to fail, as the manager will have to check and reinforce ten new behaviors. This is only doable – perhaps – with tiny teams. Instead, better to spend one month to introduce a single new procedure, consistently obsess over its implementation, and only move to the second procedure during the next month, once the first behavior will have been internalized.

同样，这项举措的范围也应限制在它旨在改变的行为数量上。一项旨在引入十项新流程的举措很可能会失败，因为管理者需要检查和强化十项新行为。这或许只有在小型团队中才可行。更好的做法是，花一个月时间引入一项新流程，持续关注其执行情况，然后在下个月，当第一项流程被员工内化之后，再推进第二项流程。

Being too ambitious and choosing a too large scope for change (too many people affected, or too many behaviors) so that managers cannot be 100% consistent in applying the Fourth Principle is the number one reason for which change initiatives fail.

目标过于远大，选择过大的变革范围（受影响的人数太多，或行为太多），导致管理者无法 100% 一致地应用第四原则，这是变革举措失败的首要原因。

Fractal hierarchy

分形层次结构

The only way to ensure that change is quickly implemented across a large company is by leveraging a fractal hierarchy.

确保变革在大公司内快速实施的唯一方法是利用分形层次结构。

Due to the necessity of achieving critical mass, a manager can only promote change over a small team – perhaps 4 to 10 people, depending to how close the manager is to them and how busy he is with other tasks. Having a manager trying to implement change over more people is bound to fail. Therefore, only companies with a very vertical structure (few subordinates per manager/supervisor) can afford to implement a company-wide change initiative in a quick amount of time – and even then, the scope of the change should be limited to 1-2 new behaviors per month.

由于变革需要达到一定的规模，管理者只能在较小的团队范围内推动变革——人数可能在4到10人之间，具体取决于管理者与团队成员的亲近程度以及他/她是否忙于其他工作。试图让管理者在更多人身上推行变革注定会失败。因此，只有组织结构非常垂直（每个经理/主管管理的下属人数很少）的公司才能在短时间内推行全公司范围的变革——即便如此，变革的范围也应限制在每月1到2项新行为之内。

During a company-wide or plant-wide change initiative, every single manager and supervisor must be involved. It is impossible that a single HSE manager, for example, rolls out a company-wide change initiative over a small amount of time. He could do so over the span of several months or few years– working a couple of teams at a time – but pretending that he’d do it in a few months is unrealistic.

在公司或工厂范围内推行变革时，每一位经理和主管都必须参与其中。例如，仅靠一位健康、安全和环境（HSE）经理不可能在短时间内完成公司范围内的变革。他或许可以分几个月甚至几年完成，每次负责几个团队，但指望他几个月就能搞定是不现实的。

Driving a change initiative, like driving a car, can only be that fast. After a certain point, a crash is inevitable. The point is not to go as fast as possible, but to arrive at the destination.

推动变革就像开车，速度只能到此为止。超过某个临界点，崩溃就不可避免。关键不在于速度，而在于到达目的地。

Involving managers

让经理人参与进来

It is necessary that the CEO sets the expectations for the change initiative. Otherwise, the change initiative will not be considered a priority and will fizzle out as soon as the CEO mentions a new priority (for example, meeting a target for the quarter).

首席执行官必须明确变革计划的预期目标。否则，变革计划将不会被视为优先事项，一旦首席执行官提出新的优先事项（例如，完成季度目标），变革计划就会不了了之。

The CEO setting the expectations for the change initiative includes at least him sending a company-wide email, informing every employee of the change initiative, of its importance, of his endorsement, and of his expectations (e.g. “I expect every manager to attend the training by the end of February, to implement the changes in his team by the end of April and to improve this and that indicator by X% by the end of June.”).

首席执行官在设定变革计划的预期时，至少会向全公司员工发送一封电子邮件，告知每位员工有关变革计划、其重要性、他的支持以及他的期望（例如，“我希望每位经理在 2 月底前参加培训，在 4 月底前在其团队中实施变革，并在 6 月底前将某项指标提高 X%。”）。

In the best case, the CEO should also do the following: talk about the initiative during “company-wide meetings” (if the company organizes any), talk about the initiative during every internal meeting with more than 5 people it participates to, participate himself to the first batch of training, and talk about the initiative during his at-least-monthly management walk. Because the CEO time is so valuable, all of these are costly signals, thus effective ones.

理想情况下，CEO还应该做到以下几点：在公司全体会议（如有）上谈论这项计划；在所有参与人数超过5人的内部会议上谈论这项计划；亲自参加第一批培训；并在至少每月一次的例行管理巡视中谈论这项计划。由于CEO的时间非常宝贵，所有这些都是成本高昂但行之有效的举措。

Every other manager and supervisor in the company should be expected to do the same: sending a team-wide email and holding a public presentation about the change initiative stating the expectations for his subordinates, talking about the change initiative during the meetings with his subordinates and during his Management Walks.

公司其他所有经理和主管都应该这样做：向全团队发送电子邮件，并就变革计划进行公开演讲，说明对下属的期望，在与下属的会议以及管理巡视期间谈论变革计划。

Of course, every manager and supervisor in the company – including the CEO, especially the CEO – is expected not to let any non-conforming-to-the-change-initiative behavior pass. This should be stated into the expectation-setting phase.

当然，公司里的每一位经理和主管——包括首席执行官，尤其是首席执行官——都不应该放任任何不符合变革举措的行为。这一点应该在预期设定阶段就明确说明。

In particular, attending trainings should be a personal objective of every employee, and failing to attend them (within a reasonable time frame) should be disciplined. As Silicon Valley entrepreneur Ben Horowitz noted, “no [team] has time to do optional things. Therefore, training must be mandatory.”

尤其重要的是，参加培训应该是每位员工的个人目标，未能（在合理时间内）参加培训应受到纪律处分。正如硅谷企业家本·霍洛维茨所指出的那样，“任何团队都没有时间去做可有可无的事情。因此，培训必须是强制性的。”

The adoption curve

采用曲线

When a new technology is adopted, it is not received equally by all customers. Similarly, when a new organizational culture, a new procedure or a new tool are introduced, they are not received equally by all employees.

一项新技术被采用时，并非所有客户都能平等接受。同样，当一种新的组织文化、新的流程或新的工具被引入时，也并非所有员工都能平等接受。

Adoption Curve Theory divides the adopters into five groups: innovators, early adopters, early majority, later majority and laggards (in order of adoption). To ensure the success of your change initiative, you need to understand the different factors that drive adoption within each different group.

采纳曲线理论将采纳者分为五类：创新者、早期采纳者、早期大众、后期大众和落后者（按采纳顺序排列）。为了确保您的变革举措取得成功，您需要了解驱动每个不同群体采纳的不同因素。

Innovators adopt the new procedure because it allows them to do something new. They are eager to try it even if it doesn’t work reliably yet. For example, if your company is about to introduce a new software to track purchase orders, these would be the few employees which ask you to see the software even before it is publicly announced. (In this context, the term “innovator” has nothing to do with performing research or development. It simply refers to people who, by personal inclination, are open to try new things which might not work.)

创新者之所以采用新流程，是因为它能让他们尝试新事物。即使新流程目前还不完善，他们也渴望尝试。例如，如果你的公司即将推出一款新的采购订单跟踪软件，那么很可能就是这些员工会在软件正式发布前就要求先睹为快。（在此语境下，“创新者”一词与研发无关，它仅仅是指那些出于个人意愿，乐于尝试可能失败的新事物的人。）

Early adopters are the employees who immediately begin using the new procedure after it is put in place. They see its value and are internally convinced of its usefulness. They do not need the manager to remind them nor they need to see that their colleagues are using it.

早期采用者是指新流程实施后立即开始使用的员工。他们看到了新流程的价值，并由衷地相信它的实用性。他们不需要经理提醒，也不需要看到同事们在使用新流程。

The early majority are the employees who use the new procedure only after they see other colleagues using it. They do not want to be the first ones. They do not want to do anything risky or anything new.

早期大多数是指那些只有在看到其他同事使用新流程后才会采用的员工。他们不想成为第一个吃螃蟹的人，也不想做任何有风险或新的事情。

The late majority are the employees who will use the new procedure only after the rest of the team will have adopted it and after their manager will have reprimanded them for not using it. Change has to be made inevitable for them to embrace it.

后知后觉的大多数员工只有在团队其他成员都采用新流程，并且他们的经理批评他们不遵守流程之后，他们才会使用新流程。必须让变革成为一种必然，他们才会接受它。

The laggards are those employees who will never use the new procedure, unless forced to do so.

那些不愿采用新流程的员工，除非被迫，否则绝不会使用新流程。

Understanding what drives adoption in the five groups is critical, because a trend emerges: whereas a small percentage of employees is able to individually adopt a new procedure (innovators and the early majority), the rest of the employees needs to see other people using it. The more an employee is towards the right of the Adoption Curve spectrum, the higher the percentage of his colleagues who need to adopt the procedure for him to be willing to do so.

了解五类员工采纳新流程的驱动因素至关重要，因为其中蕴含着一个趋势：只有一小部分员工能够独立采纳新流程（创新者和早期大众），而其余员工则需要看到其他人使用该流程。员工在采纳曲线上的位置越靠右，就越需要看到更高比例的同事采纳该流程，他才会愿意采纳。

Therefore, managers of large divisions who focus their energy towards all subordinates at the same time in the same way are bound to fail.

因此，管理大型部门的经理如果同时以同样的方式将所有精力集中在所有下属身上，就注定会失败。

Instead, change initiatives must be progressively rolled out. First, to innovators. Then, to the early majority. Only afterwards, to the majority of the team. The adoption of the former two groups is needed to recruit the latter one.

相反，变革举措必须循序渐进地推行。首先面向创新者，然后面向早期大众，最后才面向团队中的大多数成员。前两类群体的接受是争取后一类群体参与的前提。

Good managers also know that new procedures might require some adjustment to work. For example, a procedure which works great for one plant might need some adjustment to work in another plant. If the new procedure is rolled out to the whole team at the same time and it is later discovered that it needs some adjustments, some team members who are part of the late majority might think that “the procedure does not work” and might lose faith in the change initiative.

优秀的管理者也明白，新流程可能需要一些调整才能有效运作。例如，一个流程在一个工厂行之有效，在另一个工厂可能就需要进行一些调整。如果新流程同时推广到整个团队，之后才发现需要调整，那么一些属于后知后觉者的团队成员可能会认为“这个流程行不通”，从而对变革失去信心。

Therefore, good managers first recruit the help of the innovators in their team to test the procedure and see if anything has to be changed before rolling it out to the rest of the team. (Remember: in this context, the term “innovators” does not refer to a job role, but simply to people with a natural inclination to try new things.)

因此，优秀的管理者会先让团队中的创新者参与测试流程，看看是否需要做出任何调整，然后再推广到团队的其他成员。（请记住：在这里，“创新者”并非指某个职位，而仅仅是指那些天生就乐于尝试新事物的人。）

Good managers proceed as follow:

优秀的管理者会这样做：

1) First, they ask the innovators in their team to try the new procedure.

1）首先，他们要求团队中的创新者尝试新的程序。

2) If needed, they adjust the procedure.

2）如有必要，他们会调整程序。

3) They explain the procedure to the whole team, saying that it will be optional for the first week or two.

3）他们向整个团队解释了流程，并表示在前一两周内是可选的。

4) They work with the early adopters to make sure that they are implementing the new procedure and tweaking it if early feedback reveals a need to do so.

4) 他们与早期采用者合作，确保他们实施新程序，并在早期反馈表明需要进行调整时进行调整。

5) After the first week or two, when the rest of the team can see that the innovators and the early adopters are using the new procedure and that it works, the manager asks everyone in the team to adopt the new procedure.

5）经过一两周后，当团队中的其他成员看到创新者和早期采用者正在使用新流程并且该流程有效时，经理要求团队中的每个人都采用新流程。

Why not asking everyone to follow the new procedure during step 3? Because you want to present employees in the late majority with a procedure that works and this is only possible after some testing. Moreover, whenever you ask someone to do something you want them to do it without possibility to justifying themselves out of it after the objective has been agree – otherwise, you will debase your authority and people will not take your words as serious anymore – and “this procedure is not working well yet” is a valid post-hoc excuse, if true.

为什么不在第三步就要求所有人遵循新流程呢？因为你想让大多数员工在流程实施后期才能接触到真正有效的流程，而这只有经过一些测试才能实现。此外，当你要求别人做某事时，你希望他们在目标达成后能够毫无借口地执行——否则，你的权威就会受损，人们也不会再认真对待你的话——而“这个流程目前还不太有效”如果属实，倒也算是一个合理的事后借口。

Simpler procedures can be implemented all at once; the process described above refers to those procedures which have a noticeable element of novelty or which represent a major disruption from the old way of doing things.

更简单的程序可以一次性全部实施；上面描述的过程是指那些具有明显新颖性或与旧方法截然不同的程序。

Leverage points

杠杆点

Complex systems, such as an organization made of hundreds of employees, each responding to its own local environment and incentives, are changed by acting upon leverage points – parameters that individual actors in the system use to determine their behavior.

复杂的系统，例如由数百名员工组成的组织，每个员工都对其自身的本地环境和激励做出反应，通过作用于杠杆点（系统中各个参与者用来决定其行为的参数）来改变系统。

Low-leverage points are tasks and micromanagement. They should be avoided as much as possible and otherwise acknowledged as “not a solution to our problems”.

低杠杆点指的是任务和微观管理。应尽可能避免这些环节，否则就应该承认它们“并非解决问题的办法”。

The reason tasks and micromanagement should be avoided as the way to change the Operational Culture of your team is that they do not create any long-term growth in their employees and in their ability to autonomously contribute to the organization.

之所以应该避免使用任务分配和微观管理来改变团队的运营文化，是因为它们不会给员工带来任何长期的成长，也不会提高员工自主为组织做出贡献的能力。

Higher-leverage points are preferred. For example, Core Values reinforcement and delegating problems (rather than tasks). As saw in the Second and Third Principles of Operational Excellence, these are activities which both enable and require subordinates to meaningfully contribute to the organization autonomously.

应优先选择高杠杆点。例如，强化核心价值观和委派问题（而非任务）。正如卓越运营的第二和第三原则所述，这些活动既能赋能下属，又能要求下属自主地为组织做出有意义的贡献。

Higher-leverage points have the additional advantage that they achieve more with less time; freeing the time of the manager so that he will be able to work on the kind of actions that will bring long-term results – the Eight Best Practices.

高杠杆点还有一个额外的优势，那就是可以用更少的时间取得更大的成就；从而解放管理者的时间，让他能够从事能够带来长期成果的行动——八项最佳实践。

In his seminal book “High Output Management”, Andy Grove wrote that two of the highest-leverage activities a manager can perform are training and motivation. While the statement is without doubt true, it should not be interpreted literally. “Motivation” does not mean inspiring speeches like seen in movies, but creating and reinforcing the belief that good individual outcomes will necessarily follow the achievement of objectives and bad individual outcomes will necessarily follow the failure to achieve them; and this is done not through speeches but through a constant, consistent, obsessive and relentless application of the Four Principles of Operational Excellence.

安迪·格鲁夫在其开创性著作《高产出管理》中写道，管理者可以开展的两项最具杠杆效应的活动是培训和激励。这句话无疑是正确的，但不应按字面意思理解。“激励”并非指电影中常见的鼓舞人心的演讲，而是指建立并强化这样一种信念：良好的个人绩效必然伴随目标的实现，而糟糕的个人绩效则必然伴随目标的失败；而这并非通过演讲就能实现的，而是需要持续、始终如一、执着且不懈地运用卓越运营的四大原则。

Similarly, training is more effective when “pulled” by the subordinates (i.e., requested) rather than “pushed” upon them. Delegating problems and ensuring good individual outcomes to those who achieve results are great ways to get subordinates to “pull” the training they might need.

同样，培训如果是由下属“主动”要求（即请求）而不是“强加”给他们，效果会更好。将问题委派给那些取得成果的人，并确保他们获得良好的个人回报，是促使下属主动接受所需培训的有效方法。

The best kind of leverage is the one which is indirect; the one which tries not to change the employees of the organization directly, but which does so indirectly, by changing the system they find themselves operating in.

最好的杠杆作用是间接的；它不试图直接改变组织的员工，而是通过改变他们所处的系统来间接地改变他们。

# ↩

Sustaining

维持

Unless specific systems are set in place to ensure the sustenance of a change initiative over time, its results will revert back to zero in the space of a few months.

除非建立具体的系统来确保变革举措能够长期持续下去，否则其成果将在几个月内归零。

Erosion is a powerful force. Even in a company with great managers, as time passes by, events in which a negative behavior is let pass will cumulate and will erode any positive behavior that the change initiative will have built. Therefore, great companies put in place systems to fight erosion.

侵蚀是一种强大的力量。即使在拥有优秀管理者的公司里，随着时间的推移，如果放任负面行为发生，这些行为就会不断累积，最终侵蚀掉变革举措所建立的任何积极行为。因此，优秀的公司会建立相应的制度来对抗这种侵蚀。

Fighting erosion

对抗侵蚀

Mediocre companies assume that when a goal is met (for example, the injury rate falls below a given threshold), attention can be moved elsewhere.

平庸的公司认为，当目标达成时（例如，受伤率降至给定阈值以下），就可以将注意力转移到其他方面。

Great companies know that the defaults state is that Operational Culture degrades year after year, and that proactive effort has to be made to keep it from worsening.

优秀的公司都知道，默认情况下，运营文化会逐年恶化，必须采取积极主动的措施来防止这种情况继续恶化。

Therefore, great companies exhibit the following two traits . First, they keep talking about the Four Principles of Operational Excellence even when they do not seem necessary anymore. They keep educating their managers on them, organizing “refresh training sessions” and they bring them as the main topic of performance review meetings.

因此，优秀的公司具备以下两个特点。首先，即使运营卓越四大原则看似不再必要，他们也会继续强调这些原则。他们会持续对管理人员进行相关培训，组织“复习培训”，并将其作为绩效考核会议的主要议题。

Second, they keep placing costly objectives on the achievement of Core Values based goals. A “costly objective” is an objective that harms both the individuals and the company if they are not achieved. For example, the company might decide that if a manager does not achieve its safety objective, his career advancements are frozen for that year. This is a costly objective, because the company risks that the manager loses motivation or looks for another job in case he fails to achieve his objective. However, because it is costly, it is also effective in shaping behavior.

其次，他们不断将高成本目标与基于核心价值观的目标的实现挂钩。“高成本目标”是指如果未能实现，会对个人和公司都造成损害的目标。例如，公司可能决定，如果一位经理未能实现安全目标，则其当年的职业晋升将被冻结。这是一个高成本目标，因为如果经理未能实现目标，公司将面临经理失去动力或另谋高就的风险。然而，正因为成本高昂，它也确实能够有效地塑造员工行为。

Conversely, “cheap objectives” are objectives in which the individual has something to gain if he achieves them but does not lose anything if he doesn’t. These are bad, because they might incentivize managers to “tactically” forego an objective in order to achieve another one (e.g., neglecting the safety objective to focus on the production one) [19] .

相反，“廉价目标”是指个人如果实现这些目标就能获得收益，而如果未能实现也不会损失任何收益的目标。这些目标不好，因为它们可能会激励管理者“策略性地”放弃某个目标，以实现另一个目标（例如，为了专注于生产目标而忽略安全目标）[19]。

Rewarding

有回报

Good managers are unafraid of clarity. They know that, even if a blurry objective seems easier to set, it will inevitably bring larger problems down the road.

优秀的管理者不惧清晰的目标。他们明白，即使模糊的目标看似更容易设定，但最终必然会引发更大的问题。

Love for clarity and shamelessness in demanding it are strong predictors of Operational Excellence. They are the two most important qualities your organization might want to reward, be it with promotions, raises, or simple words of appreciation.

对清晰透明的追求和毫不掩饰的坚持，是卓越运营的有力预测指标。这两种品质也是贵公司最应该奖励的，无论是晋升、加薪，还是简单的赞赏。

Training

训练

Mandatory “refresher” trainings should be set at least once a year, to ensure that Core Values, rules and procedures are maintained at the top of the mind of the employees.

应至少每年进行一次强制性“复习”培训，以确保员工始终牢记核心价值观、规则和程序。

Each manager should be required to organize this at-least-yearly training for all of his subordinates. He might involve Human Resources or external experts to run them, but he should at least be accountable for his subordinates attending it and for spending a few minutes at the beginning of the training to set the expectations: what skills should the attendees learn? What new goals should they become able to achieve?

每位经理都应被要求至少每年为其所有下属组织一次培训。他可以邀请人力资源部门或外部专家来负责培训，但他至少应该对下属的参加负责，并在培训开始时花几分钟时间明确培训目标：学员应该学习哪些技能？他们应该达到哪些新的目标？

Institutionalizing your Culture

将你的文化制度化

The Culture of an organization is the sum of “how we do things here” plus the tradeoffs that its employees believe are worth taking (i.e., the Core Values).

一个组织的文化是“我们在这里做事的方式”加上其员工认为值得做出的权衡（即核心价值观）的总和。

For a Culture to be sustained over time, it must be institutionalized .

一种文化要想长期延续下去，就必须将其制度化。

“How we do things here” cannot be transferred by oral tradition only. It has to be written down. Procedures must be written. They must be stored somewhere visible. They need to be enforced. They need to become not an option, but a requirement to stay in the organization.

“我们这里做事的方式”不能只靠口头传承，必须写下来。程序必须成文，必须存放在显眼的地方，必须严格执行，必须成为留在组织中的必要条件，而不是可选项。

The same applies to Core Values. They need to be written down. They need to be conspicuously visible. Employees (and managers above all) should visibly demonstrate them. Posters should be hanged on walls, detailing the Core Values. Meetings must begin with a Core Values review. Costly objectives must be placed on Core Values.

核心价值观也同样如此。它们需要被记录下来，需要被醒目地展示出来。员工（尤其是管理者）应该以实际行动践行这些价值观。墙上应该张贴海报，详细列出核心价值观。会议必须以核心价值观回顾开始。必须将重要的目标与核心价值观挂钩。

Only institutionalized Culture lasts.

只有制度化的文化才能长久存在。

Peer accountability

同伴问责制

As organizations proceed in the journey towards Operational Excellence , they will reach a point in which Peer Accountability becomes possible.

随着组织在迈向卓越运营的道路上不断前进，它们将达到一个可以实现同侪问责的阶段。

To define Peer Accountability, I will use the words of Patrick Lencioni [20] : “ Members of great teams improve their relationship by holding one another accountable, thus demonstrating that they respect each other and have high expectation for one another’s performance. […] A team that avoids accountability creates resentment amongst team members who have different standards of performance […] and place an undue burden on the team leader as the sole source of discipline [… whereas] the team leader should be the ultimate arbiter when accountability fails.”

为了定义同伴问责制，我将引用帕特里克·兰西奥尼[20]的话：“优秀团队的成员通过互相问责来改善彼此的关系，从而展现出他们彼此尊重，并对彼此的绩效抱有很高的期望。[…] 一个回避问责制的团队会在绩效标准不同的团队成员之间造成怨恨，[…] 并给团队领导施加过重的负担，使其成为唯一的纪律来源。[…] 然而，当问责制失效时，团队领导才是最终的仲裁者。”

Peer accountability necessitates that its employees are able to independently see the importance of procedures and of Core Values. As such, it is not something that should be introduced nor expected by companies which are still at the beginning of their journey towards Operational Excellence, in which most employees depend upon their manager to realize the importance of procedures and Core Values.

同侪问责制要求员工能够独立认识到流程和核心价值观的重要性。因此，对于那些仍处于卓越运营初期、大多数员工依赖经理来理解流程和核心价值观的公司而言，同侪问责制既不应引入，也不应被期望实现。

Only once most employees (at least 70-80%) are able to independently do so, they will be able to become interdependent, keeping each other accountable.

只有当大多数员工（至少 70-80%）能够独立完成工作时，他们才能相互依存，互相监督。

This is the Holy Grail of Operational Excellence and, in my experience, a very achievable goal, if one follows consistently enough the Principles, Best Practices and Implementation Roadmap described in this book.

这是卓越运营的圣杯，而且以我的经验来看，如果能够始终如一地遵循本书中描述的原则、最佳实践和实施路线图，这是一个非常容易实现的目标。

Hiring

招聘

The better people your organization hires, the easier it will be to manage them, the easier it will be for them to manage complexity and to act autonomously, and the better will the Operational Culture ultimately be.

组织雇佣的人才越优秀，管理起来就越容易，他们就越容易应对复杂情况并自主行动，最终运营文化也会越好。

No matter your role, there are some practical actions you can take in order to improve the quality of hires in your organization.

无论你担任什么职位，你都可以采取一些切实可行的措施来提高你所在组织的员工招聘质量。

  • Write precise and compelling job descriptions. These documents will be used by Human Resources to filter candidates and to write job postings. A compelling job posting will do wonders to interest talented professionals and ambitious graduates.
    撰写精准且引人入胜的职位描述。人力资源部门将使用这些文件筛选候选人并撰写招聘启事。一份吸引人的招聘启事将极大地激发优秀人才和雄心勃勃的毕业生的兴趣。
  • Create good career plans. Depending on the size of your company, this might be your job, you might be assisted by Human Resources, or it might be Human Resources’ job. In the last case, it is your job to ask HR to create good career plans for your hires, because good candidates will demand them. Career plans should be conditional (i.e., if you achieve this and that result, you will grow in this direction). Do not accept any “we cannot make career plans” answers from HR; instead, ask them “what conditions should be in place for this career plan to exist”.
    制定良好的职业发展规划。根据公司规模，这可能是你的工作，也可能由人力资源部门协助，或者完全由人力资源部门负责。如果是后者，你需要主动要求人力资源部门为新员工制定完善的职业发展规划，因为优秀的求职者会要求获得这样的规划。职业发展规划应该具有条件性（例如，如果你达到某个目标，你就能朝着这个方向发展）。不要接受人力资源部门“我们无法制定职业发展规划”之类的回答；相反，你应该询问他们“制定这样的职业发展规划需要满足哪些条件”。
  • Meet potential hires in person. As their potential future boss, you are the person with the better perception of whether they will be a good fit for your team. Moreover, you are also the person with the better chance to influence their decision to join your team.
    与潜在候选人面对面交流。作为他们未来的潜在上司，您最能判断他们是否适合您的团队。此外，您也最有机会影响他们是否愿意加入您的团队。
  • Do not lie during the interview. Using lies to convince people to join your company will only result in having to re-hire for the position after one or two years, after the person you lied to realizes your team wasn’t a good fit for them and either quits the company or enters “I don’t care” mode.
    面试时不要撒谎。用谎言说服别人加入你的公司，只会导致一两年后你不得不重新招聘，因为被你欺骗的人会意识到你的团队并不适合他们，要么辞职，要么进入“我不在乎”的状态。
  • Meet HR and your bosses in person, asking them to recruit the talent you need for your team. Often, a few words exchanged in person can get them to recommend people they would not have contacted otherwise.
    亲自与人力资源部门和你的老板会面，请他们帮你招聘团队所需的人才。通常情况下，几次面对面的交流就能让他们推荐一些他们平时不会联系的人选。
  • Ask your subordinates to recommend potential hires. Make clear what the desired traits are – this is also an opportunity to reinforce what is important.
    请下属推荐合适的候选人。明确说明所需的特质——这也是一个重申重点的好机会。
  • If you need to hire at least two people per year, hire them together. When hiring a single person, recruiters tend to fall back on the safest choice, which might not be the best choice. When hiring more than one person, recruiters are more likely to “take little risks” and hire the talent you need.
    如果你每年至少需要招聘两人，最好同时招聘。招聘单个员工时，招聘人员往往会选择最稳妥的方案，但这未必是最佳选择。而招聘多人时，招聘人员则更倾向于“降低风险”，从而找到你真正需要的人才。
  • Screen for Core Values: refuse any hire who does not believe in your Core Values and in their uncompromisability. It might be tempting to hire a “mad genius”, but such employees often destroy more than they create.
    筛选核心价值观：拒绝任何不认同你的核心价值观及其不可妥协性的应聘者。聘用“疯狂的天才”或许很诱人，但这类员工往往破坏性大于创造性。
  • Keep a good team atmosphere. This does not mean perks and events, but an environment of fairness and respect. It will make it more likely that your subordinates recommend good hires or spread good words about working at your company.
    保持良好的团队氛围。这并非指提供福利和举办活动，而是指营造公平和尊重的工作环境。这将使你的下属更有可能推荐优秀人才，或向他人宣传在公司工作的良好体验。
  • Instead of conducting exit interviews asking people who left your team why they did so, ask them these questions while they still are your team members . For example, in a one-on-one meeting, a good question might be “if you were to leave the company over the next few years, why would it be so?”
    与其在离职面谈中询问离职员工离开的原因，不如在他们还是团队成员时就问他们这些问题。例如，在单独面谈中，一个好问题可能是：“如果你在未来几年内要离开公司，原因是什么？”

Developing peer accountability

培养同伴责任感

Good managers tell their subordinates who aim for a promotion that they do not need to wait for the promotion to act like a team leader; rather, it is by showing the traits of a team leader while in their current position that they will become one.

优秀的管理者会告诉那些渴望晋升的下属，他们不需要等到晋升才去扮演团队领导者的角色；相反，他们应该在目前的职位上展现出团队领导者的特质，这样他们才能最终成为一名团队领导者。

In particular, managers should give the following task to their most capable subordinates: to sustain Core Values in their team by reinforcing the positive behaviors they spot and asking their teammates to correct their negative behaviors. This introductory objective is excellent for it will develop the skills of using consistency and reinforcement to drive the adoption of the desired behaviors and the abandonment of undesired ones. The fact that this task is limited to reinforcing behaviors which are related to Core Values will make it easier for the teammates to receive comments from a peer. Core Values are so important, universal and beneficial that no one can argue against their enforcement.

具体来说，管理者应该将以下任务交给能力最强的下属：通过强化他们发现的积极行为，并要求团队成员纠正消极行为，来维护团队的核心价值观。这个入门目标非常有效，因为它能培养运用一致性和强化手段来推动理想行为的采纳和不良行为的摒弃的技能。由于这项任务仅限于强化与核心价值观相关的行为，因此团队成员更容易接受来自同伴的反馈。核心价值观如此重要、普适且有益，以至于没有人会反对它们的执行。

It is important that the subordinate who is given the task above focuses on reinforcing the positive behaviors rather than correcting the negative ones, except in the most important cases. Otherwise, he might be perceived as “bossy” or “pretentious” by his peers.

重要的是，负责执行上述任务的下属应着重强化积极行为，而非纠正消极行为，除非在极其特殊的情况下。否则，他可能会被同事视为“专横跋扈”或“自命不凡”。

Similarly, it is important that the subordinate restricts this exercise to behaviors related to Core Values and priorities only. He should not fully assume the role of the manager, to avoid being perceived as arrogant or to avoid him becoming a “second boss”. The latter would be problematic, as there would not be a single source of objectives anymore, and confusion would ensue.

同样重要的是，下属应将这种练习限制在与核心价值观和优先事项相关的行为范围内。他不应完全扮演经理的角色，以免被视为傲慢自大，或成为“第二老板”。后者会带来问题，因为目标来源不再统一，从而导致混乱。

Conclusion

结论

Congratulations for having made it so far! Now you know the Four Principles of Operational Excellence and the Eight Best Practices to apply them. You also received a Roadmap to implement change in your organization.

恭喜你坚持到了现在！现在你已经了解了卓越运营的四大原则以及应用这些原则的八项最佳实践。你还收到了一份在组织中实施变革的路线图。

Never forget that Operational Excellence is first and foremost about Clarity.

永远不要忘记，卓越运营的首要前提是清晰明确。

Strive for maximum clarity in all situations, avoiding any behavior and situation that might introduce confusion, ambiguity, or that can be misunderstood, and you’ll be fine.

在所有情况下都力求做到最清晰明了，避免任何可能引起混乱、歧义或被误解的行为和情况，你就会没事的。

Set up the necessary systems and take the necessary actions to ensure that everyone in the company does the above, and your organization will be fine.

建立必要的制度并采取必要的措施，确保公司里的每个人都做到以上几点，你的组织就会一切顺利。

What to do now?

现在该怎么办？

Now, the time comes for you to implement your learnings from this book into your company.

现在，是时候将你从这本书中学到的知识运用到你的公司中去了。

Have confidence, in yourself, in the Four Principles and in the Eight Best Practices.

要对自己有信心，要对四大原则和八项最佳实践有信心。

If you will be constant and relentless in their application, results will follow.

只要你坚持不懈地运用这些方法，就一定会有结果。

About the Author

作者简介

An automotive engineer by training, after having led large teams and consulted for large multinationals, Luca quit his corporate job to become an independent researcher and author and dedicate his career on shedding light on the topic of emerging human behavior. Luca believes that this topic is essential for preventing human suffering, especially as the scale of our civilization keeps increasing.

卢卡曾是一名汽车工程师，在领导过大型团队并为多家跨国公司提供咨询服务后，他辞去了企业的工作，成为一名独立研究员和作家，致力于研究新兴人类行为。卢卡认为，随着人类文明规模的不断扩大，这一课题对于预防人类苦难至关重要。

After having lived in Spain, Germany and Singapore, Luca recently moved back to his hometown of Turin (Italy). He spends his days between exercising, consulting, investing and conducting his independent research from his home, a coffee bar or a park.

卢卡曾在西班牙、德国和新加坡生活，最近搬回了家乡意大利都灵。他每天的工作包括锻炼、咨询、投资以及在家、咖啡馆或公园进行独立研究。

A few days a month, Luca also consults corporations and individuals that want to improve their businesses. Once per year he teaches a Risk Management module at Genoa University and runs a few private intensive courses for entrepreneurs, operations managers, plant managers and CEOs / COOs.

卢卡每月抽出几天时间，为希望改善业务的企业和个人提供咨询服务。他每年在热那亚大学讲授风险管理课程，并为企业家、运营经理、工厂经理和首席执行官/首席运营官开设一些私人强化课程。

The Control Heuristic, 2 nd edition

控制启发式（第二版）

“Luca’s book was so helpful to my work. Opened my eyes up to some more reasons why change is so hard.” – Chris Murman

“卢卡的书对我的工作帮助很大。它让我明白了为什么改变如此艰难。”——克里斯·默曼

At a first look, human behavior appears as an inexplicable mess. Why do we behave irrationally? Why do I behave irrationally? Why is it so hard to change? What is happiness and why does it seem to escape us?

乍看之下，人类行为似乎是一团难以解释的混乱。为什么我们会做出非理性的行为？为什么我会做出非理性的行为？为什么改变如此困难？幸福是什么？为什么它似乎总是与我们擦肩而过？

The Control Heuristic offers a new perspective to answer these questions and provides a guiding light to shed the darkness of the subconscious resistances that prevent us to behave like the man or woman we want to be.

控制启发式为我们提供了一个新的视角来回答这些问题，并为我们指明了方向，驱散了潜意识中阻碍我们成为我们想成为的人的阻力。

100 Truths You Will Learn Too Late

100个你迟到才会明白的真相

“I am amazed at Luca Dellanna’s ability to observe, compile, and articulate 99 very actionable life principles here. Each chapter describes the rule in a way that makes you think and then summarizes the Action. It’s filled with DEEP insights yet VERY readable.” – Theresia Tanzil

“卢卡·德拉纳的观察力、整理能力和阐述能力令我惊叹，他总结并阐述了99条极具实用价值的人生原则。每一章都以引人深思的方式描述原则，并总结相应的行动方案。这本书充满了深刻的见解，却又非常易读。”——特蕾西娅·坦齐尔

I wasted years of my life, because I did not know its rules.

我浪费了数年光阴，因为我不知道它的规则。

I did not know the rules of relationships, of careers, of health, of happiness.

我不懂人际关系、事业、健康和幸福的规则。

Then, through hard work, talking with mentors and trial and error, I uncovered some of them.

然后，通过努力工作、与导师交流以及反复尝试，我发现了其中一些。

Now, I lay these rules out for you. In this book, you will find 100 of the lessons I learnt.

现在，我把这些规则列出来。在这本书里，你会找到我总结出的100条经验教训。

It will still require hard work from your side to internalize them and put them into practice, but at least I hope to make this process easier for you, by letting you to avoid committing the same mistakes I did.

你仍然需要付出艰辛的努力才能将它们内化并付诸实践，但我至少希望能够让你的这个过程变得更容易，让你避免犯我曾经犯过的错误。

The Power of Adaptation

适应的力量

“This guy! Luca is amazing. So insightful with common sense applications of complexity and the ability to communicate clearly!!” – Bob Klapetzky

“这家伙！卢卡太棒了。他对复杂问题的洞察力非常敏锐，能用常识解释问题，而且沟通能力也很强！！”——鲍勃·克拉佩茨基

This book is for you if:

如果您符合以下条件，那么这本书适合您：

  • You like books dense of information.
    你喜欢信息量丰富的书籍。
  • You appreciated books such as Taleb’s Antifragile.
    你很欣赏像塔勒布的《反脆弱》这样的书。
  • You understand or are willing to accept that the world is dynamic, and that understanding how something changes is more important than understanding how something works now.
    你理解或愿意接受世界是动态的，并且了解事物如何变化比了解事物现在如何运作更重要。
  • You do not like usual business / self-help books which provide solutions which only work in the short-term.
    你不喜欢那些通常只能提供短期解决方案的商业/自助书籍。

“The Power of Adaptation” focuses on the topic of adaptation as the main force shaping the world as we know it. However, adaptation is an emergent process and thus cannot be understood with narratives nor it can be acted upon directly. This book aims to describe the basic phenomena which weave together into what we perceive as adaptation and to provide a guide to help the readers practicing the four behaviors that will help them harness, rather than fight, change.

《适应的力量》聚焦于适应这一主题，认为它是塑造我们所知世界的主要力量。然而，适应是一个涌现的过程，因此无法用叙事来理解，也无法直接干预。本书旨在描述构成我们所理解的适应的基本现象，并为读者提供指导，帮助他们实践四种行为，从而驾驭而非对抗变化。

The World Through a Magnifying Glass

透过放大镜看世界

“Thank you for helping me understand! My son was recently diagnosed and I needed to be able to understand how he views the world. Why certain things would overwhelm him and cause so much anxiety and pain. This book made it so clear and easy to understand.” – Geiger T., a reader.

“谢谢你帮我理解！我儿子最近被确诊，我需要了解他是如何看待这个世界的。为什么有些事情会让他感到不知所措，引发如此多的焦虑和痛苦。这本书让我明白了这一切，而且解释得非常清楚易懂。”——读者 Geiger T.

(note: most of the content of this book is present, for free, in a different form, on the author’s website www.autismclarified.com )

（注：本书的大部分内容以不同的形式免费发布在作者的网站 www.autismclarified.com 上）

A book to understand the Autism Spectrum Disorder.

一本帮助人们了解自闭症谱系障碍的书。

Imagine looking at the world through a magnifying glass all the time.

想象一下，你一直透过放大镜看世界。

Being able to see only a detail at a time, but to see it so well as to be hypnotized by it.

一次只能看到一个细节，但却看得如此清楚，以至于被它深深吸引。

Imagine always being slower than everyone around you.

想象一下，你总是比周围的人慢。

Imagine being unable to communicate with others, because you are talking about that detail, while they are talking about the big picture.

想象一下，你因为在谈论某个细节而无法与他人沟通，而他们却在谈论大局。

Imagine being so good at seeing the details, and feel so useless, because no one cares about them.

想象一下，你非常擅长观察细节，却觉得自己毫无用处，因为没有人关心这些细节。

This book is for parents, friend or anyone related to someone with Autism.

这本书适合自闭症患者的父母、朋友或任何与他们相关的人阅读。

This is for neurologists and psychologists to help them understand the world of ASD.

这是为了帮助神经科医生和心理学家了解自闭症谱系障碍的世界。

This book is for people on the Spectrum, to help them understand themselves.

这本书是为自闭症谱系人士编写的，旨在帮助他们更好地了解自己。

Some of the topics covered inside:

本书涵盖的部分主题包括：

  • The Magnifying Glass: a metaphor to understand perception under the Spectrum
    放大镜：理解光谱下感知的一种隐喻
  • Why people on the Spectrum are impaired in contextual fields (such as personal communication) and advantaged in mastering detailed fields (such as computer science).
    为什么自闭症患者在情境领域（例如人际沟通）存在缺陷，而在掌握细节领域（例如计算机科学）则具有优势。
  • Peripheral Functionality Blindness: the reason people on the Spectrum do not develop appropriate body language and facial expressivity.
    周边功能障碍：自闭症谱系人士无法发展出适当的肢体语言和面部表情的原因。
  • Prioritization by Specificity: the reason literal meaning is the only thing which matters, for people on the Spectrum.
    按具体性进行优先排序：对于自闭症谱系人士来说，字面意义是唯一重要的事。
  • The High-Pass filter: a novel hypothesis for the Autism Spectrum Disorder, coherent with previous theories and experimental results.
    高通滤波器：自闭症谱系障碍的一个新假设，与之前的理论和实验结果相一致。

(Reading time is about 1h30)

（阅读时间约1小时30分钟）
